title: Amino-Acid Availability & Prioritisation

scientific_finding_classification_notes.PM1-F3: Physiological tyrosine-supply contribution remains subject to SEC appraisal. The established PAH reaction is documented separately as Scientific Principle PM1-SP1; the earlier biochemical-provenance-only assessment is retained as history.

scientific_principles.title: Phenylalanine hydroxylase reaction
scientific_principles.proposition: Phenylalanine-4-hydroxylase catalyses conversion of L-phenylalanine to L-tyrosine.
scientific_principles.scope_limitations: Reaction identity does not quantify physiological conversion flux, dietary contribution to tyrosine supply or brain catecholamine synthesis. Those propositions remain subject to scientific appraisal in SF3.
scientific_principles.classification_rationale: Only the established reaction identity is a Principle; the original mixed physiological proposition remains an active Finding.

scientific_principles.historical_proposition: Tyrosine and tryptophan supply the precursor pathways for catecholamines and serotonin, respectively. Their biochemical identity does not demonstrate that additional meal protein improves brain transmitter synthesis, attention, mood or reward.
scientific_principles.title: Tyrosine and tryptophan precursor identities
scientific_principles.proposition: Tyrosine is a precursor in catecholamine biosynthesis; tryptophan is a precursor in serotonin biosynthesis.
scientific_principles.mechanism: Precursor identity for downstream pathways, distinct from circulating supply and brain transport.
scientific_principles.scope_limitations: These identities do not establish that additional dietary protein raises brain neurotransmitter synthesis or improves functional or clinical outcomes. Intervention, transport and flux propositions remain Findings requiring separate appraisal.
scientific_principles.classification_rationale: Foundational precursor identities are presented as a Principle; historical dietary-effect boundaries remain limitations, not a newly adjudicated negative intervention Finding.

mission: Ensure meal-level protein supply delivers the amino-acid foundation neurotransmitter pathways depend on.
summary: Food protein supplies indispensable amino acids—the amino acids the body cannot make in sufficient amounts—including phenylalanine and tryptophan. Phenylalanine can also be converted to tyrosine. After a protein meal, dietary phenylalanine appears in the circulation. Tyrosine and tryptophan are precursors later signalling can use for dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin. Protein that covers those amino acids is the supported dietary route.
dose_sensitivity: Not established as a neurotransmitter dose. Protein type, dose and age change how much dietary phenylalanine reaches the circulation. Extra protein is not shown to raise brain monoamines.

dietary_input_traceability.dietary_input_note: Accepted dietary provision or constituent supply relationship; no efficacy or quantity claim added.
dietary_input_traceability.biological_role: Coverage of the indispensable amino-acid set, including phenylalanine, that sets the circulating pool neurotransmitter pathways can draw on. Meals contribute measurable amino-acid composition; this is not a requirement that each meal provide complete coverage
dietary_input_traceability.evidence_limitation: Protein-quality scoring and vegetarian-diet amino-acid coverage do not establish that increasing protein raises brain monoamine synthesis or improves attention or mood. The indispensable set includes phenylalanine; tyrosine is not an indispensable amino acid.

dietary_input_traceability.dietary_input_note: 2026-10-26 recovery: admitted Type A capacity under the functional-dependency and dietary-supply gate. The original biochemical-only record and its rationale are preserved in the recovery history. No additional-intake efficacy is asserted.
dietary_input_traceability.biological_role: Catecholamine precursor in the circulating pool this PM prioritises. Tyrosine is normally formed from indispensable phenylalanine and can become conditionally indispensable when phenylalanine availability is limited
dietary_input_traceability.evidence_limitation: Dietary supply to a circulating pool is distinct from brain transport, catecholamine synthesis or clinical benefit. A small human study found higher plasma tyrosine during protein-containing meals and after a large tyrosine supplement; it does not define ordinary-food efficacy or a need for extra tyrosine when supply is adequate. Tyrosine is not an indispensable amino acid.

dietary_input_traceability.dietary_input_note: Accepted dietary provision or constituent supply relationship; no efficacy or quantity claim added.
dietary_input_traceability.biological_role: Indispensable serotonergic precursor this PM prioritises in the circulating precursor pool
dietary_input_traceability.evidence_limitation: Pool presence of tryptophan is not evidence for increased brain serotonin, brain entry, or an attention or mood benefit.

dietary_lever_atoms.permitted_wording: Indispensable amino-acid supply is a Direct Dietary Requirement of this PM. Coverage of the indispensable set can be assessed in meals and across the diet; this is not a rule that each meal must be complete, and it is not a monoamine-dosing rule.
dietary_lever_atoms.evidence_limitation: Protein-quality scoring and vegetarian-diet amino-acid coverage do not establish that increasing protein raises brain monoamine synthesis or improves attention or mood. The indispensable set includes phenylalanine; tyrosine is not an indispensable amino acid.

dietary_lever_atoms.permitted_wording: Dietary tyrosine supplies the circulating tyrosine precursor pool, alongside endogenous phenylalanine hydroxylation, sustaining substrate availability for downstream pathways.
dietary_lever_atoms.evidence_limitation: Dietary supply to a circulating pool is distinct from brain transport, catecholamine synthesis or clinical benefit. A small human study found higher plasma tyrosine during protein-containing meals and after a large tyrosine supplement; it does not define ordinary-food efficacy or a need for extra tyrosine when supply is adequate. dietary_lever_atoms.permitted_wording: Tryptophan is an indispensable Direct substrate in the pool this PM governs. Presence in meals is not a serotonin-dosing rule.
dietary_lever_atoms.evidence_limitation: Pool presence of tryptophan is not evidence for increased brain serotonin, brain entry, or an attention or mood benefit.

kc_applicability_adjudications.applicability_proposition: Imbalance of LAT1 competitive large-neutral-amino-acid balance can constrain this mechanism’s governed circulating amino-acid pool.
established_links: This mechanism’s overview treats circulating pool sufficiency as independent of blood–brain-barrier transport.
Fernstrom 2013 locates LNAA competition at LAT1, which is the transport mechanism.
inferred_links: LAT1 imbalance would therefore reduce the circulating pool this PM governs.
kc_applicability_adjudications.rationale: The named competitive state is brain-entry competition, not circulating-pool availability. That is a different process. Neither assessed arm is admitted as a mapping to the current KC1 definition.

kc_change_control_flags.proposition: Candidate PM↔KC1 mapping on the amino-acid quality arm. Shared IAA/protein-quality pool may constrain this PM; competitive LAT1 balance is not this PM's relationship. Input overlap with §4.1.1 is not a rejection criterion. Public §4.1.3 has no mapping. Dual-arm iKC remains KC-owned.

phenome_relationships.rationale: Meal protein supplies circulating phenylalanine, and phenylalanine can be converted to tyrosine. Tyrosine and tryptophan are precursors later catecholamine and serotonin pathways can use. These studies do not measure attention.
Phenylalanine from dietary protein can be converted to tyrosine, the dopamine precursor. That supply is not a measurement of motivation or drive, and it is not dopaminergic signalling.
Tryptophan is an indispensable amino acid and the serotonin precursor. Coverage of that amino acid is not a measurement of emotional regulation, and serotonin signalling is a later step.

scientific_findings_intro: Dietary protein supplies the circulating precursor pool; food structure and source can alter delivery kinetics without proving superior neurotransmitter function. Curated reaction identity, whole-diet adequacy and experimental intervention findings are distinguished below.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Dietary protein and amino-acid availability
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Human tracer studies establish dietary delivery. Cross-study source/dose comparisons and variable age results require qualified interpretation.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Scope is circulating provision and the exact measured endpoint, not brain entry, neurotransmitter efficacy or a clinical recommendation.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Dietary protein supplies phenylalanine to the human circulation, with delivery kinetics varying by the tested protein source, dose and meal context. The pooled age association is context-dependent, not proof that ageing uniformly impairs absorption or that greater availability increases brain neurotransmitters.
scientific_findings.synthesis: The pooled dairy corpus establishes dietary tracer appearance but is not 18 independent research-group replications. Independent human source comparisons support context-dependent plasma responses. An individual exercise study and the newer six-source crossover did not show a uniform age-related decrement; plasma profiles and dietary tracer appearance are not identical measurements.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Mostly male dairy-tracer cohorts; between-study source/dose contrasts, nonrandomised age comparisons and different matrices limit generalisation. No brain transport, neurotransmitter or ADHD endpoint.

evidence_considered.label: Gorissen et al. (2020)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: dietary whey, casein or milk protein
evidence_considered.directional_finding: About half of dietary protein-derived phenylalanine appeared in the circulation over five hours. The fraction was lower for casein, higher with a larger dose, and slightly lower in older adults.

assessment.study: Pooled analysis of 18 randomised trials using intrinsically labelled whey, casein or milk protein.
assessment.population: 602 participants, mean age 53 years. The age comparison used 82 young adults and 83 older adults.
assessment.result: Dietary phenylalanine entered the circulation. Protein type, dose and age changed the fraction that appeared.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Mean appearance 50% ± 14% over five hours. Casein 45% ± 11%, whey 57% ± 10%, milk 65% ± 13%. Older adults 45% ± 10% versus young adults 51% ± 14%.
assessment.evidence_summary: A protein meal delivers phenylalanine into the circulation, and the amount depends on the protein, the dose and age.
assessment.limitations: Phenylalanine appearance is not the full indispensable set, not tryptophan, and not a brain or clinical endpoint.

evidence_considered.label: Non-animal protein-source crossover (2024)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: 30 g protein as milk, mycoprotein, pea, lupin, spirulina or chlorella; five-hour sampling; at least seven-day washout.
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Source-specific plasma profiles; some non-animal sources produced higher essential-amino-acid responses than the tested milk beverage. Integrated responses did not show a uniform age decrement.

assessment.study: Independent Exeter programme; randomised double-blind six-period crossover, 12 young and 10 older adults, both sexes.
assessment.population: Independent Exeter programme; randomised double-blind six-period crossover, 12 young and 10 older adults, both sexes.
assessment.result: Source-specific plasma profiles; some non-animal sources produced higher essential-amino-acid responses than the tested milk beverage. Integrated responses did not show a uniform age decrement.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Source-specific endpoint and uncertainty: Small cohorts; composition and food matrix differ, so no isolated digestibility estimate or universal ranking follows.
assessment.evidence_summary: Source-specific plasma profiles; some non-animal sources produced higher essential-amino-acid responses than the tested milk beverage. Integrated responses did not show a uniform age decrement.
assessment.limitations: Small cohorts; composition and food matrix differ, so no isolated digestibility estimate or universal ranking follows. Independent of Maastricht pooled dairy corpus; age analyses and six visits within a person are not six independent replications.

evidence_considered.label: Pennings et al. (2011): exercise before protein
evidence_considered.exposure_context: Resistance-type exercise before labelled protein versus rest; six-hour tracer follow-up.
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Dietary phenylalanine availability did not differ detectably with exercise although muscle incorporation increased.

assessment.study: Young/older men, rest/exercise comparisons; 48 participants total.
assessment.population: Young/older men, rest/exercise comparisons; 48 participants total.
assessment.result: Dietary phenylalanine availability did not differ detectably with exercise although muscle incorporation increased.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Source-specific endpoint and uncertainty: Muscle utilisation is not circulating-pool enhancement; a nonsignificant contrast is not equivalence.
assessment.evidence_summary: Dietary phenylalanine availability did not differ detectably with exercise although muscle incorporation increased.
assessment.limitations: Muscle utilisation is not circulating-pool enhancement; a nonsignificant contrast is not equivalence. NCT00557388 is part of Gorissen2020; no double-counting.

evidence_dependency: Shared sources with PM1-F1 and PM1-F2 are reused for distinct propositions, not independent replication. Pooled studies, thesis chapters and journal reports may overlap.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Diet-wide amino-acid adequacy does not require identical complete meals
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Retain nutritional adequacy, but separate whole-diet coverage from acute food-specific kinetics.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Scope is circulating provision and the exact measured endpoint, not brain entry, neurotransmitter efficacy or a clinical recommendation.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Varied adult diets can provide digestible indispensable amino acids without requiring every meal to supply the full set. This nutritional-adequacy proposition does not establish an optimal neurotransmitter dose or demonstrate that all plant and animal foods have identical postprandial responses.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Existing vegetarian-diet and DIAAS reviews support adequacy across a varied diet. New human source and faba-bean studies qualify single-food composition/digestibility; they do not contradict adequate mixed diets. The recent systematic requirement review concerns quantitative requirements, not neurotransmitter enhancement.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Requirement reviews are not direct tests of neurotransmitter response or every possible plant diet. Energy sufficiency, variety, age and clinical context remain relevant.

evidence_considered.label: Mariotti and Gardner (2019)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: vegetarian and vegan dietary patterns
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Adult vegetarian diets that include protein-rich plant foods can meet protein and amino-acid requirements. Amino-acid deficiency is described as overstated.

assessment.study: Review of protein and amino-acid intakes from vegetarian and vegan diets in Western adults.
assessment.population: Adults, including older adults, eating vegetarian or vegan diets. Children are discussed separately.
assessment.result: Protein-rich plant foods can achieve protein and amino-acid adequacy in adults.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No single intake-response estimate. The result is adequacy against requirements, not a change in brain transmitters.
assessment.evidence_summary: Dietary patterns can cover the indispensable amino acids this pool requires.
assessment.limitations: Requirement coverage is not a plasma time course and not a neurotransmitter outcome.

evidence_considered.label: Moughan and Lim (2024)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: protein-quality scoring
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Protein quality is scored by digestible indispensable amino acids rather than by protein grams alone.

assessment.study: Review of the digestible indispensable amino acid score a decade after its introduction.
assessment.population: Not a new human trial. The score is applied to foods and diets.
assessment.result: Quality depends on digestible indispensable amino acids.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No neurotransmitter effect size.
assessment.evidence_summary: Coverage of those amino acids is the quality claim this mechanism can use.
assessment.limitations: A scoring review does not measure circulating or brain amino acids.

evidence_considered.label: Marsh et al. (2013)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: vegetarian dietary pattern
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Varied plant-protein sources across the diet can cover indispensable amino acids without combining complementary proteins in each meal.

assessment.study: Review of protein in vegetarian diets.
assessment.population: People eating vegetarian diets.
assessment.result: Completeness can be reached across the day rather than inside every meal.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No meal-level neurotransmitter measurement.
assessment.evidence_summary: Each meal does not have to supply the full indispensable set.
assessment.limitations: The review does not test brain precursor availability.

evidence_considered.exposure_context: Average daily protein and indispensable-amino-acid requirements across life stages.
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Evidence gaps in exact requirement estimates do not negate indispensable-amino-acid biology.

assessment.study: Systematic review of studies January 2000-May 2024; duplicate screening and risk-of-bias appraisal.
assessment.population: Systematic review of studies January 2000-May 2024; duplicate screening and risk-of-bias appraisal.
assessment.result: Evidence gaps in exact requirement estimates do not negate indispensable-amino-acid biology.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Source-specific endpoint and uncertainty: Not a PM-specific intake prescription, postprandial tracer experiment or neurotransmitter trial.
assessment.evidence_summary: Evidence gaps in exact requirement estimates do not negate indispensable-amino-acid biology.
assessment.limitations: Not a PM-specific intake prescription, postprandial tracer experiment or neurotransmitter trial. Review plus included studies are not independent replications.

evidence_considered.label: True ileal amino-acid digestibility of faba bean (2024)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: Cooked dehulled faba mash providing 20 g protein; eight-hour collection.
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Individual amino-acid digestibility and limiting-amino-acid content differ; a single food score is not a whole-diet inadequacy diagnosis.

assessment.study: Healthy-human single-food tracer/intubation study, NCT05047757.
assessment.population: Healthy-human single-food tracer/intubation study, NCT05047757.
assessment.result: Individual amino-acid digestibility and limiting-amino-acid content differ; a single food score is not a whole-diet inadequacy diagnosis.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Source-specific endpoint and uncertainty: Ileal digestibility, systemic appearance and brain transport are distinct endpoints.
assessment.evidence_summary: Individual amino-acid digestibility and limiting-amino-acid content differ; a single food score is not a whole-diet inadequacy diagnosis.
assessment.limitations: Ileal digestibility, systemic appearance and brain transport are distinct endpoints. Different endpoint and protocol; no replication credit for a dairy-source comparison and no independence score assigned.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Phenylalanine conversion and endogenous tyrosine supply
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Established conversion chemistry; dietary admission and downstream catecholamine effects remain separate decisions.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Scope is circulating provision and the exact measured endpoint, not brain entry, neurotransmitter efficacy or a clinical recommendation.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Phenylalanine-4-hydroxylase (PAH) converts L-phenylalanine to L-tyrosine. This endogenous route contributes to tyrosine supply but does not make tyrosine absent from foods or establish an independent requirement for extra dietary tyrosine.
scientific_findings.synthesis: UniProt P00439 and Rhea 20273 establish reaction identity; the Matthews human kinetic review remains linked for physiological context. No new intake-response or clinical conclusion is inferred.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Curated enzyme annotation does not quantify whole-body dietary contribution or human brain catecholamine flux. Do not automatically add every PAH cofactor as a PM1-specific dietary requirement.

evidence_considered.label: Matthews (2007)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: human tracer infusions
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Phenylalanine is hydroxylated to tyrosine in humans. Tyrosine is normally dispensable and can become conditionally indispensable when phenylalanine availability is limited.

assessment.study: Overview of human phenylalanine and tyrosine tracer kinetics.
assessment.population: Human tracer studies in people with ordinary hydroxylation and in disorders that block it.
assessment.result: Phenylalanine is converted to tyrosine. The conversion depends on phenylalanine availability.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Kinetic rates are reviewed. No dietary dose for a brain catecholamine change is given.
assessment.evidence_summary: Dietary phenylalanine can supply tyrosine through a conversion that has been measured in humans.
assessment.limitations: Conversion kinetics are not brain dopamine or noradrenaline synthesis.

evidence_dependency: Shared sources with PM1-F1 and PM1-F2 are reused for distinct propositions, not independent replication. Pooled studies, thesis chapters and journal reports may overlap.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Downstream precursor identity is not a dietary efficacy result
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Preserve precursor identity and the downstream PM2-PM5 boundary.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Scope is circulating provision and the exact measured endpoint, not brain entry, neurotransmitter efficacy or a clinical recommendation.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Tyrosine and tryptophan supply the precursor pathways for catecholamines and serotonin, respectively. Their biochemical identity does not demonstrate that additional meal protein improves brain transmitter synthesis, attention, mood or reward.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Retain Aquili and existing precursor evidence as biochemical/contextual support, not evidence that ordinary dietary coverage reproduces depletion or pharmacological supplementation experiments.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Transport competition, regional synthesis, release and clinical outcomes require their own evidence. No score is inherited from this elementary relationship.

evidence_considered.label: Aquili (2020)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: narrative review of depletion and supplementation studies
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Tryptophan is named as the serotonin precursor and tyrosine as the dopamine precursor. The reviewed behavioural effects come from depletion and supplementation, not from meal-protein coverage.

assessment.study: Narrative review of tryptophan and tyrosine in executive function and reward.
assessment.population: The behavioural studies are mostly acute depletion or supplementation experiments.
assessment.result: The precursor relationship is stated. Cognitive effects in the review are not effects of this dietary pool.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No effect size for meal protein on brain transmitters.
assessment.evidence_summary: The precursor names are supported. The cognitive conclusions are not a result for this mechanism.
assessment.limitations: Depletion and isolated supplements are not indispensable-amino-acid coverage.

evidence_dependency: Shared sources with PM1-F1 and PM1-F2 are reused for distinct propositions, not independent replication. Pooled studies, thesis chapters and journal reports may overlap.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Food texture and amino-acid appearance
scientific_findings.finding_statement: In a randomised crossover study of ten older men, 135 g minced beef produced greater six-hour dietary phenylalanine appearance than the same quantity of steak. Total plasma essential-amino-acid concentrations and muscle protein synthesis did not differ detectably between preparations.
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Texture affected source-specific tracer delivery, not every circulating or functional outcome.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Scope is circulating provision and the exact measured endpoint, not brain entry, neurotransmitter efficacy or a clinical recommendation.
scientific_findings.synthesis: The matched-food crossover supports a preparation effect on dietary tracer appearance. Null total-concentration and muscle outcomes prevent a generic better-protein or neurotransmitter interpretation. The thesis and publication describe one dataset.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: One small older-male trial; no independent replication of the exact matched-beef protocol was established in this assessment. No claim that all foods should be minced or that this improves attention.

evidence_considered.label: Pennings et al. (2013): minced beef versus steak
evidence_considered.exposure_context: 135 g intrinsically labelled lean beef, same cut, minced patty versus steak; six-hour tracer follow-up.
evidence_considered.directional_finding: More dietary phenylalanine appeared after mincing. Total plasma essential-amino-acid concentrations and muscle synthesis did not differ detectably.

assessment.study: Randomised crossover; ten older men, mean age 74 years; two visits at least 14 days apart.
assessment.population: Randomised crossover; ten older men, mean age 74 years; two visits at least 14 days apart.
assessment.result: More dietary phenylalanine appeared after mincing. Total plasma essential-amino-acid concentrations and muscle synthesis did not differ detectably.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Six-hour dietary phenylalanine appearance: minced 61% ± 3% versus steak 49% ± 3% (means ± SEM), P < 0.01; 12 percentage-point difference. No paired confidence interval calculated or inferred.
assessment.evidence_summary: More dietary phenylalanine appeared after mincing. Total plasma essential-amino-acid concentrations and muscle synthesis did not differ detectably.
assessment.limitations: Small single trial; mean estimates and standard errors available, paired effect interval not extracted; no equivalence claim for null outcomes. Single empirical dataset; thesis and journal article are the same experiment, not replications.

evidence_dependency: Shared sources with PM1-F1 and PM1-F2 are reused for distinct propositions, not independent replication. Pooled studies, thesis chapters and journal reports may overlap.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Extrusion altered early amino-acid kinetics, not demonstrated total loss
scientific_findings.finding_statement: In a randomised crossover of nine healthy young adults, the tested high-moisture-extruded mycoprotein/pea blend delayed selected early plasma amino-acid responses relative to the dry blend. Total five-hour grouped amino-acid availability was not significantly different; the study does not establish poorer overall nutrition for all meat alternatives.
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Preserve both temporal differences and the null integrated endpoint.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Scope is circulating provision and the exact measured endpoint, not brain entry, neurotransmitter efficacy or a clinical recommendation.
scientific_findings.synthesis: The human beverage experiment and in-vitro analyses address different endpoints. Selected phenylalanine/tyrosine peaks changed, while grouped integrated responses were statistically inconclusive. Composition, matrix and sampling constrain interpretation.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Single small trial, no dietary tracer, numerous secondary endpoints and laboratory reconstituted products. Not proof of equal total absorption or a reason to avoid all processed plant foods.

evidence_considered.label: High-moisture extrusion crossover (2024)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: 25 g protein, 39% mycoprotein/61% pea; extruded versus dry-milled blend in drinks; five-hour samples.
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Extrusion delayed early responses and reduced selected peaks, including phenylalanine and tyrosine. Total five-hour grouped amino-acid availability was not significantly different.

assessment.study: Randomised double-blind counterbalanced crossover; nine young adults, five men/four women; minimum five-day separation.

title: LAT1 Competitive Transport Modulation
mission: Influence competition for transport across the blood–brain barrier so neurotransmitter precursors can reach the brain after meals.
summary: Large neutral amino acid transporter 1 (LAT1) helps control which amino acids can enter the brain. Tyrosine, tryptophan and other large neutral amino acids (LNAAs) compete for this shared route. Human feeding experiments show that meal composition and protein source can alter their relative availability in blood. The response depends on the tested meal and sampling period, rather than a universal carbohydrate-to-protein rule. This transport step connects circulating precursor supply with downstream neurotransmitter pathways.
key_constraints: BRS1(KC1) - Amino Acid Quality & Competitive Balance
dose_sensitivity: Pattern target rather than single nutrient threshold; depends on protein/carbohydrate composition
scientific_findings_intro: LAT1 transport identity is separated from the experimental finding that meal composition changes plasma precursor ratios. Breakfast, evening-meal and protein-source results show why a between-meal difference must not be described as a universal rise above baseline. Plasma ratios do not directly measure brain transport or neurotransmitter production. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) [[3]](#pm-ref-3) [[7]](#pm-ref-7) [[8]](#pm-ref-8)

scientific_findings.finding_label: Shared LAT1 transport and precursor competition
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Large neutral amino acid transporter 1 (LAT1) carries competing amino acids as part of an exchanger complex. Blood ratios describe substrate presentation, not measured transport flux.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: This establishes competitive transport biology. It does not show that eating more tyrosine or tryptophan increases brain monoamines or improves function.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Large neutral amino acids share competitive transport through LAT1 (SLC7A5) with the SLC3A2 heavy chain; plasma composition helps shape substrate availability but is not a direct measurement of net brain uptake.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Curated human SLC3A2 annotation and the deposited human LAT1 complex support transporter identity; the inherited Fernstrom review supplies the physiological competition context. Exchange, substrate affinity and cellular context qualify the simple plasma-ratio model. No numerical score is assigned merely for curated identity.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Curated transporter and structural records do not quantify an ordinary meal effect in the human brain. The plasma-ratio proxy is not the sole determinant of net flux. The original Finding ID and source history are retained.

assessment.limitations: Review synthesis; does not by itself demonstrate that ordinary meals change human brain monoamines or function.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Meal composition and protein source alter plasma precursor ratios
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Human feeding experiments demonstrate context-dependent plasma-ratio changes. A higher ratio after one meal than another is not necessarily an increase above baseline.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Retain the admitted meal-composition regulatory relationship at its plasma-ratio ceiling. Protein-source experiments qualify generalisation; they do not establish a best ratio, an additional nutrient requirement or a clinical protocol.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: In the studied healthy adults, meal composition and tested protein sources can alter plasma tryptophan relative to competing large neutral amino acids; the direction and tyrosine response depend on the exposure and sampling context, without establishing increased human brain transport or neurotransmitter synthesis.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Breakfast contrasts and separate protein-source experiments support meal-responsive precursor ratios, but not one universal direction. The recovered Wurtman table shows lower tryptophan and tyrosine ratios after the protein-rich breakfast, not an increased tyrosine ratio. Evening-meal null results and a starch-control null constrain extrapolation. Brain uptake and downstream effects were not measured by those plasma experiments.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Small acute healthy-adult samples; different meals, ratio denominators and sampling windows; incomplete historical methods retrieval. No population-wide optimum or direct human brain-flux estimate. Evening null results limit generalisation but are not equivalence evidence.

scientific_findings.finding_statement: The ordinary-meal studies assessed here measured plasma amino-acid ratios, not brain transport or ADHD outcomes; findings from enriched-protein attention studies do not establish ordinary-meal efficacy.
scientific_findings.synthesis: The original meal studies do not measure functional outcomes. Markus et al. (2005) measured morning attention after an enriched-protein protocol, while a newer athlete trial reported null sleep/performance results. These contexts cannot validate a general ordinary-meal benefit or prove mediation by LAT1.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: This is an assessment-scope boundary, not a claim that functional evidence is absent from the entire literature. The enriched-protein trials are not ordinary-meal or ADHD trials; no equivalence or mediation is inferred.

title: Dopaminergic Signalling Regulation
mission: Maintain appropriately regulated dopamine synthesis, storage, release, receptor signalling, reuptake and metabolism across changing functional demand.
summary: Dopamine signalling is set by how much is made, stored, released, sensed, taken back up and broken down. The result depends on brain region, receptor type, baseline state and the task, so more signalling is not always better. Tests of synthesis, release, receptors and transporters are not one dopamine level. This regulation supports cognitive control and willingness to spend mental effort.
dose_sensitivity: No intake-response range established; dopamine effects are baseline-, region- and task-dependent
scientific_findings_intro: Human pharmacology and PET evidence supports context-dependent dopamine regulation: baseline synthesis capacity, receptor involvement and cognitive demand influence motivation and flexibility, so effects are not uniformly enhancing. [[4]](#pm-ref-4) [[5]](#pm-ref-5) [[7]](#pm-ref-7) Exercise, sleep deprivation and dietary restriction studies demonstrate changes in different dopaminergic endpoints—release and receptor availability must be distinguished. [[15]](#pm-ref-15) [[16]](#pm-ref-16) [[17]](#pm-ref-17) Biochemical and deficiency evidence separately supports synthesis requirements, without establishing that extra precursor intake improves human signalling. dietary_input_traceability.evidence_limitation: Substrate necessity does not establish that additional dietary tyrosine increases brain dopamine or improves a functional or clinical outcome.

dietary_input_traceability.dietary_input_note: Accepted intracellular/endogenous participant; no dietary supply relationship is admitted for this entry in this PM.
dietary_input_traceability.biological_role: Endogenous cofactor required by tyrosine hydroxylase during conversion of tyrosine to L-DOPA
dietary_input_traceability.evidence_limitation: BH4 is synthesised and recycled in vivo; this is not evidence for dietary BH4 provision or increased dopamine synthesis.

dietary_input_traceability.dietary_input_note: Accepted dietary provision or constituent supply relationship; no efficacy or quantity claim added.
dietary_input_traceability.biological_role: Folate supplies the methyl group through [BRS2 PM1 — Folate/B12 remethylation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm1-folate-b12-dependent-homocysteine-remethylation), replenishing methionine used by [BRS2 PM3 — MAT/SAM synthesis](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm3-same-synthesis). SAM is the methyl donor used by COMT during dopamine metabolism.
dietary_input_traceability.evidence_limitation: This requires functional B12-dependent remethylation. The connected reaction chain does not measure dietary folate contribution to regional brain SAM or clearance; alternative methionine supply and tissue turnover matter. A limiting effect and benefit from extra intake remain unresolved.

dietary_input_traceability.dietary_input_note: Accepted dietary provision or constituent supply relationship; no efficacy or quantity claim added.
dietary_input_traceability.biological_role: Betaine donates methyl groups through [BRS2 PM2 — BHMT remethylation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm2-betaine-bhmt-remethylation), predominantly in liver and kidney, replenishing methionine upstream of [BRS2 PM3 — SAM synthesis](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm3-same-synthesis). SAM is used by COMT during dopamine metabolism.
dietary_input_traceability.evidence_limitation: This is peripheral BHMT supply, not neuronal BHMT activity or measured delivery into neural SAM. Dietary methionine and folate remethylation provide alternatives. Homocysteine lowering does not establish regional clearance, a limiting constraint or benefit from extra intake.

dietary_input_traceability.dietary_input_note: Accepted dietary provision or constituent supply relationship; no efficacy or quantity claim added.
dietary_input_traceability.biological_role: Choline can be oxidised to betaine for [BRS2 PM2 — BHMT remethylation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm2-betaine-bhmt-remethylation), predominantly in liver and kidney, replenishing methionine upstream of [BRS2 PM3 — SAM synthesis](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm3-same-synthesis). SAM is used by COMT during dopamine metabolism.
dietary_input_traceability.evidence_limitation: Only choline-to-betaine methyl supply is admitted, not membrane or acetylcholine roles. Oxidation, peripheral BHMT, alternative methionine supply and local neural SAM turnover limit interpretation. Neural delivery, increased clearance, a limiting constraint and extra-intake benefit are not measured.

dietary_input_traceability.dietary_input_note: Accepted dietary provision or constituent supply relationship; no efficacy or quantity claim added.
dietary_input_traceability.biological_role: Phenylalanine is hydroxylated to tyrosine in peripheral tissues, replenishing the circulating tyrosine available to [LAT1 transport](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm2-lat1-competitive-transport-modulation) upstream of dopamine synthesis.
dietary_input_traceability.evidence_limitation: Human peripheral conversion supplies circulating tyrosine; neuronal delivery uses the separately supported transport chain. This does not establish increased dopamine/noradrenaline output, a limiting intake or benefit from extra phenylalanine. Hydroxylation, renal/hepatic function and LNAA competition matter; high phenylalanine is not interchangeable with tyrosine.

dietary_input_traceability.biological_role: Riboflavin supplies FMN and FAD formation; FAD sustains monoamine oxidase in dopamine metabolism capacity.
dietary_input_traceability.evidence_limitation: Rat enzyme capacity, not measured human neurotransmitter clearance, synaptic output or benefit above adequacy. No conclusion about which flavin analogue is effective is taken from the internally inconsistent abstract. The same experiment is shared across the three monoamine PMs, not independent replication.
dietary_input_traceability.dietary_input_note: 2026-10-26 mission-specific dietary recovery: admitted under the existing Type A gate; food composition does not establish an effective intervention dose.

dietary_input_traceability.biological_role: FAD is the bound flavin cofactor of monoamine oxidase.
dietary_input_traceability.evidence_limitation: This is a biochemical cofactor target, not an independent oral FAD admission or food-content claim.
dietary_input_traceability.dietary_input_note: Target of the separately admitted riboflavin activation route; not duplicated as a primary dietary presentation.

dietary_input_traceability.biological_role: Magnesium supplies the catalytic metal required by COMT for SAM-dependent catechol O-methylation within this PM’s metabolism arm.
dietary_input_traceability.evidence_limitation: Catalytic capacity does not show that extra dietary magnesium increases regional catecholamine clearance or improves function. COMT isoforms, genotype, SAM availability and tissue homeostasis constrain interpretation; increased clearance is not universally desirable.
dietary_input_traceability.dietary_input_note: 2026-10-26 mission-specific dietary recovery: admitted under the existing Type A gate; food composition does not establish an effective intervention dose.

dietary_lever_atoms.permitted_wording: Iron is a Direct cofactor requirement for tyrosine hydroxylase. This does not establish that additional iron increases brain dopamine when iron status is adequate.
dietary_lever_atoms.evidence_limitation: Human intake-to-dopamine responsiveness and clinical benefit were not established; the direct dopamine-metabolite evidence assessed here is preclinical deficiency evidence.

dietary_lever_atoms.permitted_wording: PLP is the Direct cofactor requirement for aromatic L-amino-acid decarboxylase. PLP is formed in the body from vitamin B6 vitamers; this classification does not establish dietary PLP provision or intake-responsive human brain dopamine synthesis.
dietary_lever_atoms.evidence_limitation: Kennedy reviews B-vitamin roles in neurochemical synthesis; this does not establish dietary PLP provision or an intake-to-dopamine response in humans.

dietary_lever_atoms.permitted_wording: Vitamin B6 is a Derived Dietary Requirement because dietary B6 vitamers are converted to PLP, the Direct cofactor requirement for aromatic L-amino-acid decarboxylase. It is the dietary route to PLP, not a second independent dopamine cofactor. This does not establish that increasing B6 intake increases dopamine synthesis or improves cognition or ADHD.
dietary_lever_atoms.evidence_limitation: Dietary B6 can supply PLP precursors, including vitamers that enter the central nervous system, but increasing B6 intake has not been shown to increase human brain dopamine synthesis.

dietary_lever_atoms.permitted_wording: Tyrosine is a Direct substrate requirement for tyrosine-hydroxylase conversion to L-DOPA. This does not establish that additional dietary tyrosine increases brain dopamine or improves a functional or clinical outcome.
dietary_lever_atoms.evidence_limitation: Substrate necessity does not establish that additional dietary tyrosine increases brain dopamine or improves a functional or clinical outcome.

dietary_lever_atoms.permitted_wording: BH4 is the endogenous cofactor required for tyrosine hydroxylation. It is not a dietary BH4 recommendation.
dietary_lever_atoms.evidence_limitation: BH4 is synthesised and recycled in vivo; this is not evidence for dietary BH4 provision or increased dopamine synthesis.

dietary_lever_atoms.permitted_wording: Phenylalanine is hydroxylated to tyrosine in peripheral tissues, replenishing the circulating tyrosine available to [LAT1 transport](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm2-lat1-competitive-transport-modulation) upstream of dopamine synthesis.
dietary_lever_atoms.evidence_limitation: Human peripheral conversion supplies circulating tyrosine; neuronal delivery uses the separately supported transport chain. This does not establish increased dopamine/noradrenaline output, a limiting intake or benefit from extra phenylalanine. Hydroxylation, renal/hepatic function and LNAA competition matter; high phenylalanine is not interchangeable with tyrosine.

Riboflavin supplies FMN and FAD formation; FAD sustains monoamine oxidase in dopamine metabolism capacity.
dietary_lever_atoms.evidence_limitation: Rat enzyme capacity, not measured human neurotransmitter clearance, synaptic output or benefit above adequacy. No conclusion about which flavin analogue is effective is taken from the internally inconsistent abstract. The same experiment is shared across the three monoamine PMs, not independent replication.
