scientific_findings_intro: Human-pathway evidence establishes methionine synthase’s folate-substrate and methylcobalamin requirements and distinguishes them from upstream flavin-dependent enzymes. [[9]](#pm-ref-9) In an adult observational study, riboflavin status modified the association between an MTHFR variant and circulating homocysteine. [[10]](#pm-ref-10) Together, these findings clarify enzyme-specific dependence and a status–genotype interaction; the circulating marker does not directly measure tissue remethylation flux.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Methionine synthase remethylates homocysteine
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Methionine synthase transfers the methyl group of 5-methyltetrahydrofolate to homocysteine, producing methionine and tetrahydrofolate. Methylcobalamin carries that methyl group. Betaine remethylation, SAMe synthesis, transsulfuration and phospholipid methylation are different reactions.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: This defines the reaction and its direct participants. It does not show that eating more folate or vitamin B12 speeds the reaction in human tissues, and it does not make riboflavin a cofactor of the synthase.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase transfers the methyl group of 5-methyltetrahydrofolate to homocysteine, producing methionine and tetrahydrofolate, and uses methylcobalamin as its cofactor. Betaine-dependent remethylation, methionine adenosyltransferase, transsulfuration and phosphatidylethanolamine methylation are separate reactions.
scientific_findings.synthesis: A human-pathway review states the reaction directly: methionine synthase (MTR) converts homocysteine plus 5-methyltetrahydrofolate to methionine plus tetrahydrofolate and requires the methylated form of cobalamin. Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase produces that folate substrate. Betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase is a separate, mainly liver and kidney route. Methionine adenosyltransferase then converts methionine to SAMe, and cystathionine beta-synthase starts transsulfuration. The review also traces dietary folate, including folic acid reduced by dihydrofolate reductase, into 5-methyltetrahydrofolate, and dietary cobalamin through absorption and intracellular processing onto the enzyme as methylcobalamin.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: The primary source is a biochemical review, not a new human flux study. Reaction identity does not show that ordinary dietary intake controls tissue remethylation rate, and it does not assign clinical benefit. Phosphatidylethanolamine methylation is a later SAMe-consuming reaction, not part of this step.

evidence_considered.label: Froese et al. (2019)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Methionine synthase uses methylcobalamin to remethylate homocysteine with 5-methyltetrahydrofolate, producing methionine and tetrahydrofolate. Parallel and downstream reactions are named separately.

assessment.study: Narrative review of cobalamin absorption, intracellular cofactor processing, folate-mediated one-carbon metabolism and methionine-cycle regulation.
assessment.population: No new participants. The review synthesises human pathway biochemistry and inherited disorders of cobalamin and folate metabolism.
assessment.result: Methionine synthase (MTR, EC 2.1.1.13) catalyses homocysteine plus 5-methyltetrahydrofolate to methionine plus tetrahydrofolate and requires methylcobalamin. Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase produces 5-methyltetrahydrofolate. Betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase is an alternative remethylation enzyme, mainly in liver and kidney. Methionine adenosyltransferase converts methionine and ATP to SAMe. Cystathionine beta-synthase combines homocysteine with serine to start transsulfuration. Dietary folic acid is reduced to tetrahydrofolate by dihydrofolate reductase, and dietary cobalamin is processed to methylcobalamin on the synthase.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No new numeric effect size. The result is reaction identity and pathway separation.
assessment.evidence_summary: Direct statement of the human methionine synthase reaction, its methylcobalamin cofactor, the folate route to its substrate, and the neighbouring reactions this PM does not include.
assessment.limitations: A review does not measure tissue remethylation flux, ordinary-diet dose response, or a cognitive or attention outcome.

evidence_considered.label: Wolthers et al. (2007)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: Purified enzyme and coenzymes.
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Purified human methionine-synthase reductase contains both flavins and transfers reducing equivalents to methionine synthase.

assessment.study: Human reductase module crystallography and coenzyme-binding experiments.
assessment.population: Recombinant human enzyme; no dietary participant cohort.
assessment.result: Purified human methionine-synthase reductase contains both flavins and transfers reducing equivalents to methionine synthase.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No additional magnitude inferred.
assessment.evidence_summary: Purified human methionine-synthase reductase contains both flavins and transfers reducing equivalents to methionine synthase.
assessment.limitations: Foundational human-enzyme cofactor provenance supports capacity; it is not a measurement of dietary riboflavin-induced remethylation flux, brain methylation or benefit above adequacy. FMN is also required; FAD is the endpoint of the displayed activation chain, not its sole functional cofactor.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Primary abstract retrieved 26 October 2026; full methods and supplements not extracted.

connected_supportive_evidence.label: Aragão et al. (2024)
connected_supportive_evidence.why_relevant: Riboflavin is often discussed beside folate-cycle enzymes, so this review was checked against the synthase reaction.
connected_supportive_evidence.why_excluded: Its abstract describes general riboflavin physiology. It does not state the methionine synthase reaction, methylcobalamin dependence, or separation from betaine remethylation.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Riboflavin is not the synthase cofactor
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Riboflavin supplies the flavin cofactor of methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase, which makes 5-methyltetrahydrofolate, and of methionine synthase reductase, which repairs inactive cobalamin. Methionine synthase itself uses methylcobalamin.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Riboflavin can matter upstream of the substrate and in enzyme repair. It is not a cofactor bound at the methionine synthase catalytic site.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Flavin adenine dinucleotide derived from riboflavin is a cofactor of methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase and of methionine synthase reductase, not of the methionine synthase catalytic site, which uses methylcobalamin.
scientific_findings.synthesis: The human-pathway review assigns methylcobalamin, not a flavin, to methionine synthase, and places methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase upstream as the source of 5-methyltetrahydrofolate. An adult cross-sectional study states the same split: methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase uses FAD, methionine synthase reductase binds flavin mononucleotide and FAD, and methionine synthase uses methylcobalamin. In that study, riboflavin status modified the association of an MTHFR variant with blood homocysteine. That is a circulating-marker interaction at the upstream enzyme, not evidence that riboflavin occupies the synthase cofactor site.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: The flavin assignment for the two neighbouring enzymes is stated in the study introduction from prior enzymology, and the new data are genotype associations with blood homocysteine. Neither source shows that dietary riboflavin changes tissue methionine-synthase flux.

evidence_considered.label: García-Minguillán et al. (2014)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: dietary
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Riboflavin status modified MTHFR-linked differences in blood homocysteine. The synthase cofactor named in the paper is methylcobalamin, while FAD is assigned to MTHFR and to MTRR.

assessment.study: Cross-sectional analysis of whether fasting plasma total homocysteine associations with MTHFR 677C>T, MTRR 66A>G and MTRR 524C>T depend on riboflavin status, measured by the erythrocyte glutathione reductase activation coefficient.
assessment.population: 771 adults aged 18–75 years in Tarragona province, Spain, excluding B-vitamin users and pregnant or lactating women. Recruitment was in 1998–2002, before mandatory folic acid fortification of flour in that setting.
assessment.result: The paper states that FAD is a cofactor of MTHFR, that MTRR binds flavin mononucleotide and FAD, and that methionine synthase uses methylcobalamin and is reactivated by MTRR. Among MTHFR 677T carriers with plasma folate below 14.7 nmol/L, blood homocysteine was 8.2% higher than in the 677CC genotype, and that difference was not seen when riboflavin status was optimal (interaction p = 0.048).
assessment.effect_magnitude: 8.2% higher blood homocysteine in the specified MTHFR contrast (p < 0.01), eliminated at optimal riboflavin status (interaction p = 0.048). No methionine-synthase activity or tissue-flux estimate is reported.
assessment.evidence_summary: Separates the riboflavin-dependent enzymes (MTHFR and MTRR) from the methylcobalamin cofactor of methionine synthase, and shows a riboflavin-status interaction with an MTHFR variant on blood homocysteine.
assessment.limitations: Observational genotype analysis. The endpoint is plasma homocysteine, not enzyme rate. Optimal riboflavin status did not identify riboflavin as a prosthetic group of methionine synthase.

connected_supportive_evidence.label: Froese et al. (2019)
connected_supportive_evidence.why_relevant: States that methionine synthase requires methylcobalamin and that methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase produces its folate substrate.
connected_supportive_evidence.why_excluded: It does not itself test riboflavin status or assign FAD to MTHFR or MTRR, so it is not the study that adjudicates the riboflavin split.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Plasma homocysteine is not remethylation flux
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Folic acid lowers blood homocysteine, and vitamin B12 adds a further reduction. That change is in a circulating marker. It does not measure how fast methionine synthase runs in tissues.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Blood homocysteine can move when folate or vitamin B12 status changes. It still cannot be read as tissue remethylation rate, methylation output, or a clinical benefit.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: A reduction in blood homocysteine after folic acid or vitamin B12 does not measure tissue methionine-synthase flux.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Individual data from 12 randomised trials show that folic acid lowers blood homocysteine, with a larger effect at higher starting homocysteine and lower starting folate, and that vitamin B12 produces a further reduction while vitamin B6 does not. The measured endpoint is blood homocysteine concentration. A separate small trial also lowered plasma homocysteine with vitamin B12, fish oil, or both, which mixes this marker with a fatty-acid exposure that is not a synthase substrate.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Standardised percentage reductions describe blood concentration after supplements, often at doses above ordinary food intake. They do not report tissue methionine appearance, SAMe production, or a clinical outcome. Fish oil co-administration shows that the marker can move for reasons outside this reaction.

evidence_considered.label: Collaboration (1998)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: supplemental-formulation
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Folic acid lowered blood homocysteine, vitamin B12 added a further reduction, and vitamin B6 did not. The endpoint was blood concentration, not tissue enzyme flux.

assessment.study: Meta-analysis of randomised trials of folic-acid-based supplements, using individual data and multivariate regression to separate folic acid dose from added vitamin B12 or vitamin B6.
assessment.population: 1114 people in 12 trials. Results were standardised to pretreatment blood homocysteine of 12 µmol/L and blood folate of 12 nmol/L, described as approximate Western-population averages.
assessment.result: After that standardisation, dietary folic acid reduced blood homocysteine by 25% (95% confidence interval 23% to 28%). Effects were similar from 0.5 to 5 mg folic acid daily. Vitamin B12 (mean 0.5 mg daily) produced an additional 7% reduction (3% to 10%). Vitamin B6 (mean 16.5 mg daily) had no significant additional effect. Reductions were larger at higher pretreatment homocysteine and lower pretreatment folate.
assessment.effect_magnitude: 25% (23% to 28%) blood homocysteine reduction with folic acid; additional 7% (3% to 10%) with vitamin B12; no significant added effect of vitamin B6.
assessment.evidence_summary: Direct human evidence that folic acid and vitamin B12 lower a circulating homocysteine marker, with the folate effect depending on starting folate and homocysteine.
assessment.limitations: Supplement doses, blood concentration only, no tissue remethylation-flux measurement, and no clinical-outcome test in this meta-analysis.

connected_supportive_evidence.label: Tao Huang et al. (2015)
connected_supportive_evidence.why_relevant: A randomised comparison also reported lower plasma homocysteine after vitamin B12.
connected_supportive_evidence.why_excluded: Thirty-eight participants were assigned to vitamin B12, fish oil, or both, and plasma homocysteine fell by 22%, 19% and 39%. Fish oil is not a methionine-synthase substrate, and plasma homocysteine is still not tissue flux.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Attention studies do not test this reaction
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Studies in children with ADHD report lower folate or vitamin B12, and sometimes higher homocysteine, than comparison groups. They do not measure methionine synthase activity or test whether changing it improves attention.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: These associations are a ceiling on the attention relationship. They are not evidence that this reaction is impaired, and they are not a treatment result.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Attached ADHD biomarker and MTHFR-genotype studies do not establish that folate- and B12-dependent methionine synthase activity modulates Focus / Attention Stability.
scientific_findings.synthesis: A meta-analysis of observational studies found lower vitamin B9 and vitamin B12 in children with ADHD than in comparison children. A case-control study of boys found higher homocysteine and lower vitamin B12. A Taiwanese case-control study found lower serum folate and vitamin B12 together with a less favourable dietary pattern. A polymorphism meta-analysis linked an MTHFR variant to ADHD occurrence. None of these studies assayed methionine synthase, traced tissue remethylation, or tested folate or vitamin B12 as an attention treatment.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: This is a bounded reading of the studies already attached to the attention relationship. It does not prove that no attention relationship exists. Heterogeneity is high in the vitamin meta-analysis, and the genotype paper concerns MTHFR, which is upstream of this reaction.

evidence_considered.label: Razavinia et al. (2024)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: dietary
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Children with ADHD had lower vitamin B9 and vitamin B12 than comparison children. Methionine synthase activity was not measured.

assessment.study: Systematic review and meta-analysis of case-control or cross-sectional studies of plasma vitamins B9 and B12 in children with ADHD, searched through June 2023.
assessment.population: Six studies, 982 children aged about 6–12 years (204 girls and 744 boys; mean age 8.86 ± 2.03 years).
assessment.result: Vitamin B9 differed between children with and without ADHD (standardised mean difference −0.80, 95% confidence interval −1.55 to −0.04). Vitamin B12 was lower in ADHD (standardised mean difference −0.29, 95% confidence interval −0.42 to −0.16). After sensitivity analysis the B12 difference remained (standardised mean difference −0.19, 95% confidence interval −0.34 to −0.04).
assessment.effect_magnitude: Vitamin B9 standardised mean difference −0.80 (−1.55 to −0.04). Vitamin B12 standardised mean difference −0.29 (−0.42 to −0.16), and −0.19 (−0.34 to −0.04) after sensitivity analysis. Heterogeneity for the B12 analysis was I² = 93% before that sensitivity analysis, then 21%.
assessment.evidence_summary: Observational evidence of lower circulating folate and vitamin B12 in children with ADHD, without an enzyme or treatment measurement.
assessment.limitations: Blood levels only, high heterogeneity before sensitivity analysis, no methionine-synthase assay and no supplementation outcome.

evidence_considered.label: Lukovac et al. (2024)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Boys with ADHD had higher homocysteine and lower vitamin B12 than age-matched boys. This was a diagnostic-marker comparison, not a synthase-flux or treatment study.

assessment.study: Cross-sectional serum comparison of homocysteine, vitamin B12, vitamin D, ferritin and iron, with behavioural and cognitive assessments.
assessment.population: 133 boys aged 6.5–12.5 years, 67 with DSM-V ADHD and 66 age-matched boys without ADHD.
assessment.result: Homocysteine was higher and vitamin B12 was lower in the ADHD group. Multiple logistic regression identified homocysteine as a potential prognostic indicator for ADHD.
assessment.effect_magnitude: The abstract reports statistically significant differences and does not give means, confidence intervals, or an enzyme-activity effect.
assessment.evidence_summary: A single-sex paediatric case-control difference in two blood markers associated with one-carbon metabolism.
assessment.limitations: Boys only, no folate measurement in the reported panel, no methionine-synthase assay, and no intervention. A prognostic association is not a causal test of this reaction.

evidence_considered.label: Wang et al. (2019)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: dietary
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Children with ADHD had lower serum folate and vitamin B12 and a dietary pattern poorer in vegetables, fruit and protein-rich foods. The path model links diet, nutrient markers and ADHD; it does not measure methionine synthase.

assessment.study: Case-control study of food-frequency intake and fasting nutritional biochemistry, with a structural equation model linking diet, markers and ADHD.
assessment.population: 216 children with ADHD and 216 age-, height- and sex-matched controls from 31 elementary schools in Taiwan.
assessment.result: Compared with controls, children with ADHD had lower serum vitamin B12, folate, vitamin B6, ferritin and monounsaturated fatty acids, and higher saturated fatty acids, n-6/n-3 ratio and inorganic phosphorus. They reported more nutrient-poor, high-sugar and high-fat foods and less vegetable, fruit and protein-rich food. The model treated poor nutritional biochemistry as a link between unhealthy diet and ADHD.
assessment.effect_magnitude: The abstract reports significant group differences and does not give mean differences for folate or vitamin B12, or any synthase-flux estimate.
assessment.evidence_summary: Human observational evidence that diet pattern and several blood nutrients, including folate and vitamin B12, differ by ADHD status.
assessment.limitations: Cross-sectional path analysis cannot show that methionine synthase activity changed, or that correcting folate or vitamin B12 improves attention. Several non-B-vitamin markers differed as well.

evidence_considered.label: Meng et al. (2022)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: An MTHFR 1298A>C meta-analysis was associated with ADHD occurrence. The paper does not measure methionine synthase.

assessment.study: Random-effects meta-analysis of case-control studies of MTHFR 677C>T and 1298A>C in ADHD, bipolar disorder and schizophrenia.
assessment.population: Five ADHD studies (434 cases and 670 controls), plus separate bipolar and schizophrenia study sets. Cases and controls were defined by the included psychiatric studies, not by a shared remethylation assay.
assessment.result: MTHFR 677C>T was associated with bipolar disorder and schizophrenia. MTHFR 1298A>C was related to ADHD and bipolar disorder. Sensitivity analyses were described as stable. No methionine-synthase genotype or enzyme activity was analysed.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Associations were summarised as odds ratios. The abstract does not give the ADHD odds ratio, and it reports no remethylation-flux effect.
assessment.evidence_summary: Genetic association of an upstream folate-cycle enzyme variant with ADHD occurrence, not a test of methionine synthase capacity.
assessment.limitations: MTHFR is upstream of 5-methyltetrahydrofolate supply. Genotype association does not establish enzyme flux, dietary response, or an attention benefit from folate or vitamin B12.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Cognitive effects are not synthase flux
scientific_findings.finding_summary: In older adults with mild cognitive impairment, B vitamins were associated with slower cognitive decline only when omega-3 status was higher. That interaction does not measure methionine synthase flux.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: A conditional cognitive signal in mild cognitive impairment is not evidence that this reaction modulates cognitive clarity, and it is not an attention-treatment result.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: B-vitamin effects on cognitive decline in mild cognitive impairment, including an interaction with omega-3 status, do not measure methionine synthase flux or establish that this reaction modulates Cognitive Clarity.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Re-analysis of a two-year trial in mild cognitive impairment found better cognitive and clinical scores with B vitamins as baseline omega-3 status rose, and no B-vitamin effect on cognitive decline when omega-3 status was low. The intervention combined folic acid, vitamin B6 and vitamin B12. Blood homocysteine lowering by folic acid and vitamin B12 is a separate circulating-marker result. Neither dataset isolates methionine synthase activity from other B-vitamin actions or from omega-3-dependent membrane biology.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: One re-analysis in adults aged 70 years and older with mild cognitive impairment, using a three-vitamin intervention. It does not test children, attention outcomes, or tissue remethylation rate. The omega-3 interaction places part of the signal outside this reaction.

evidence_considered.label: Oulhaj et al. (2016)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: combination-formulation
evidence_considered.directional_finding: B vitamins slowed cognitive decline in mild cognitive impairment only when baseline omega-3 status was higher. Methionine synthase flux was not measured.

assessment.study: Re-analysis of the VITACOG randomised trial testing whether baseline plasma omega-3 status interacted with B-vitamin treatment on cognitive and clinical scores.
assessment.population: 266 participants with mild cognitive impairment, aged 70 years or older, randomised to folic acid plus vitamins B6 and B12, or placebo, for 2 years.
assessment.result: Final verbal delayed recall, global cognition and clinical dementia rating improved in the B-vitamin group as baseline omega-3 concentration increased, with little relation to omega-3 status in the placebo group. Among participants with good omega-3 status, 33% on B vitamins had a global clinical dementia rating above 0, compared with 59% on placebo. Docosahexaenoic acid, more than eicosapentaenoic acid, carried the interaction. When omega-3 status was low, B vitamins had no effect on cognitive decline.
assessment.effect_magnitude: 33% versus 59% with global clinical dementia rating above 0 in the good omega-3 stratum. No methionine-synthase activity or tissue-flux estimate is reported.
assessment.evidence_summary: Human outcome evidence that a combined B-vitamin intervention interacts with omega-3 status on cognitive decline in mild cognitive impairment.
assessment.limitations: Not a test of methionine synthase alone. Vitamin B6, which acts in transsulfuration rather than this reaction, was part of the intervention. The result is conditional on omega-3 status and does not establish a general cognitive-clarity benefit.

connected_supportive_evidence.label: Collaboration (1998)
connected_supportive_evidence.why_relevant: Shows that folic acid and vitamin B12 lower blood homocysteine, the marker often used to interpret B-vitamin cognitive trials.
connected_supportive_evidence.why_excluded: The meta-analysis measured blood homocysteine, not cognitive clarity and not tissue methionine-synthase flux. That marker limit is assessed in PM1-IC1.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Pharmacological folic acid changes measured whole-body methyl flux
scientific_findings.finding_summary: A small human tracer study measured increased whole-body remethylation and transmethylation after three weeks of folic acid; concentration changes did not establish those rates.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: A small human tracer study measured increased whole-body remethylation and transmethylation after three weeks of folic acid; concentration changes did not establish those rates.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Pharmacological folic acid, not ordinary food folate, a deprivation trial or isolated tissue/whole-pool effect. Evidence access: Primary abstract.
scientific_findings.synthesis: A small human tracer study measured increased whole-body remethylation and transmethylation after three weeks of folic acid; concentration changes did not establish those rates.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Pharmacological folic acid, not ordinary food folate, a deprivation trial or isolated tissue/whole-pool effect. Evidence access: Primary abstract.

evidence_considered.label: Stam et al. (2005)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Whole-body remethylation increased 59% and transmethylation 20%; concentrations did not track kinetic changes.

assessment.study: Three-week before/after folic acid with stable-isotope methionine kinetics
assessment.population: 12 healthy subjects; 5 mg/day folic acid
assessment.result: Whole-body remethylation increased 59% and transmethylation 20%; concentrations did not track kinetic changes.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No general dietary efficacy or tissue-uniform effect is inferred.
assessment.evidence_summary: Whole-body remethylation increased 59% and transmethylation 20%; concentrations did not track kinetic changes.
assessment.limitations: Pharmacological folic acid, not ordinary food folate, a deprivation trial or isolated tissue/whole-pool effect. Evidence access: Primary abstract.

pm_kc_relationships.pm_biological_role: The folate member of KC1 supplies folate forms converted to 5-methyltetrahydrofolate for PM1 methionine synthase.
pm_kc_relationships.evidence_limitation: This is the folate provision relationship already disclosed on PM1, not a new reaction or proof of a limiting effect on tissue flux. Functional B12 is required. Betaine and choline support a parallel BHMT route, not this enzyme’s donor reaction.

constituent_relationships.rationale: Individually evidenced KC membership and PM applicability. The full provision disclosure is already retained on this PM; no second identical atom is published.

dietary_input_assessments.operation: Recycle homocysteine to methionine through folate and B12 so methyl-donor supply and homocysteine control stay supported.
dietary_input_assessments.assessment_limitations: Foundational human-enzyme cofactor provenance supports capacity; it is not a measurement of dietary riboflavin-induced remethylation flux, brain methylation or benefit above adequacy. FMN is also required; FAD is the endpoint of the displayed activation chain, not its sole functional cofactor.

food_target_research.sufficient_coverage_rationale: Existing structured composition and provisional food research for this exact canonical input were inspected. Reuse these source/form-qualified foods; do not infer an effective food dose or invent additional relationships.

functional_dependency.statement: Riboflavin supplies FMN and FAD used by methionine-synthase reductase to regenerate active B12-dependent methionine synthase.

dietary_supply.statement: The same canonical nutrient is supplied by the inspected food records. Tissue uptake and homeostasis remain distinct from an effect of extra intake.

conversion_pathway.process: Riboflavin kinase (RFK) phosphorylates riboflavin to FMN using ATP.
conversion_pathway.limitations: Enzyme identity does not quantify tissue cofactor supply or flux after a meal.

evidence.statement: Human RFK catalyses riboflavin phosphorylation; UniProt Q969G6 entry 195 retrieved 2026-10-26, Rhea 14357.

conversion_pathway.limitations: FAD production and enzyme loading depend on cellular context; no fixed food-to-FAD yield is inferred.

evidence.statement: Human FLAD1 catalyses FMN adenylation; UniProt Q8NFF5 entry 182 retrieved 2026-10-26, Rhea 17237.

title: Betaine/BHMT Remethylation
mission: Provide a parallel homocysteine clearance route so methionine and SAMe supply remain resilient when folate demand is high.
summary: Betaine–homocysteine methyltransferase transfers a methyl group from betaine to homocysteine, forming methionine and dimethylglycine. A bound zinc ion activates homocysteine. Folate and vitamin B12 are not part of that reaction. Betaine may come from the diet or from oxidation of choline. In healthy men, controlled choline depletion lowered plasma betaine and reduced homocysteine-handling reserve, and repletion reversed that change.

kc_applicability_adjudications.applicability_proposition: Inadequacy of the folate donor route can indirectly constrain BHMT-dependent remethylation capacity by changing demand on the betaine route or the betaine-to-DMG state.
established_links: BHMT transfers a methyl group from betaine to homocysteine and does not use folate or vitamin B12 in that reaction (PM2-F1).
The flow of methyl groups through BHMT is not dependent on folate or vitamin B12 (PM2-F1).
The canonical KC review admits folate as a methyl-group input into the shared pool.
In folate-deprived rats, hepatic betaine fell, dimethylglycine rose, and betaine supplementation increased hepatic BHMT activity but only partly corrected hyperhomocysteinaemia.

Liu 2012 full Methods/Results: hepatic extracted BHMT activity was unchanged by folate deprivation; betaine supplementation increased activity. Higher hepatic DMG and partial homocysteine rescue support interaction but do not isolate DMG inhibition in vivo.

Liu 2012 full Methods/Results: hepatic extracted BHMT activity was unchanged by folate deprivation; betaine supplementation increased activity. Higher hepatic DMG and partial homocysteine rescue support interaction but do not isolate DMG inhibition in vivo.
inferred_links: The proposed DMG inhibition link at relevant intracellular concentrations, distinguishing unchanged extracted enzyme activity from impaired in-vivo BHMT function and alternative clearance routes.
kc_applicability_adjudications.rationale: Full text narrows the earlier inference. An animal supported chain is allowed; the unresolved issue is causal inhibition and competing explanations, not absence of a human assay.
kc_applicability_adjudications.evidence_gap: The proposed DMG inhibition link at relevant intracellular concentrations, distinguishing unchanged extracted enzyme activity from impaired in-vivo BHMT function and alternative clearance routes.

kc_applicability_adjudications.applicability_proposition: Inadequacy or imbalance of the methionine–cysteine sulfur-amino-acid pool constrains BHMT-dependent remethylation capacity.
established_links: BHMT produces methionine and does not use cysteine in its reaction (PM2-F1).
In rats, methionine restriction increased rather than decreased hepatic BHMT expression and activity when a methyl donor was available.
inferred_links: Reduced methionine intake necessarily reduces the capacity of BHMT to remethylate an available homocysteine load.
The rat regulatory response establishes a human intake recommendation.
kc_applicability_adjudications.rationale: The named KC2 pool is not a required input pool for this PM: methionine is the product and cysteine is absent from the reaction. Methionine restriction can increase BHMT capacity when methyl donor is available, which is a compensatory response rather than evidence that KC2 inadequacy constrains the governed remethylation capacity. No KC2 mapping is established.

established_links: KC1’s betaine/choline route supplies BHMT methyl donor; demonstrated choline depletion can reduce remethylation reserve under a methionine challenge.

dose_sensitivity: Betaine is the reaction substrate. Supplemental betaine lowers plasma homocysteine, but no human dose-response for tissue BHMT flux is established.

dietary_input_assessments.operation: Provide a parallel homocysteine clearance route so methionine and SAMe supply remain resilient when folate demand is high.

functional_dependency.statement: Zinc supplies the catalytic metal that activates the homocysteine thiol in human BHMT; removing enzyme-bound zinc abolishes activity and reconstitution restores it.

dietary_supply.statement: The same mineral has established dietary supply through the canonical composition records. Cellular uptake and homeostasis mediate enzyme loading; this is maintenance of capacity, not a claim that extra intake accelerates the reaction.

dietary_input_assessments.assessment_limitations: Human purified-enzyme metal removal/reconstitution and ligand mutants establish zinc-dependent capacity. Dietary zinc supplies the same element, but no human extra-intake BHMT flux response, intake threshold or cognitive benefit is established.

phenome_relationships.rationale: Reviews of ADHD diets and of choline in neurodevelopment discuss attention, but they do not test BHMT activity or betaine supplementation as an attention treatment {{cite:millichap_diet_2012,derbyshire_role_2023}}. The enzyme reaction is established separately, and a change in plasma homocysteine is not an attention outcome {{cite:evans_betaine_2002,olthof_low_2003}}. Direct evidence that this remethylation route changes Focus / Attention Stability remains a gap.

Lower plasma homocysteine after betaine supplements is a blood measurement, not a test of cognitive clarity or of tissue BHMT activity {{cite:olthof_low_2003}}. A choline review discusses neurodevelopment rather than an effect of this reaction on clarity {{cite:derbyshire_role_2023}}. The relationship remains an indirect bridge with no direct outcome evidence.

scientific_findings_intro: Human structure and mutagenesis studies establish BHMT’s betaine-dependent reaction and catalytic zinc requirement. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) Controlled human choline depletion lowered plasma betaine and worsened the homocysteine response to a methionine challenge in participants who developed hepatic steatosis; repletion restored that response. [[6]](#pm-ref-6) Animal depletion and enzyme-inhibition studies complement this supported dependency chain, but human tissue BHMT flux and cognitive outcomes were not measured. scientific_findings.finding_label: BHMT remethylates homocysteine with betaine and catalytic zinc
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Human betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase (BHMT) transfers one methyl group from betaine to homocysteine. The products are methionine and dimethylglycine. A zinc ion bound by three cysteines activates homocysteine. Folate and vitamin B12 are not part of this reaction.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: This is the reaction boundary. It does not include folate-dependent remethylation, the later conversion of methionine to SAMe, whole-cycle throughput, phosphatidylethanolamine methyltransferase, or acetylcholine formation. It also does not show that dietary zinc intake changes the reaction in people.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: BHMT transfers a methyl group from betaine to homocysteine, forming methionine and dimethylglycine, without folate or vitamin B12 in that reaction, and uses an active-site zinc ion to activate homocysteine.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Human crystal structures show that BHMT makes methionine from betaine and homocysteine and uses zinc to activate homocysteine. Mutating any of the three zinc-binding cysteines to alanine abolishes activity and sharply reduces zinc binding, and the same biochemical work states the products as methionine and dimethylglycine. A methyl-donor review states that methyl flow through this pathway does not depend on folate or vitamin B12. Together these sources identify the reaction and its metal. They do not test ordinary dietary control or human tissue flux.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: The enzyme evidence uses purified or recombinant human protein, not intact human metabolism. Loss of activity after removing zinc ligands does not show that dietary zinc usually limits the enzyme. The review statement that the pathway is independent of folate and vitamin B12 is not a new flux experiment. Quantitative claims in that review about choline deficiency and liver methionine were not re-checked in the primary animal papers.

evidence_considered.label: Evans et al. (2002)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Human BHMT structures show methionine formation from betaine and homocysteine, with zinc activating homocysteine; oxidation that expels zinc rearranges the active site.

assessment.study: X-ray structures of human BHMT in an oxidised zinc-free form and a reduced zinc-bound form with a homocysteine-like bisubstrate analog.
assessment.population: Purified crystallised human BHMT; no cells, animals or human participants.
assessment.result: The enzyme forms methionine from betaine and homocysteine. Zinc activates homocysteine. The zinc-binding sequences sit at the ends of barrel strands, and a Cys217–Cys299 disulfide expels zinc.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Structures at 2.15 Å (zinc-free) and 2.05 Å (zinc-bound). No physiological effect size applies.
assessment.evidence_summary: Direct structural evidence for the human reaction and for catalytic zinc.
assessment.limitations: Static structures establish catalytic geometry, not in-vivo flux, dietary zinc responsiveness, or a clinical outcome.

evidence_considered.label: Breksa and Garrow (1999)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Replacing any of Cys217, Cys299 or Cys300 with alanine abolished human BHMT activity and reduced zinc binding. The reaction produces methionine and dimethylglycine from betaine and homocysteine.

assessment.study: Site-directed mutagenesis of recombinant human liver BHMT, with activity and zinc-binding measurements.
assessment.population: Recombinant human BHMT protein expressed in bacteria; no human participants.
assessment.result: Cys217, Cys299 and Cys300 were identified as zinc ligands. Mutation of any one to alanine caused complete loss of activity and a significant reduction in zinc binding. The catalysed transfer is from betaine to homocysteine, yielding dimethylglycine and methionine.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Complete loss of activity for each alanine substitution. No human effect size applies.
assessment.evidence_summary: Direct evidence that catalytic activity of human BHMT depends on those zinc ligands, and a clear statement of the reaction products.
assessment.limitations: Bacterial expression and purified-protein assays do not show that dietary zinc limits BHMT in human tissues.

evidence_considered.label: Obeid (2013)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Methyl-group flow through BHMT does not depend on folate or vitamin B12, although the pathway is most active in liver and kidney and talks to the folate route.

assessment.study: Narrative review of methyl-donor deficiency with emphasis on the BHMT pathway.
assessment.population: Review of human and animal methyl-donor studies; not a new experiment.
assessment.result: BHMT transfers a methyl group from betaine to homocysteine. The review states that methyl flow through this pathway is not dependent on folate or vitamin B12, while several cross-talk mechanisms exist. BHMT is particularly active in liver and kidney.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No new effect size. The review cites other studies for homocysteine and metabolite changes.
assessment.evidence_summary: Explicit pathway-level statement that folate and vitamin B12 are not required for methyl flow through BHMT.
assessment.limitations: A review cannot replace a flux assay. Some quantitative deficiency claims are attributed to other papers and were not re-adjudicated here.

evidence_dependency: Obeid (2013) is also primary evidence in PM2-F2 for choline oxidation. That reuse is one review, not a second experiment.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Choline oxidation supplies betaine and is not the BHMT reaction
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Choline can be oxidised to betaine aldehyde and then to betaine. That sequence can supply the BHMT substrate. It is not the methyl transfer that BHMT carries out, and betaine is not turned back into choline.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Choline is a precursor of the substrate, not a cofactor or substrate of BHMT. Acetylcholine formation and phosphatidylethanolamine methylation use choline or SAMe in other reactions.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Irreversible oxidation of choline to betaine is an upstream supply route for the BHMT substrate and is not itself the BHMT reaction.
scientific_findings.synthesis: A methyl-donor review states that betaine is produced by irreversible oxidation of choline through choline dehydrogenase and betaine-aldehyde dehydrogenase, and that BHMT then uses betaine. A choline-dehydrogenase review places the human enzyme in the inner mitochondrial membrane, mainly in kidney and liver, and separates the first oxidation to betaine aldehyde from the second oxidation to betaine. Betaine then donates a methyl group in the homocysteine-to-methionine reaction. The two steps are supply, not the BHMT reaction.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Purified, stable human choline dehydrogenase has been difficult to obtain, so some catalytic detail is inferred from related enzymes and from tissue activity rather than from a complete human kinetic characterisation. The reviews do not show that raising choline intake increases BHMT flux in people.

evidence_considered.label: Obeid (2013)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Betaine can be formed by irreversible oxidation of choline via choline dehydrogenase and betaine-aldehyde dehydrogenase, and BHMT then uses that betaine to remethylate homocysteine.

assessment.study: Narrative review of methyl-donor metabolism centred on BHMT.
assessment.population: Review of human and animal evidence; not a new enzyme assay.
assessment.result: The review states the two-enzyme oxidation of choline to betaine and the subsequent BHMT reaction. It treats the oxidation as irreversible.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No new effect size for the oxidation steps.
assessment.evidence_summary: Pathway-level evidence that choline oxidation supplies betaine upstream of BHMT.
assessment.limitations: Review synthesis, not a direct demonstration of human choline dehydrogenase kinetics or of dietary choline increasing BHMT flux.

evidence_considered.label: Salvi and Gadda (2013)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Human choline dehydrogenase oxidises choline to betaine aldehyde, and betaine-aldehyde dehydrogenase completes formation of betaine, which can donate a methyl group to homocysteine.

assessment.study: Review of human choline dehydrogenase localisation, physiological role and biochemical characterisation.
assessment.population: Review of human tissue activity and comparative biochemistry; not a dietary trial.
assessment.result: The enzyme sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane and is found mainly in kidney and liver. It oxidises choline to betaine aldehyde. A second enzyme, betaine-aldehyde dehydrogenase, oxidises that aldehyde to betaine. Betaine is described as a methyl donor for methionine formation from homocysteine. Purified active human enzyme has been difficult to obtain.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Tissue activity was reported mainly in kidney, with about six-fold lower activity in liver. No dietary dose-response was measured.
assessment.evidence_summary: Enzyme-level support for the two-step oxidation that supplies betaine.
assessment.limitations: Incomplete purification of human choline dehydrogenase limits kinetic detail. Localisation and pathway role do not show that dietary choline changes BHMT flux.

evidence_dependency: Obeid (2013) is also primary evidence in PM2-F1 for folate- and vitamin B12-independence of BHMT. That reuse is one review, not a second experiment.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Plasma homocysteine is not tissue BHMT flux
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Betaine supplements lower plasma homocysteine, and severe choline depletion can raise it after a methionine load. The same blood measurement also falls after vitamin B12 and fish oil, which are not BHMT substrates. The number is not the enzyme's rate in tissue and is not a clinical benefit.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: A homocysteine change can be consistent with this route and still fail to prove it. Read supplement and depletion studies as blood results unless enzyme activity or traced methyl flux was measured.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Changes in plasma homocysteine after betaine supplementation, choline depletion, or vitamin B12 and fish-oil treatment do not measure tissue BHMT flux and do not establish a clinical benefit of this reaction.
scientific_findings.synthesis: In healthy adults, six weeks of supplemental betaine lowered fasting plasma homocysteine relative to placebo, and it also blunted the rise after a methionine load. The authors inferred faster betaine-dependent remethylation, but they did not measure BHMT activity, tissue methionine formation or dimethylglycine flux. In mice, choline deficiency doubled post-load plasma homocysteine, and a small male pilot found a higher post-load value after clinical choline depletion, yet mouse liver betaine did not fall and BHMT was not assayed. A separate trial lowered plasma homocysteine with vitamin B12, fish oil or both, without betaine. The biomarker is therefore real, shared and non-specific.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: The betaine trial selected healthy adults with relatively high homocysteine still in a broad reference range. The human choline study was a pilot of eight men. None of the three studies measured tissue BHMT flux, attention or cognition.

evidence_considered.label: Olthof et al. (2003)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: supplemental-formulation
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Daily betaine at 1.5, 3 and 6 g lowered fasting plasma homocysteine by about 12%, 15% and 20% versus placebo after six weeks, without a measurement of tissue BHMT flux.

assessment.study: Randomised, placebo-controlled trial of anhydrous betaine for six weeks, with methionine-load tests.
assessment.population: Four groups of 19 healthy adults selected for higher plasma homocysteine within a broad reference range.
assessment.result: Fasting plasma homocysteine after 1.5, 3 and 6 g/day was about 12%, 15% and 20% lower than placebo. The post-load rise was also smaller. The discussion infers increased betaine-dependent remethylation.
assessment.effect_magnitude: About 12% (P < 0.01), 15% (P < 0.002) and 20% (P < 0.0001) lower fasting homocysteine than placebo at six weeks for 1.5, 3 and 6 g/day.
assessment.evidence_summary: Direct human evidence that supplemental betaine lowers plasma homocysteine. The endpoint is a circulating metabolite, not enzyme flux.
assessment.limitations: No BHMT activity, tissue methionine flux, dimethylglycine production rate, or clinical symptom outcome was measured.

evidence_considered.label: da Costa et al. (2005)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: dietary
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Choline deficiency raised post-methionine-load plasma homocysteine in mice and in a small human pilot, but did not measure BHMT activity, and mouse liver betaine did not fall.

assessment.study: Three-week mouse diets with 0, 10 or 35 mmol choline/kg, plus a depletion-repletion pilot in men, each with an oral methionine load.
assessment.population: Male C57BL/6J mice and eight healthy men aged 20–46 years.
assessment.result: Two hours after the load, choline-deficient mice had about twice the plasma homocysteine of choline-fed mice. Fasting values did not differ. Four hours after the load, clinically choline-depleted men had plasma homocysteine about 35% higher than when not depleted. Hepatic betaine in the mice was not significantly lower.
assessment.effect_magnitude: About twofold higher post-load homocysteine in deficient mice. About 35% higher post-load homocysteine in depleted men. Mouse liver betaine 1.3 ± 0.3 versus 1.1 ± 0.3 nmol/mg protein.
assessment.evidence_summary: Dietary choline depletion can change post-load plasma homocysteine. It does not isolate BHMT flux, and the mouse betaine pool was not shown to fall.
assessment.limitations: Human sample of eight men, clinical depletion rather than ordinary intake, and no enzyme or tracer measurement.

evidence_considered.label: Huang et al. (2015)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: supplemental-formulation
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Vitamin B12, fish oil and their combination lowered plasma homocysteine without any betaine intervention, so the biomarker is not specific to BHMT.

assessment.study: Randomised trial of vitamin B12, fish oil, or both, with plasma homocysteine as an endpoint.
assessment.population: Thirty-eight participants randomised to three groups.
assessment.result: The repository abstract reports plasma homocysteine reductions of about 22% with vitamin B12, 19% with fish oil, and 39% with the combination. Betaine and BHMT were not the interventions.
assessment.effect_magnitude: About 22%, 19% and 39% lower plasma homocysteine in the three arms.
assessment.evidence_summary: Shows that plasma homocysteine can fall through inputs that are not the BHMT substrate.
assessment.limitations: The attached abstract does not report BHMT activity, betaine status or a clinical neurological outcome. Design detail beyond the abstract was not re-extracted.

scientific_findings.finding_label: ADHD diet reviews do not test BHMT
scientific_findings.finding_summary: The attached attention reviews discuss dietary patterns, supplements and choline in neurodevelopment. They do not measure BHMT or test betaine as a treatment for attention.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: An attention relationship can remain a framework bridge. It should not be read as evidence that this remethylation route changes focus.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: The repository ADHD diet review and choline neurodevelopment review do not directly demonstrate that BHMT-dependent remethylation changes Focus / Attention Stability.
scientific_findings.synthesis: One review surveys sugar restriction, additive-free diets, elimination diets, fatty acids, iron and zinc in ADHD. Another surveys choline status in autism, ADHD and dyslexia. Neither assigns an attention outcome to BHMT activity or to betaine supplementation. The biochemical reaction can be true while this phenome link stays untested.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: This is a gap in the attached reviews, not proof that no attention relationship exists. The sources are narrative reviews and mix many dietary exposures.

evidence_considered.label: Millichap and Yee (2012)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Reviews dietary approaches to ADHD symptoms, including fatty acids, iron and zinc, and does not test BHMT or betaine supplementation.

assessment.study: Narrative clinical review of diet as a treatment factor in ADHD.
assessment.population: Children with ADHD in the reviewed literature; not a BHMT cohort.
assessment.result: Discusses restriction diets, fatty-acid supplements, iron, zinc and dietary pattern. No betaine dose, BHMT assay or homocysteine remethylation endpoint is the basis of the conclusions.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No BHMT or betaine effect size is reported.
assessment.evidence_summary: Shows why an ADHD diet review cannot be used as direct evidence for this reaction.
assessment.limitations: Narrative review spanning many exposures and outcomes. Not a mechanism test.

evidence_considered.label: Derbyshire and Maes (2023)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Reviews choline in autism, ADHD and dyslexia, without measuring BHMT activity or betaine-dependent remethylation.

assessment.study: Narrative review of choline and neurodevelopmental disorders.
assessment.population: Pregnancy, children with autism, and people with ADHD or dyslexia in the reviewed literature.
assessment.result: Low choline intake or altered choline status is discussed for those groups. The review does not test BHMT, betaine supplementation or tissue remethylation flux against attention scores.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No BHMT effect size is reported.
assessment.evidence_summary: Choline neurodevelopment context is not a BHMT outcome study.
assessment.limitations: Narrative review. Choline has membrane and neurotransmitter roles outside this reaction.

evidence_dependency: Derbyshire and Maes (2023) is also primary evidence in PM2-F4. That reuse is one review, not independent replication.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Homocysteine and choline reviews do not test cognitive clarity
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Betaine can lower plasma homocysteine, and choline is discussed in neurodevelopment. Neither result shows that BHMT activity changes cognitive clarity.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Cognitive clarity stays an indirect bridge. Do not treat a homocysteine change, or a choline review, as a clarity outcome for this PM.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Plasma homocysteine lowering after betaine, and narrative choline reviews, do not directly demonstrate that BHMT-dependent remethylation changes Cognitive Clarity.
scientific_findings.synthesis: The betaine trial measured plasma homocysteine in healthy adults and did not measure cognition. The choline review discusses neurodevelopmental conditions rather than clarity as an outcome of this reaction. Both can sit near methyl-donor biology without testing the phenome claim.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Bounded to the attached sources. Absence of a clarity endpoint in these papers is not a universal negative finding.

evidence_considered.label: Olthof et al. (2003)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: supplemental-formulation
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Lowers plasma homocysteine in healthy adults and does not measure cognitive clarity or BHMT flux.

assessment.study: Six-week randomised betaine supplementation trial with methionine loads.
assessment.population: Healthy adults in four groups of 19.
assessment.result: Fasting and post-load plasma homocysteine fell relative to placebo. No cognitive clarity scale was used.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Fasting homocysteine about 12%, 15% and 20% lower than placebo at 1.5, 3 and 6 g/day. No cognitive effect size exists in the study.
assessment.evidence_summary: Human homocysteine evidence without a clarity endpoint.
assessment.limitations: Healthy adults, circulating endpoint, no cognitive measurement.

evidence_considered.label: Derbyshire and Maes (2023)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Discusses choline and neurodevelopment, not BHMT-dependent cognitive clarity.

assessment.study: Narrative review of choline in autism, ADHD and dyslexia.
assessment.population: Developmental cohorts in the reviewed literature.
assessment.result: Considers choline status and neurodevelopmental conditions. It does not isolate BHMT or measure cognitive clarity as a remethylation outcome.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No BHMT or clarity effect size for this reaction is reported.
assessment.evidence_summary: Neurodevelopment review, not a test of this PM against cognitive clarity.
assessment.limitations: Narrative review with several choline roles outside BHMT.

evidence_dependency: Olthof et al. (2003) is also primary evidence in PM2-IC1. Derbyshire and Maes (2023) is also primary evidence in PM2-F3. Neither reuse is a second study.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Betaine availability and choline supply can constrain remethylation reserve
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Controlled human choline depletion lowered plasma betaine and reduced challenged remethylation reserve in participants who developed clinical depletion. In rats, choline deprivation lowered hepatic betaine and the phenotype was suppressed by choline or betaine; specific BHMT inhibition independently produced the expected pathway failure.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Together with the established BHMT reaction, these intervention, pool, rescue and specific-inhibition edges support a constraint on betaine-dependent remethylation capacity. They do not directly measure human tissue BHMT flux or show a benefit from intake above adequacy.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Inadequate betaine availability, including from conditional failure of choline provision, can constrain BHMT-dependent homocysteine remethylation capacity.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Da Costa et al. fed eight healthy men a 550 mg/day choline baseline diet followed by 50 mg/day for up to 42 days. Plasma choline and betaine fell by about 30% and 47% while folate remained adequate. In the four participants who developed hepatic steatosis, post-load homocysteine was 5.2 µmol/L higher and returned to the baseline response after repletion. In rats under low-methionine conditions, Setoue et al. found that choline deprivation markedly lowered hepatic betaine and raised plasma homocysteine, while either choline or betaine restored hepatic betaine and suppressed the increase. Strakova et al. independently showed that a specific BHMT inhibitor reduced liver BHMT activity by more than 90%, raised plasma homocysteine two- to five-fold and lowered liver SAM by more than 40%. Human BHMT biochemistry establishes betaine as the methyl donor. These edges form a supported constraint chain.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: The human study was a pilot in eight men, with the challenged response confined to four clinically depleted participants. The pool-rescue and specific-inhibition evidence is from rat liver, and neither study measured isotope-resolved human BHMT flux. Choline partitioning, endogenous synthesis and methionine/folate state modify the provision route. The chain supports capacity constraint under demonstrated depletion, not universal limitation on ordinary diets, benefit from supplementation above adequacy, or a cognitive outcome.

evidence_considered.label: da Costa et al. (2005)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: dietary
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Controlled choline depletion lowered plasma betaine and reduced post-methionine-load homocysteine-handling reserve in the participants who developed clinical depletion; both the phenotype and challenge response reversed with repletion.

assessment.study: Controlled depletion–repletion pilot with a methionine-load challenge.
assessment.population: Eight healthy men aged 20–46 years; four developed hepatic steatosis during depletion.
assessment.result: Plasma choline and betaine fell about 30% and 47% in the full group. In the four clinically depleted men, post-load homocysteine increased by 5.2 µmol/L (95% CI 1.2–9.1; P = 0.025) relative to the 550 mg/day baseline phase and returned to the baseline response after repletion. Folate did not fall.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Betaine fell from 66 ± 7 to 35 ± 2 nmol/mL in all eight men; clinically depleted participants had a 5.2 µmol/L greater post-load homocysteine response.
assessment.evidence_summary: Human intervention evidence linking choline inadequacy, lower betaine availability and reduced remethylation reserve under challenge.
assessment.limitations: Small male-only pilot, severe controlled depletion, shared circulating endpoint, and no direct tissue or isotope-resolved BHMT flux.

evidence_considered.label: Evans et al. (2002)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Human BHMT structures establish the betaine-to-homocysteine methyl transfer that links betaine availability to the challenged remethylation response.

assessment.study: X-ray structural analysis of human BHMT.
assessment.population: Purified human BHMT; no participants.
assessment.result: BHMT transfers a methyl group from betaine to homocysteine to form methionine and dimethylglycine.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No human intervention effect size.
assessment.evidence_summary: Provides reaction-specific attribution for the donor-pool intervention chain.
assessment.limitations: Purified-enzyme evidence does not itself establish dietary constraint.

evidence_considered.label: Setoue et al. (2008)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: dietary
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Under low-methionine conditions, choline deprivation depleted hepatic betaine and raised plasma homocysteine; either choline or betaine suppressed the phenotype.

assessment.study: Controlled rat feeding experiments varying choline, methionine context and lipotrope rescue.
assessment.population: Male Wistar rats fed casein- or soybean-protein-based diets.
assessment.result: On the choline-deprived soybean-protein diet, hepatic betaine fell from about 3.65 to 0.13 µmol/g and plasma homocysteine rose from about 12.5 to 33.5 µmol/L. Choline or betaine supplementation restored hepatic betaine to about 9.81 or 13.3 µmol/g and lowered plasma homocysteine to about 7.3 or 7.7 µmol/L. Ex-vivo BHMT activity did not decline.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Approximately 96% lower hepatic betaine with deprivation; rescue restored the pool above control and suppressed hyperhomocysteinaemia.
assessment.evidence_summary: Pool depletion and rescue connect conditional choline inadequacy to loss of substrate-supported remethylation capacity rather than loss of BHMT protein competence.
assessment.limitations: Rat liver model under low-methionine conditions; homocysteine removal also involved transsulfuration, and no in-vivo isotope-resolved BHMT flux was measured.

evidence_considered.label: Strakova et al. (2011)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: isolated-substance
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Specific pharmacological BHMT inhibition produced the pathway direction expected when BHMT-dependent capacity fails.

assessment.study: Rat feeding study using the potent and specific BHMT inhibitor S-(δ-carboxybutyl)-L-homocysteine for 3 or 14 days across adequate, cysteine-free and methionine-deficient diets.
assessment.population: Rats; no human participants.
assessment.result: The inhibitor reduced liver BHMT activity by more than 90%, increased plasma homocysteine two- to five-fold and lowered hepatic SAM by more than 40% across dietary conditions.
assessment.effect_magnitude: >90% lower BHMT activity; 2–5-fold higher plasma homocysteine; >40% lower liver SAM.
assessment.evidence_summary: Specific perturbation confirms that impaired BHMT capacity can generate the observed remethylation and methylation-state direction.
assessment.limitations: Pharmacological inhibition in rats does not quantify the effect of ordinary human betaine or choline intake.

evidence_dependency: Da Costa et al. (2005) is also used in PM2-IC1. PM2-IC1 establishes that plasma homocysteine alone is non-specific; PM2-F5 relies on the combined depletion, pool, challenge, repletion and reaction chain rather than treating that biomarker alone as BHMT flux.
Evans et al. (2002) is also primary evidence in PM2-F1. Its reuse in PM2-F5 supplies the same reaction-specific link and is not independent replication.

decisions.applicability_proposition: Inadequacy of the folate donor route can indirectly constrain BHMT-dependent remethylation capacity by changing demand on the betaine route or the betaine-to-DMG state.
established_links: BHMT transfers a methyl group from betaine to homocysteine and does not use folate or vitamin B12 in that reaction (PM2-F1).
The flow of methyl groups through BHMT is not dependent on folate or vitamin B12 (PM2-F1).
The canonical KC review admits folate as a methyl-group input into the shared pool.
In folate-deprived rats, hepatic betaine fell, dimethylglycine rose, and betaine supplementation increased hepatic BHMT activity but only partly corrected hyperhomocysteinaemia.
inferred_links: The higher hepatic dimethylglycine concentration inhibited BHMT enough in vivo to make folate inadequacy a BHMT-capacity constraint.
The rat interaction generalises to human BHMT capacity under nutritionally relevant folate inadequacy.
decisions.rationale: Folate is not a BHMT reactant, so pathway proximity cannot establish this arm. The prior non-application decision was nevertheless too strong: rat evidence shows a material cross-route interaction through lower hepatic betaine, higher dimethylglycine and a limited response to betaine. Because in-vivo BHMT flux was inferred and the evidence is not human, indirect folate-to-PM2 applicability remains unresolved. decisions.rationale: User-approved KC1 mapping withdrawal on 2026-10-02 supersedes the prior established admission of BRS2-FM1-PM2-KCR-1. title: SAMe Synthesis
mission: Maintain methionine adenosyltransferase capacity to convert methionine and ATP into SAMe, sustaining the methyl-donor pool used by downstream methyltransferases.
summary: Methionine adenosyltransferase forms S-adenosylmethionine from methionine and ATP. Magnesium and potassium ions coordinate that ATP-dependent catalysis. This reaction supplies the methyl donor used by many later enzymes. Upstream methionine regeneration and later methyl-transfer reactions remain separate processes. Circulating SAMe and the SAM:SAH ratio describe pool balance rather than synthesis speed.

phenome_relationships.rationale: SAMe supplies methyl groups used by many downstream pathways relevant to neural function, but this is an inferred downstream bridge rather than evidence that MAT-dependent SAMe synthesis itself modulates Cognitive Clarity. The attached methylation review establishes SAMe's donor role, not a cognitive outcome or endogenous synthesis-flux effect {{cite:chiang_s-adenosylmethionine_1996}}. Circulating SAMe or SAM:SAH measurements cannot isolate MAT synthesis from utilisation and clearance {{cite:corrillero_bravo_analysis_2022}}. Direct relationship evidence remains a gap.

SAMe-dependent methylation is biologically relevant to downstream neurotransmitter and membrane chemistry, but the attached mood-disorder review concerns exogenous SAMe and combined folate/B12 treatment rather than endogenous MAT activity or SAMe synthesis flux {{cite:cicero_combined_2022}}. It therefore does not directly demonstrate that this PM modulates Emotional Regulation; the relationship remains an indirect framework bridge with a direct-evidence gap.
