title: Gut-Derived Inflammatory Signalling
mission: Limit gut-derived endotoxin spillover so barrier dysfunction does not drive systemic inflammatory load.
summary: The evidence supports gut-derived inflammatory load as a barrier-related process. Glutathione participates in oxidant-sensitive epithelial protection, but is not a universal barrier constraint. A defined prebiotic intervention changed permeability and circulating LPS in obese mice; this does not establish a generic fibre requirement or a human intake target.
dose_sensitivity: No human intake target is established. Experimental epithelial and obese-mouse effects must retain their exposure and endpoint boundaries.

evidence_qualification.label: Diet-Supported
evidence_qualification.rationale: A defined oligofructose exposure influenced permeability and plasma LPS in obese mice. This is bounded preclinical intervention evidence, not a human dietary requirement.
evidence_qualification.scope_note: KC1 upstream supply does not itself establish intervention responsiveness. A human protocol and principal route remain unestablished.

principal_route_selection.rationale: Preclinical influence does not establish which intervention group deserves principal prominence.
principal_route_selection.comparative_limitations: Comparative dominance and human implementation remain unestablished.

kc_applicability_adjudications.applicability_proposition: KC1 provides cysteine and glycine for glutathione used in oxidant-sensitive epithelial barrier protection. This resource connection is distinct from the downstream NF-κB response to gut-derived signals.
established_links: Cysteine and glycine are glutathione constituents; combined provision increased red-cell glutathione synthesis.
Glutathione/redox manipulations alter oxidant-induced epithelial paracellular permeability in Caco-2 cells.
inferred_links: Transfer from human red-cell precursor provision to intestinal epithelial provision.
Contribution of this experimentally supported barrier route to gut-derived endotoxin spillover in humans.
kc_applicability_adjudications.rationale: The supported chain qualifies as upstream resource supply at its stated experimental scope. It does not establish a general limiting constraint.

kc_applicability_adjudications.applicability_proposition: Precursor inadequacy limits barrier protection and increases endotoxin spillover in a specified context.
kc_applicability_adjudications.evidence_gap: Establish inadequate precursor provision, the relevant intestinal glutathione/redox consequence and increased endotoxin entry in a defined context, accounting for compensation. Salmonella-rat depletion did not establish this barrier limitation.
kc_applicability_adjudications.rationale: Permeability, bacterial translocation and circulating LPS are different endpoints. Endotoxin need not first reduce glutathione synthesis; the previous rationale reversed the proposed dependency.

kc_change_control_flags.proposition: Canonical KC1 constituent identity reconciled; cysteine and glycine admitted as supported upstream supply, while conditional spillover limitation remains unresolved.

scientific_findings.finding_summary: The gut lining normally keeps lipopolysaccharide out of the blood. Dietary change can alter that lining. Lipopolysaccharide that gets through activates Toll-like receptor 4 and is reviewed as a route to low-grade systemic inflammation.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: This is the exposure route. It is a review, not a measurement of how much lipopolysaccharide crosses after a fibre intake.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Metabolic endotoxemia is lipopolysaccharide reaching the blood after a change in the gut barrier, with downstream inflammatory signalling through Toll-like receptor 4.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Mohammad and Thiemermann review diet-linked metabolic endotoxemia. The gut epithelium normally limits lipopolysaccharide absorption. Structural change in that lining lets lipopolysaccharide into the bloodstream. Lipopolysaccharide then activates Toll-like receptor 4 and pro-inflammatory cytokines. The review suggests dietary interventions might reduce that inflammation. It does not test one.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: A narrative review of the route is not a human translocation-flux trial and not a fibre-dose result.

evidence_considered.label: Mohammad and Thiemermann (2021)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: narrative review of diet-linked endotoxemia
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Barrier change can raise plasma lipopolysaccharide, and that lipopolysaccharide activates Toll-like receptor 4.

assessment.study: Narrative review of metabolic endotoxemia, barrier change, and inflammatory signalling.
assessment.population: Animal and human literature. No new cohort.
assessment.result: Lipopolysaccharide that crosses a changed gut lining is reviewed as a contributor to low-grade systemic inflammation.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No single translocation rate or intake effect is pooled.
assessment.evidence_summary: Endotoxin spillover is a barrier-to-blood route, not a nutrient reaction.
assessment.limitations: The review does not measure translocation after fermentable fibre, and it does not test butyrate as a requirement.

connected_supportive_evidence.label: Cavaliere et al. (2022)

scientific_findings.finding_label: Glutathione supports oxidant-sensitive epithelial protection, with context-dependent barrier effects
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Glutathione prevented oxidant-induced permeability in epithelial cells, but depletion did not increase permeability or bacterial translocation in infected rats.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: KC1 provides cysteine and glycine for glutathione used in oxidant-sensitive epithelial barrier protection. This resource connection is distinct from the downstream NF-κB response to gut-derived signals.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Supported upstream resource supply is distinct from an established dietary constraint on endotoxin entry.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Precursor provision, epithelial permeability and infectious translocation measure different links. The chain supports bounded resource relevance; the negative depletion result prevents a universal glutathione-barrier constraint claim.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Supported upstream supply through glutathione-dependent epithelial redox protection, not an established dietary constraint on endotoxin spillover. Human precursor tracing measured red-cell glutathione after combined glycine and N-acetylcysteine; epithelial experiments measured oxidant-induced paracellular permeability. In Salmonella-infected rats, glutathione depletion did not increase permeability or bacterial translocation. Neither intestinal precursor inadequacy, individual constituent limitation, human LPS reduction nor benefit from additional intake is established.

title: Nrf2-Mediated Cellular Defence Regulation
mission: Regulate the expression of cellular defence genes in response to oxidative and electrophilic stress.
summary: Nrf2 is held by Keap1 until oxidative or electrophilic stress lets it reach defence genes. A three-day broccoli sprout homogenate raised phase II enzyme RNA in nasal cells of healthy adults. That is airway gene expression, not brain Nrf2, and sulforaphane is not a nutrient this regulation requires.
dose_sensitivity: No ordinary crucifer intake is set. The gene result is a three-day myrosinase-completed sprout homogenate. A four-week broccoli-sprout extract capsule did not raise Nrf2 target-gene expression in the lungs of people with COPD.

evidence_qualification.label: Diet-Supported
evidence_qualification.rationale: A prepared broccoli sprout homogenate changed nasal phase II enzyme RNA. That is conditional food-preparation influence on a defence-gene endpoint. It does not establish that diet is the principal route for this switch.

routes.intervention_effect: Three daily doses of a broccoli sprout homogenate, prepared with added daikon myrosinase, increased phase II enzyme RNA in nasal cells.
routes.context: Healthy nonsmoking adults. Nasal cells were sampled two hours after the third dose. Alfalfa sprout homogenate did not produce the increase.
routes.limitations: Nasal enzyme RNA is not Nrf2 protein, brain Nrf2 activation, or a cognitive result. The COPD capsule trial does not erase this food result, and this food result does not erase that null.

principal_route_selection.rationale: Sulforaphane is admitted separately as a Direct Regulatory Modulator in 3.1. The compound is the principal dietary lever. The preparation practice remains separately in 3.2 and is not jointly promoted or counted as another intervention supply. Lifestyle was not shown to change this switch.
principal_route_selection.comparative_limitations: The homogenate changed nasal enzyme RNA. It is not ordinary broccoli, not a capsule, and not brain Nrf2.

assessments.relevance: The practice raises phase II enzyme RNA, the defence-gene class this switch is about, in human nasal cells.
assessments.directness: Sulforaphane is the admitted regulatory modulator. The tested delivery was the homogenate, specified as an exposure limitation rather than the dietary input. The authors inferred Nrf2-linked induction from phase II enzyme RNA; they did not measure Nrf2 protein or nuclear translocation.
assessments.extent: Three daily doses in healthy nonsmoking adults, sampled in nasal cells. This is not brain Nrf2 activation, an ordinary broccoli serving, or the four-week sprout-extract capsules in COPD.

kc_applicability_adjudications.applicability_proposition: Vitamin C availability constrains the Nrf2 activation step on this page.
established_links: Verlaet lists vitamin C as a water-soluble non-enzymatic antioxidant, beside the antioxidant enzymes.
Houghton reports ascorbic acid as a weak inducer of NQO1 compared with sulforaphane, and treats ascorbate as a direct antioxidant used up in the reaction.
inferred_links: Antioxidant substrate sufficiency would have to be in place before Nrf2 could switch defence genes on.
kc_applicability_adjudications.rationale: General antioxidant status, and a weak comparison of inducer strength, do not show that vitamin C availability constrains this activation step. Public mapping is not published.

The human exposure changed phase II enzyme RNA in nasal cells. It does not show that ordinary repeated eating changes attention, and the sources do not compare repeated exposure with a single dose.
Nrf2-dependent detoxification and antioxidant gene programmes may intersect stress-buffering redox context; direct ADHD stress-outcome evidence remains limited.

dietary_input_traceability.evidence_limitation: Human target engagement varies by formulation, tissue and population. The positive study used a myrosinase-completed broccoli sprout homogenate for three days in healthy nonsmokers and measured nasal phase II enzyme RNA, not Nrf2 protein or nuclear translocation. Extract capsules did not increase lung target-gene expression in COPD. An ordinary broccoli meal, direct activation of Nrf2 in the human brain and clinical ADHD benefit remain unestablished. Sulforaphane is not an essential nutrient.

system_optimisation_practices.biological_role: Three daily doses of broccoli sprouts, blended with water and daikon sprouts and held at 37°C so myrosinase could finish forming sulforaphane, increased phase II enzyme RNA in nasal cells of healthy adults. The authors read that shared pattern as Nrf2-linked induction. They did not measure Nrf2 protein or its movement into the nucleus.

scientific_findings_intro: Keap1 holds Nrf2 until oxidative or electrophilic stress lets defence genes be transcribed. A three-day myrosinase-completed broccoli sprout homogenate raised phase II enzyme RNA in nasal cells. Extracted sulforaphane capsules did not raise that class of genes in COPD lung cells. Sulforaphane is not a nutrient this regulation requires.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Keap1 holds Nrf2 until stress lets defence genes be read
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Keap1 binds Nrf2 and keeps defence-gene transcription off. Electrophiles and oxidative stress release that hold. Keap1 also sends Nrf2 for disposal, and sulforaphane or oxidative stress slows that disposal. Turning the response up is not, by itself, the aim.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: This is the control step. It is not a nutrient requirement, and it is not evidence that more activity is always useful.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Keap1 represses Nrf2 until oxidative or electrophilic stress allows defence-gene transcription. Sulforaphane can slow Keap1-directed disposal of Nrf2 in cells. That is regulation, not a dietary requirement.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Itoh and colleagues identified Keap1 as the protein that binds Nrf2 and represses antioxidant-response-element activity. Electrophilic agents opposed that repression and let Nrf2 move toward the nucleus. Zhang and colleagues showed Keap1 is the adaptor that marks Nrf2 for disposal, and that oxidative stress or sulforaphane inhibits that marking. Neither paper is a dietary trial.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Both results are cell biology. They do not measure brain Nrf2, and they do not show that eating more of any nutrient improves this regulation.

evidence_considered.label: Itoh et al. (1999)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: transfected cells and electrophilic agents
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Keap1 binds the Neh2 domain of Nrf2 and represses antioxidant-response-element activity. Electrophiles oppose that repression.

assessment.study: Identification of Keap1 as the repressor of Nrf2, with tests of electrophilic agents in cells.
assessment.population: Transfected cell lines. No human cohort.
assessment.result: Keap1 holds Nrf2 back, and electrophiles release that hold so defence genes can be transcribed.
assessment.effect_magnitude: The paper reports repression and its release. It does not give a human fold change.
assessment.evidence_summary: Defence-gene transcription is a regulated response to oxidative and electrophilic stress.
assessment.limitations: Cell identification of the sensor is not a food result and not a brain measurement.

evidence_considered.label: Zhang et al. (2004)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: cells exposed to oxidative stress or sulforaphane
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Keap1 marks Nrf2 for disposal. Oxidative stress and sulforaphane inhibit that marking. A cysteine-151 mutant of Keap1 resists that inhibition.

assessment.study: Cell and biochemical tests of Keap1 as the adaptor that marks Nrf2 for disposal.
assessment.population: Cultured cells. No human dietary cohort.
assessment.result: Stress or sulforaphane slows disposal of Nrf2. Changing cysteine 151 of Keap1 blocks that effect.
assessment.effect_magnitude: The paper reports inhibition of ubiquitination, not a dietary dose.
assessment.evidence_summary: Sulforaphane acts on the Keap1 sensor in cells. It is not a nutrient the regulation requires.
assessment.limitations: Cell exposure to sulforaphane is not the sprout homogenate and not brain Nrf2.

scientific_findings.finding_label: A prepared sprout homogenate raised airway defence-gene RNA
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Healthy nonsmokers drank a broccoli sprout homogenate, finished with daikon myrosinase, once a day for three days. Phase II enzyme RNA rose in nasal cells. Alfalfa did not do this. Capsules of extracted sulforaphane for four weeks did not raise Nrf2 target genes in COPD lung cells.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: The homogenate is a preparation that changed an airway readout of this gene programme. It is not a nutrient requirement, not brain Nrf2, and not evidence that a capsule does the same thing.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: A myrosinase-completed broccoli sprout homogenate raised phase II enzyme RNA in nasal cells of healthy adults. Extracted sulforaphane capsules did not raise Nrf2 target-gene expression in COPD lung cells.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Riedl, Saxon and Diaz-Sanchez gave healthy nonsmokers a broccoli sprout homogenate blended with daikon sprouts and held at 37°C, once a day for three days. Nasal phase II enzyme RNA rose with dose. Alfalfa sprout homogenate did not. Wise and colleagues gave people with COPD 25 or 150 micromoles of extracted sulforaphane, or placebo, for four weeks. Nrf2 target-gene expression in alveolar macrophages and bronchial epithelium did not rise, and inflammation and lung function did not change.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Nasal RNA after three days is not brain Nrf2. The capsule null is a different preparation in COPD, so it does not cancel the homogenate result, and the homogenate result does not make capsules work.

evidence_considered.label: Riedl, Saxon and Diaz-Sanchez (2009)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: myrosinase-completed broccoli sprout homogenate
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Nasal phase II enzyme RNA rose with dose after three days of the homogenate. Alfalfa homogenate did not do this.

assessment.study: Placebo-style food comparison in healthy nonsmokers. Broccoli sprout homogenate versus alfalfa sprout homogenate, once daily for three days.
assessment.population: Healthy nonsmoking adults. Nasal cells sampled after the third dose.
assessment.result: Phase II enzyme RNA in nasal cells rose with the broccoli sprout dose and did not rise with alfalfa.
assessment.effect_magnitude: The rise was dose-related. Nrf2 protein was not measured, so no Nrf2 fold change is available.
assessment.evidence_summary: A defined sprout preparation can raise airway defence-gene RNA.
assessment.limitations: Airway RNA is not brain Nrf2, not an ordinary broccoli serving, and not a clinical outcome.

evidence_considered.label: Wise et al. (2016)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: capsules of sulforaphane extracted from broccoli sprouts
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Four weeks of 25 or 150 micromoles of extracted sulforaphane did not raise Nrf2 target genes in COPD lung cells.

assessment.study: Randomised comparison of two sulforaphane capsule doses with placebo for four weeks.
assessment.population: People with COPD.
assessment.result: Nrf2 target-gene expression in alveolar macrophages and bronchial epithelium did not rise. Inflammation markers and lung function did not differ.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No rise in the measured target genes at either 25 or 150 micromoles a day.
assessment.evidence_summary: Extracted sulforaphane capsules did not reproduce the homogenate gene result.
assessment.limitations: COPD lung cells are not healthy nasal cells, and capsules are not the myrosinase-completed homogenate.

evidence_gaps.title: Other phytochemicals cannot inherit the sprout-formulation result
evidence_gaps.establishes: A defined sprout preparation increased selected airway defence-gene transcripts; the COPD trial supplied relevant null evidence.
evidence_gaps.cannot_establish: These observations do not establish quercetin, catechin or ellagitannin food-level engagement of the same Nrf2 operation.
evidence_gaps.missing_link: These observations do not establish quercetin, catechin or ellagitannin food-level engagement of the same Nrf2 operation.
evidence_gaps.required_evidence: Compound- and formulation-specific dietary exposure plus operation engagement; distinguish isolated cell concentrations from achievable tissue exposure.
evidence_gaps.affected_relationship: Other phytochemicals cannot inherit the sprout-formulation result

title: ROS Generation vs Clearance Balance
mission: Balance reactive oxygen species production and clearance so net oxidative pressure stays within tolerable limits.
summary: Cells generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) during ordinary immune and metabolic activity, and enzymatic clearance uses selenium, zinc, copper, and manganese. Net oxidative pressure is the balance of generation and clearance, not the level of one marker. When generation outruns clearance, oxidative damage accumulates across membranes, proteins, and mitochondria. High-heat cooking can add advanced glycation end products that raise this pressure.
dose_sensitivity: Not established. Selenium and copper restore clearance-enzyme activity when status is low. Extra intake when status is adequate is not shown.

scientific_findings_intro: Net oxidative pressure is the balance of reactive-oxygen generation and enzymatic clearance. Superoxide dismutase, catalase and glutathione peroxidase do that clearance. Selenium and copper are the dietary provision routes. Manganese supplies MnSOD catalytic capacity; zinc and glutathione participate in these reactions, but this manganese evidence does not establish their dietary supply relationships. Extra intake when status is adequate is not established.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Three enzymes clear superoxide and hydrogen peroxide
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide. Catalase and glutathione peroxidase convert hydrogen peroxide to water. Copper-zinc superoxide dismutase holds copper and zinc. Mitochondrial superoxide dismutase holds manganese. Glutathione peroxidase is a selenoprotein and uses glutathione.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Enzyme metals and the peroxidase thiol are biochemical participants. They are not, by themselves, proof that eating more of them changes the balance.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Mammalian cells clear superoxide and hydrogen peroxide with superoxide dismutase, catalase and glutathione peroxidase. Copper, zinc, manganese, selenium and glutathione belong to those enzymes. That membership is not an intake result.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Weydert and Cullen describe the three primary antioxidant enzymes, the copper-zinc and manganese superoxide dismutases, catalase, and glutathione peroxidase as a selenoprotein that requires glutathione. That places the metals and glutathione in the clearance reactions. It does not test dietary intake.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: A methods review states the enzyme chemistry. It does not show that raising intake of these participants changes net oxidative pressure.

evidence_considered.label: Weydert and Cullen (2010)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: isolated-substance
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Superoxide dismutase, catalase and glutathione peroxidase are the three primary clearance enzymes. Copper-zinc and manganese forms of superoxide dismutase are named, and glutathione peroxidase requires glutathione and is a selenoprotein.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Glutathione is the thiol used in peroxidase clearance
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Glutathione is the thiol used when glutathione peroxidase clears peroxides. It is made in the body. It is not a dietary glutathione target.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: The enzyme uses glutathione that the cell has already made. That does not show that oral glutathione sets clearance rate.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Glutathione participates in peroxidase clearance of peroxides. That role is biochemical. It is not evidence for eating glutathione.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Weydert and Cullen state that glutathione peroxidase requires reduced glutathione to remove hydrogen peroxide. Glutathione on this page stays a biochemical participant.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: The source describes the enzyme requirement. It does not test dietary glutathione.
evidence_dependency: Weydert and Cullen (2010) is reused from PM4-F1 to describe the glutathione requirement of peroxidase; it is not independent replication or dietary-response evidence.

evidence_considered.label: Weydert and Cullen (2010)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: isolated-substance
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Glutathione peroxidase requires reduced glutathione. The paper does not test eating glutathione.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Selenium intake restores glutathione peroxidase up to a plateau
scientific_findings.finding_summary: In adults eating very little selenium, plasma glutathione peroxidase activity rose with selenomethionine and levelled off at a total intake of about 35 micrograms a day. More selenium did not raise that enzyme further.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Selenium is required for glutathione peroxidase when status is low. Extra selenium after the enzyme has levelled off is not shown to improve this balance.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Dietary selenium restores plasma glutathione peroxidase activity in selenium-deficient adults up to a plateau near 35 micrograms a day. Intake above that plateau did not raise the enzyme further.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Xia and colleagues studied healthy Chinese adults whose usual diet supplied about 14 micrograms of selenium a day. Plasma glutathione peroxidase activity was optimised by a total intake of about 35 micrograms a day. Selenoprotein P needed more, about 49 micrograms a day. The trial measured those biomarkers, not net oxidative pressure and not a clinical outcome.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: The result is repletion of a low-selenium diet. It is not evidence that extra selenium helps when glutathione peroxidase is already fully expressed.

evidence_considered.label: Xia et al. (2010)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: isolated-substance
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Plasma glutathione peroxidase activity in selenium-deficient adults levelled off at about 35 micrograms of selenium a day. Higher doses did not raise it further.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Copper repletion raises red-cell superoxide dismutase when copper is low
scientific_findings.finding_summary: In infants recovering from malnutrition with marginal copper intake, copper supplementation raised red-cell superoxide dismutase together with plasma copper.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Copper is required for that enzyme when copper status is low. The study does not show a benefit from extra copper when status is already adequate, and it is not an adult balance trial.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Copper repletion raised erythrocyte superoxide dismutase in infants with marginal copper status. Adding copper to the assay tube did not raise the enzyme, so the change tracked copper nutrition rather than copper in the test.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Uauy and colleagues studied 17 infants recovering from malnutrition. After copper supplementation, plasma copper, ceruloplasmin and red-cell superoxide dismutase rose, and the enzyme correlated with plasma copper. Copper added in the assay did not change the activity. The setting is infant malnutrition, not ordinary adult intake.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Marginal copper in infants is not evidence that more copper improves reactive-oxygen balance in people who are already replete.

evidence_considered.exposure_context: isolated-substance
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Red-cell superoxide dismutase rose after copper supplementation in infants with marginal copper status and correlated with plasma copper.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Dietary manganese depletion lowers MnSOD activity in selected rat tissues
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Reducing dietary manganese lowered mitochondrial manganese-superoxide-dismutase activity in heart and kidney in a controlled rat feeding experiment.
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Dietary supply affected the activity of a defined ROS-clearance enzyme in a tissue-dependent animal experiment.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Supports a Type A manganese capacity relationship alongside curated human SOD2 cofactor dependence, without defining a human optimisation dose.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Paynter tested six dietary manganese concentrations for ten weeks in weanling male rats. Heart and kidney MnSOD activity fell at lower manganese supply. Effects differed by tissue and time; Cu-containing SOD and glutathione peroxidase did not significantly change in the examined tissues.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Human SOD2 requires manganese; dietary depletion experiments measured lower heart and kidney MnSOD activity in rats. This establishes a bounded enzyme-capacity dependency, not a human dose recommendation, universal tissue response, measured net ROS balance or benefit above adequate intake. Publisher abstract and bibliographic identity retrieved; full-text assay methods and group sample sizes remain unextracted, so numerical SEC is not assigned.

assessment.evidence_summary: Direct dietary supply-to-enzyme activity evidence in rats, not a generic oxidative biomarker.

scientific_findings.finding_summary: In a rat dietary-iron restriction experiment, kidney catalase activity was lower at the lowest intake, while many hepatic enzyme activities remained largely unaffected.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Iron supplies haem-bound catalytic capacity for catalase-mediated hydrogen-peroxide clearance; this does not imply that extra iron improves net redox balance.

title: Lipid Peroxidation Control
mission: Protect membrane fats from oxidative damage so vulnerable polyunsaturated fatty acids remain intact.
summary: Peroxyl radicals can keep oxidising polyunsaturated fats in membranes. Vitamin E is the main lipophilic antioxidant that breaks that chain. That role is the vitamin function of protecting those fats. Extra vitamin E was not shown to lower peroxidation, and a long trial found more prostate cancers with 400 IU a day.
dose_sensitivity: No intake was shown to lower membrane peroxidation. In a large prevention trial, 400 IU of vitamin E a day was associated with more prostate cancers than placebo.

dietary_input_traceability.evidence_limitation: Vitamin E breaks peroxyl-radical chains in membranes. That chemistry does not show that extra vitamin E lowers peroxidation in people. A prevention trial found more prostate cancers with 400 IU a day.

scientific_findings_intro: Vitamin E breaks peroxyl-radical chains in membranes and is placed there to protect polyunsaturated fats. Extra vitamin E was not shown to lower peroxidation. A long trial found more prostate cancers with 400 IU a day.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Vitamin E breaks peroxyl-radical chains in membranes
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Vitamin E is the main lipophilic antioxidant that stops peroxyl radicals from continuing to oxidise polyunsaturated fats. It does that job efficiently for peroxyl radicals, not for every oxidant. The vitamin function is protection of those fats in membranes.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: This is why vitamin E belongs to membrane peroxidation. It is not a trial of extra vitamin E, and lutein is not this antioxidant.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Vitamin E interrupts lipid peroxidation by scavenging peroxyl radicals in the lipid phase. Its vitamin function is protection of polyunsaturated fats in membranes.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Niki reviews the kinetic and in vivo evidence that vitamin E is the principal lipophilic peroxyl-radical scavenger and that it inhibits lipid peroxidation by breaking chain propagation. The same review states that vitamin E is not an efficient scavenger of hydroxyl, alkoxyl, nitrogen dioxide, or thiyl radicals in vivo. Traber and Atkinson argue that the vitamin function of alpha-tocopherol is that peroxyl-radical scavenging, which maintains polyunsaturated fats in membranes.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: These are mechanistic reviews. They do not test a vitamin E dose against membrane peroxidation in people.

evidence_considered.label: Niki (2014)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: in vitro lipid peroxidation and in vivo kinetic evidence
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Vitamin E breaks peroxyl-radical chain propagation in vitro and in vivo, and is not an efficient scavenger of several other radicals in vivo.

assessment.study: Review of kinetic and physiological evidence for vitamin E as a peroxyl-radical scavenger.
assessment.population: Chemical systems and the in vivo molar ratio of vitamin E to its substrates. No new human cohort.
assessment.result: Vitamin E inhibits lipid peroxidation by breaking peroxyl-radical chains. Other radicals are not scavenged efficiently at physiological ratios.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No dietary dose-response. The claim is which radical vitamin E can stop.
assessment.evidence_summary: Vitamin E is the chain-breaking antioxidant in the lipid phase.
assessment.limitations: A review of chemistry is not an intake trial and not a brain-outcome trial.

evidence_considered.label: Traber and Atkinson (2007)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: review of the in vivo vitamin function
evidence_considered.directional_finding: The vitamin function of alpha-tocopherol is peroxyl-radical scavenging that protects polyunsaturated fats in membranes.

assessment.study: Review arguing that the in vivo actions of alpha-tocopherol follow from peroxyl-radical scavenging.
assessment.population: Mammalian vitamin E biology. No new trial.
assessment.result: Protecting polyunsaturated fats in membranes is the vitamin function.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No intake threshold for peroxidation is set.
assessment.evidence_summary: The membrane job of vitamin E is protection of polyunsaturated fats.
assessment.limitations: The review does not measure peroxidation after a change in intake.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Extra vitamin E is not a peroxidation benefit
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Men in a large prevention trial who took 400 IU of vitamin E a day had more prostate cancers than men who took placebo. The trial did not measure membrane peroxidation.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: This blocks a high-dose reading of the vitamin E requirement. It is not evidence about the chain-breaking chemistry.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: A long prevention trial found more prostate cancers with 400 IU of vitamin E a day than with placebo. That result is not a peroxidation measurement, and it is a reason not to treat extra vitamin E as a benefit.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Klein and colleagues reported the SELECT prevention trial. Men assigned vitamin E, 400 IU a day, had a higher prostate-cancer risk than men assigned placebo. The endpoint is cancer incidence, not membrane peroxidation.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Prostate cancer is not lipid peroxidation. The result limits high-dose claims. It does not remove the biochemical role of vitamin E.

evidence_considered.label: Klein et al. (2011)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: 400 IU vitamin E a day in a prevention trial
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Vitamin E assignment was associated with more prostate cancers than placebo.

assessment.study: SELECT prevention trial of selenium and vitamin E, with extended follow-up for prostate cancer.
assessment.population: Men without prostate cancer at entry, assigned vitamin E, selenium, both, or placebo.
assessment.result: Vitamin E, 400 IU a day, was associated with a higher prostate-cancer risk than placebo.
assessment.effect_magnitude: The paper reports a higher risk. It does not report a peroxidation marker.
assessment.evidence_summary: Extra vitamin E at this dose is not a benefit.
assessment.limitations: Cancer incidence is not membrane peroxidation, so the trial does not test the chain-breaking reaction.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Dietary selenium supports phospholipid-peroxidase capacity
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Dietary selenium deprivation lowered PH-GPx activity in mouse organs, with slower loss than classical GPx and tissue-dependent residual activity.
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Dietary selenium deprivation lowered PH-GPx activity in mouse organs, with slower loss than classical GPx and tissue-dependent residual activity.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Dietary selenium supplies the selenocysteine-dependent phospholipid-hydroperoxide glutathione-peroxidase capacity that removes membrane lipid hydroperoxides.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Dietary selenium deprivation lowered PH-GPx activity in mouse organs, with slower loss than classical GPx and tissue-dependent residual activity.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Mouse whole-organ enzyme assays do not identify mitochondrial isoforms, a human food dose or benefit above selenium adequacy. scientific_findings_intro: Vitamin C can reduce the vitamin E radical and return vitamin E to its working form. That regeneration is distinct from vitamin E breaking peroxyl-radical chains. It is not a high-dose rule.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Vitamin C reduces the vitamin E radical
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Pulse radiolysis showed vitamin C reacting with the vitamin E radical. The interaction can return vitamin E toward its working form. Kinetic reviews describe the same partnership as extending vitamin E capacity. This is not an intake trial.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: This is the recycling job. It is different from vitamin E stopping peroxyl radicals in the membrane, and it is not a reason to take high doses.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Vitamin C can reduce the vitamin E radical. That regeneration is a biochemical partnership. It does not set a high-dose intake.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Packer, Slater and Willson observed a free-radical interaction between vitamin E and vitamin C by pulse radiolysis: ascorbate reduced the tocopheroxyl radical. Niki states that the synergistic interaction of vitamin E and vitamin C enhances the antioxidant capacity of vitamin E. Neither source is a feeding trial.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: The observation is chemical. It does not show that eating more vitamin C or vitamin E speeds recycling in people.

evidence_considered.label: Packer, Slater and Willson (1979)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: pulse radiolysis of vitamin E and vitamin C radicals
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Ascorbate reduced the vitamin E radical in a direct free-radical observation.

assessment.study: Pulse-radiolysis observation of the vitamin E radical reacting with vitamin C.
assessment.population: Chemical solution. No human participants.
assessment.result: Vitamin C reduced the vitamin E radical.
assessment.effect_magnitude: A direct radical-radical observation. No intake effect.
assessment.evidence_summary: Vitamin C can regenerate vitamin E from its radical.
assessment.limitations: A chemical observation is not a dietary dose and not a clinical outcome.

evidence_considered.label: Niki (2014)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: review of vitamin E and vitamin C interaction
evidence_considered.directional_finding: The synergistic interaction of vitamin E and vitamin C enhances the antioxidant capacity of vitamin E.

assessment.study: Review of vitamin E as a peroxyl-radical scavenger, including its interaction with vitamin C.
assessment.population: Kinetic and in vivo ratio evidence. No new feeding trial.
assessment.result: Vitamin C is described as extending vitamin E capacity.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No recycling rate after a change in intake.
assessment.evidence_summary: The partnership is part of how vitamin E keeps working.
assessment.limitations: The same review is used elsewhere for chain-breaking. Here only the vitamin C interaction is the claim.

connected_supportive_evidence.label: Packer et al. (1997)
connected_supportive_evidence.why_relevant: Places vitamin E in a network in which other antioxidants, including thiols, can regenerate it.
connected_supportive_evidence.why_excluded: A network chapter is not the direct observation of the vitamin C reaction, and it does not test intake.

connected_supportive_evidence.label: Klein et al. (2011)
connected_supportive_evidence.why_relevant: A prevention trial found more prostate cancers with 400 IU of vitamin E a day than with placebo.
connected_supportive_evidence.why_excluded: Cancer incidence is not a recycling measurement. It only blocks reading this chemistry as a high-dose rule.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Human glutathione reductase has defined flavin-dependent machinery
scientific_findings.finding_statement: The human glutathione-reductase structure contains FAD, and inherited GSR defects can abolish blood-cell enzyme activity.
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Structural and human genetic evidence identify machinery supporting the glutathione arm of thiol regeneration.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: This adds evidence for a defining thiol-regeneration step alongside vitamin C–E recycling. Enzyme machinery is not itself a new dietary admission.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Primary human-enzyme crystallography resolves the bound FAD cofactor. A separate inherited-deficiency investigation identifies loss of glutathione-reductase activity in patient blood cells and impaired protein stability in a recombinant variant. UniProtKB P00390 records the NADPH-dependent GSSG-to-GSH reaction (Rhea 11740), providing curated pathway context rather than an additional experiment.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: The experiments concern structure and rare genetic deficiency, not ordinary dietary exposure or neuronal recycling flux. They do not establish that additional riboflavin or another food improves this PM, cognition or ADHD. Thioredoxin-system coverage and a possible dietary FAD-precursor route remain separate research questions.

evidence_considered.label: Karplus and Schulz (1987)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: purified human glutathione reductase crystal; no dietary intervention
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Primary X-ray crystallography resolves the FAD prosthetic group in human glutathione reductase.

assessment.study: Primary structural experiment: refinement of human glutathione reductase at 1.54 angstrom resolution.
assessment.population: Purified human enzyme crystal; no dietary intervention or clinical cohort.
assessment.result: The refined structure includes bound FAD and resolves its active-site environment.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Structural resolution 1.54 angstrom; no dietary effect size or recycling flux.
assessment.evidence_summary: Direct structural support for the FAD-containing machinery of glutathione reductase.
assessment.limitations: A bound cofactor does not establish dietary limitation, human brain flux or benefit from extra riboflavin. Structural and database records describe the same protein, not independent replications.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Primary publication abstract and deposited experimental structure RCSB PDB 3GRS, entry version 1.4 (revision 2024-10-30), retrieved 2026-10-23; full publisher methods not re-extracted.

evidence_considered.label: Kamerbeek et al. (2007)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: inherited GSR variants; human blood-cell assays and recombinant enzyme
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Inherited GSR defects were associated with absent red-cell glutathione-reductase activity; residual leukocyte activity and protein instability varied with genotype.

assessment.study: Primary molecular case investigation of inherited glutathione-reductase deficiency with blood-cell activity/protein assays, genetic analysis and recombinant G330A characterization.
assessment.population: Two affected relatives and one unrelated patient; blood cells and recombinant enzyme, not a nutrition trial.
assessment.result: Affected red cells lacked detectable GR activity; the deletion and compound-heterozygous variants impaired protein expression or stability.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Absent detectable red-cell enzyme activity in the described cases; no population treatment or food effect estimate.
assessment.evidence_summary: Human loss-of-function evidence complements the structural finding at the level of enzyme capacity.
assessment.limitations: Rare genetic loss of enzyme is not a dietary deficiency model and does not identify an effective food, nutrient dose, neuronal effect or ADHD benefit.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Primary PubMed abstract PMID 17185460; full publisher methods not re-extracted. UniProtKB P00390 entry version 273, sequence version 2, annotation 2026-09-02 checked separately as curated pathway context on 2026-10-23.

evidence_dependency: PDB 3GRS and its primary Karplus–Schulz paper are the same structural evidence. UniProt curation is not counted as an independent primary experiment. The Kamerbeek human genetic investigation tests a different proposition and is not a replication of crystallographic structure.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Dietary riboflavin supports red-cell glutathione-reductase activity
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Oral riboflavin increased erythrocyte glutathione-reductase activity in the reported human experiments, with response dependent on prior riboflavin intake.
scientific_findings.finding_summary: The dietary precursor can influence flavin-dependent red-cell enzyme capacity; this is distinct from measuring antioxidant recycling flux in brain tissue.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Supports Type A riboflavin supply for the glutathione-reductase arm of antioxidant regeneration, without an extra-intake or clinical-benefit claim.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Beutler reported stimulation of red-cell glutathione reductase after 5 mg/day riboflavin for eight days. FAD activated the enzyme in hemolysates. A related report describes response after two days and declining activity after cessation; these same-author reports are not assumed independent cohorts.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Human red-cell enzyme evidence supports flavin-dependent capacity. It does not establish neuronal or whole-body recycling flux, benefit above adequacy, or equivalence between an ordinary food and a 5 mg/day supplement. Retrieval covered primary abstracts and curated human reaction records; full-text methods and participant-level data remain to be recovered before numerical SEC assessment.

mission: Tune downstream cytokine signalling intensity so inflammatory tone does not remain chronically elevated.
summary: IL-6 and TNF-α are messenger signals of inflammatory tone. CRP is a blood marker linked to that tone, not the messenger step. An endotoxin challenge in healthy adults has been used to read these responses. EPA plus DHA did not significantly change IL-6 or TNF-α in that challenge.

Postprandial inflammatory patterns in ADHD metabolic overlap may modulate cognitive clarity through cytokine-network context rather than single-mechanism claims.

Persistent inflammatory signalling through IL-6- and TNF-α-linked cytokine networks is a recognised contributor to anxious and perseverative cognition within neuroimmune framing (Slavich & Irwin, 2014; Marsland et al., 2017). Human omega-3 intervention reduced inflammatory markers and anxiety symptoms alongside resolution-phase cytokine remodelling (Kiecolt-Glaser et al., 2011; Ferguson et al., 2014). This PM governs cytokine-network tone — not omega-3 treatment — and attached anxiety outcomes require one inferential step to PH016 rather than direct perseverative-thought measurement.

Mitochondrial dysfunction is a recurrent theme in depression pathophysiology reviews; cytokine-network inflammatory tone may intersect reward-related mitochondrial biology without a direct anhedonia measurement.

Individual cytokine responses, including IL-6 and TNF-α, were not statistically different from placebo.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: A stress review and an endotoxin challenge do not show that a food intake sets this cytokine step. Upstream transcription is a separate mechanism.

title: Electron Transport Chain Function
mission: Sustain efficient electron transport so mitochondria generate ATP without excessive electron leakage.
summary: Mitochondria make ATP by passing electrons from NADH and from succinate through five enzyme complexes. Ubiquinone and cytochrome c carry electrons between the complexes, and the proton gradient drives ATP synthase. Iron–sulfur clusters, haem, copper and flavin mononucleotide (FMN) take part in the transfers. Defined sites can also leak electrons to oxygen and form superoxide. That chemistry does not show that a meal pattern changes attention or cognitive energy.
dose_sensitivity: Iron, riboflavin-derived flavin mononucleotide (FMN), ubiquinone and copper participate in electron transfer. None of the assessed studies shows that raising an already adequate intake increases chain activity or improves attention.

dietary_input_assessments.operation: Sustain efficient electron transport so mitochondria generate ATP without excessive electron leakage.

functional_dependency.statement: Copper supplies the CuA/CuB centres required for complex-IV electron transfer and oxygen reduction. Dietary copper deficiency impairs cardiac cytochrome-c-oxidase capacity in rats.

dietary_supply.statement: The same mineral has established dietary supply through the canonical composition records. Cellular uptake and homeostasis mediate enzyme loading; this is maintenance of capacity, not a claim that extra intake accelerates the reaction.

dietary_input_assessments.assessment_limitations: Specific complex-IV metal dependence and dietary-deficiency evidence support capacity supply. Rat cardiac protein/activity effects are not a human optimisation dose, a universal tissue response or proof that extra copper improves electron transport when status is adequate.

Verified plant/animal sources are reused with preparation qualifiers; no new food edge, effective food dose or enzyme-response inference is created.

scientific_findings_intro: Electron transport is the transfer of electrons from NADH and succinate to oxygen, coupled to ATP synthesis. The findings separate that chemistry, the sites that can leak electrons to oxygen, and the small ADHD cybrid result. They do not show that ordinary meals or extra cofactors change attention or cognitive energy.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Five complexes and two carriers make ATP
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Electrons from NADH and from succinate pass through five enzyme complexes. Ubiquinone and cytochrome c carry them between complexes. The proton gradient drives ATP synthase. Iron–sulfur clusters, haem, copper and flavin mononucleotide (FMN) take part in the transfers.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: These are the working parts of the chain. Identifying a part does not show that eating more of its dietary source raises electron transport or ATP production.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Mammalian oxidative phosphorylation oxidises mitochondrial reducing equivalents through five complexes and two mobile carriers, uses iron, copper, haem and flavin mononucleotide (FMN) in the transfers, and couples the proton gradient to ATP synthesis.
scientific_findings.synthesis: The respiratory-chain review describes five complexes and two mobile carriers. Oxidation of reducing equivalents builds a proton gradient that ATP synthase uses to make ATP. Iron–sulfur clusters and haem irons transfer electrons, and complex IV has two copper centres. A separate review places flavin mononucleotide (FMN) at the NADH entry site of complex I. Coenzyme Q10 reviews describe ubiquinone as the electron carrier used for that mitochondrial transfer and for related proton movement. Together they define the participants. They do not measure a dietary dose.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: The sources are reviews of enzyme structure and function, not human feeding trials. Flavin mononucleotide (FMN) abundance has not been shown to limit complex I in ordinary conditions. Endogenous ubiquinone synthesis is not separated here from dietary coenzyme Q10. Copper and iron centres are not evidence that supplements raise chain activity.

evidence_considered.label: Vercellino and Sazanov (2022)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Five complexes and two mobile carriers couple oxidation of reducing equivalents to a proton gradient and ATP synthesis, using iron–sulfur clusters, haem and copper centres.

assessment.study: Review of assembly, structure and function of the mammalian mitochondrial respiratory chain.
assessment.population: No human participants. Review of structural and biochemical studies.
assessment.result: The chain comprises five complexes and two mobile electron carriers. Proton pumping is coupled to ATP synthesis. Iron–sulfur clusters, haem and the two copper centres of complex IV transfer electrons.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No human effect size.
assessment.evidence_summary: Defines the complexes, carriers and metal centres used for electron transport and ATP synthesis.
assessment.limitations: A review does not test dietary intake, brain ATP, or clinical outcomes.

evidence_considered.label: Curtabbi and Enríquez (2022)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Flavin mononucleotide (FMN) in complex I accepts the electrons that NADH donates at the start of the chain.

assessment.study: Review of the flavin mononucleotide (FMN) site of respiratory complex I.
assessment.population: No human feeding cohort. Review of enzyme and mitochondrial studies.
assessment.result: Electrons from NADH enter complex I at flavin mononucleotide (FMN). The review does not establish that flavin mononucleotide (FMN) abundance limits assembly or activity.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No intake effect size.
assessment.evidence_summary: Places flavin mononucleotide (FMN) as the NADH-entry cofactor of complex I.
assessment.limitations: Does not test riboflavin intake in healthy people or show that more flavin mononucleotide (FMN) increases ATP synthesis.

evidence_considered.label: Crane (2001)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Coenzyme Q10 functions in mitochondrial electron transport and in proton movement linked to ATP synthesis.

assessment.study: Narrative review of biochemical functions of coenzyme Q10.
assessment.population: No new human participants.
assessment.result: The review assigns coenzyme Q10 a role in electron transport and proton translocation, and an antioxidant role in membranes.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No dietary effect size.
assessment.evidence_summary: Supports ubiquinone as an electron carrier. It does not test food or supplement intake.
assessment.limitations: A biochemical review cannot show that dietary coenzyme Q10 changes chain rate.

connected_supportive_evidence.why_relevant: Reviews B vitamins, iron and magnesium in energy-yielding metabolism and fatigue.
connected_supportive_evidence.why_excluded: It does not measure respiratory-complex activity or separate each cofactor's job in this chain.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Defined sites leak electrons to oxygen
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Eleven mitochondrial sites can pass electrons to oxygen and form superoxide or hydrogen peroxide. In resting-like muscle mitochondria, two sites in complex I and one site each in complexes II and III account for most of that leak.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Electron leak is a property of particular sites and conditions. It is not evidence that a diet has made the chain leaky, and stopping leak is not the same measurement as making ATP.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Mammalian mitochondria produce superoxide or hydrogen peroxide at defined sites associated with substrate oxidation and the respiratory chain, including complexes I, II and III, rather than by a single uncontrolled leak from the whole chain.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Brand reviews eleven sites that leak electrons to oxygen. They include the oxoacid dehydrogenases that feed NAD, complexes I and III, and ubiquinone-linked dehydrogenases including complex II. In skeletal-muscle mitochondria studied in a medium resembling resting muscle cytosol, two complex I sites and the sites in complexes II and III dominate. Complex III can release superoxide on both sides of the inner membrane. Other sites release it in the matrix. The rate depends on which substrates are present and on the antioxidant systems.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: The measurements are in isolated mitochondria and reconstructed substrate mixtures, not in the human brain and not during meals. Leak at these sites is not an ADHD biomarker and is not a prescription to take antioxidants.

evidence_considered.label: Brand (2016)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Eleven defined mitochondrial sites leak electrons to oxygen. Under resting-like muscle conditions, sites in complexes I, II and III dominate.

assessment.study: Review of site-specific mitochondrial superoxide and hydrogen peroxide production.
assessment.population: Isolated mitochondria and enzyme studies. No human clinical cohort.
assessment.result: Eleven sites are distinguished. In skeletal-muscle mitochondria in a resting-like medium, two complex I sites plus complex II and complex III dominate. Specific suppressors of the complex III outer quinone site and of reverse electron transport at complex I lower that leak without stopping oxidative phosphorylation.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Site capacities differ. No human dietary effect size.
assessment.evidence_summary: Electron leak is site-specific and condition-specific.
assessment.limitations: Not a human feeding study, not brain tissue, and not a clinical outcome.

scientific_findings.finding_label: ADHD cybrids respired less
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Cells carrying platelet mitochondria from three boys with ADHD used less oxygen, had lower complex V activity, a lower membrane potential and more mitochondrial superoxide than control cybrids.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: This is a small cell model of mitochondrial DNA from platelets. It does not show that food, iron, riboflavin or coenzyme Q10 changes attention.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Cybrid cells carrying platelet mitochondria from three boys with ADHD showed lower respiration, lower complex V activity, loss of membrane potential and higher mitochondrial superoxide than control cybrids, without a dietary or attention-outcome test.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Verma and colleagues fused platelets from three boys with ADHD, aged 10 and 13, with mitochondria-depleted SH-SY5Y cells. The methods describe two healthy control donors, while a figure labels four control cybrid lines. ADHD cybrids had lower whole-cell and mitochondrial respiration, lower ATPase 6/8 transcripts, lower complex V in-gel activity, lower membrane potential and higher MitoSOX signal. Serotonin was about twofold higher in differentiated cybrid neurons. Monoamine oxidase levels were unchanged. The authors infer a mitochondrial contribution to ADHD. The study did not change diet and did not measure attention.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: The sample is a handful of cybrid lines, not a population study. Platelet mitochondria in a neuroblastoma cell are not brain electron transport during attention. The control count is not stated the same way in the methods and the figure. No dietary exposure was tested.

evidence_considered.label: Verma et al. (2016)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: ADHD cybrids had lower respiration, lower complex V activity, a lower membrane potential and higher mitochondrial superoxide than control cybrids.

assessment.study: Platelets from boys with ADHD and control donors were fused with mitochondria-depleted SH-SY5Y cells. Respiration, membrane potential, MitoSOX, ATPase transcripts and complex V activity were measured.
assessment.population: Three boys with ADHD (one aged 10, two aged 13). Methods name two control donors; the figure labels four control cybrid lines.
assessment.result: ADHD cybrids showed lower cellular and mitochondrial respiration, lower ATPase 6/8 transcripts, lower complex V activity, loss of membrane potential and a higher MitoSOX signal. Differentiated cybrid neurons had about twofold higher serotonin.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Directions were reported as significant at p ≤ 0.05. Exact respiration rates are figure-based and are not restated as a single effect size here. Serotonin was about twofold higher.
assessment.evidence_summary: A small cybrid model links ADHD platelet mitochondria with lower respiratory activity.
assessment.limitations: Tiny sample, cell model, no diet, no attention test, and an inconsistent control count between methods and figure.

connected_supportive_evidence.label: Öğütlü et al. (2022)
connected_supportive_evidence.why_relevant: Reviews mitochondrial findings in ADHD, including this cybrid study.
connected_supportive_evidence.why_excluded: It does not add an independent electron-transport measurement.

evidence_dependency: Verma et al. (2016) is also the primary evidence in PM1-F4. The two findings use one study for two phenome questions.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Cognitive energy was not measured
scientific_findings.finding_summary: The ADHD cybrid cells respired less. Cognitive energy, fatigue and meal effects were not measured.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Lower respiration in a cell model is not a demonstration that this chain sets cognitive energy, and it is not a reason to supplement.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: The assessed human cell evidence does not show that electron-transport capacity changes Cognitive Energy Stability.
scientific_findings.synthesis: The only human measurement attached to this phenome is the Verma cybrid study. Those cells respired less and had lower complex V activity. The study did not measure cognitive energy, fatigue, or a dietary change. A narrative vitamin review discusses fatigue when micronutrient status is poor, but it does not measure this chain or this phenome.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Absence of a direct test is not evidence that the chain is irrelevant to energy supply. It does block claims that foods or cofactor supplements stabilise cognitive energy through this mechanism.

evidence_considered.directional_finding: Respiration was lower in ADHD cybrids. Cognitive energy was not an endpoint.

assessment.study: Cybrid respiration, complex V activity and oxidative-stress staining.
assessment.population: Three boys with ADHD and a small control donor set, studied as cybrid cell lines.
assessment.result: Respiratory measures were lower. Cognitive energy was not measured.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No cognitive-energy effect size.
assessment.evidence_summary: Shows a cell respiration difference, not a cognitive-energy outcome.

title: NAD⁺ Metabolism
mission: Maintain NAD⁺ availability so redox reactions and mitochondrial signalling stay adequately powered.
summary: NAD⁺ helps cells release energy from nutrients and supports enzymes involved in maintenance and repair. Cells must continually recycle and replenish this molecule to keep those functions available. This PM focuses on maintaining that cellular resource. Dietary vitamin B3 forms and tryptophan provide building material, while exercise can influence part of the recycling machinery. Supporting normal availability is different from assuming that raising NAD⁺ improves cognition or wellbeing.
dose_sensitivity: Nicotinamide, nicotinic acid and tryptophan are biosynthetic precursors. High-dose niacin raised NAD⁺ in mitochondrial myopathy. None of the assessed studies shows that raising an already adequate intake improves attention.
cofactors: Nicotinic acid (a form of vitamin B3)

scientific_findings_intro: NAD⁺ and NADH interconvert in dehydrogenase reactions. Separately, synthesis and salvage replenish the pool when consuming enzymes break NAD⁺ down. Nicotinamide salvage, the nicotinic-acid route and hepatic tryptophan conversion are major pathways, not every precursor entry. The findings separate that chemistry from a high-dose niacin study in mitochondrial myopathy, from a muscle-enzyme response to training, and from the absence of an NAD⁺ measurement in the ADHD papers.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Three major pathways maintain the NAD⁺ pool
scientific_findings.finding_summary: NAD⁺ accepts electrons to form NADH, and that NADH can be oxidised back to NAD⁺. Separately, nicotinamide salvage, the nicotinic-acid route and hepatic conversion of tryptophan are major pathways that replenish the pool when consuming enzymes break NAD⁺ down.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: These are major maintenance pathways, not every precursor entry. Identifying them does not show that eating more of a precursor, once intake is adequate, raises NAD⁺ or improves attention.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Major pathways that maintain the mammalian NAD⁺ pool are de novo synthesis from tryptophan, the Preiss–Handler route from nicotinic acid, and salvage of nicotinamide. Most cells outside the liver depend on salvage. These are not the only precursor entry routes.
scientific_findings.synthesis: The review describes NAD⁺ as the coenzyme that accepts a hydride in redox reactions. It is synthesised de novo from tryptophan through the kynurenine pathway, from nicotinic acid by the Preiss–Handler pathway, and by salvage of nicotinamide. Outside the liver, most cells do not express the full tryptophan route. The liver can convert tryptophan to nicotinamide, release it, and leave other cells to salvage that nicotinamide. The review states that the share of the pool coming from tryptophan is not established. Most NAD⁺ is described as coming from nicotinamide salvage.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: This is a review of pathways, not a human feeding trial. It does not measure how much an ordinary meal changes NAD⁺, and it does not test attention or cognitive energy. Nicotinamide riboside and nicotinamide mononucleotide, as supplement doses, are outside this dietary assessment.

evidence_considered.label: Covarrubias et al. (2021)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: NAD⁺ is made from tryptophan, from nicotinic acid, and by salvage of nicotinamide, with salvage as the main route outside the liver.

assessment.study: Review of NAD⁺ biosynthesis and of NAD⁺-dependent enzymes in energy metabolism and ageing.
assessment.population: No new human feeding cohort. Review of biochemical and organism studies.
assessment.result: Three biosynthetic routes are distinguished. Nicotinamide salvage supplies most NAD⁺ outside the liver. The contribution of tryptophan is not established.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No ordinary-diet effect size.
assessment.evidence_summary: Defines major pathways that maintain the NAD⁺ pool, not every precursor entry.
assessment.limitations: A review does not test meals, adequate versus extra intake, or cognitive outcomes.

connected_supportive_evidence.why_excluded: It does not define the NAD⁺ biosynthetic enzymes or measure NAD⁺.
