scientific_findings.finding_label: Sirtuins and related enzymes consume NAD⁺
scientific_findings.finding_summary: NAD⁺ is not only a redox cofactor. Sirtuins, CD38 and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases consume it during protein deacylation, signalling and repair.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Consumption explains why the pool can fall. It does not show that blocking these enzymes, or eating more niacin, improves attention.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: NAD⁺ is a substrate of non-redox enzymes, including sirtuins, CD38 and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases, as well as a hydride acceptor in energy metabolism.
scientific_findings.synthesis: The NAD⁺ review identifies sirtuins, CD38 and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases as enzymes that use NAD⁺ itself, separate from its redox role. A sirtuin review describes SIRT1 as an NAD⁺-dependent deacetylase that links this consumption to metabolic regulation. Together they place consumption on the same pool that biosynthesis rebuilds. They do not measure a dietary dose.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Both sources are reviews. They do not show that sirtuin activity in the human brain is limited by ordinary niacin intake, or that changing that activity improves cognitive energy.

evidence_considered.label: Covarrubias et al. (2021)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Sirtuins, CD38 and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases consume NAD⁺ in addition to its use as a redox cofactor.

assessment.study: Review of NAD⁺ metabolism, including non-redox consumers of the cofactor.
assessment.population: No new human cohort.
assessment.result: NAD⁺ is required by sirtuins, CD38 and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases. Ageing-related decline and the benefit of restoring NAD⁺ in people are left unresolved by the review.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No human intake effect size.
assessment.evidence_summary: Establishes enzymatic consumption of NAD⁺.
assessment.limitations: Does not test diet or cognitive outcomes.

evidence_considered.label: Chang and Guarente (2014)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: SIRT1 uses NAD⁺ as the cofactor for protein deacetylation linked to metabolic regulation.

assessment.study: Review of SIRT1 and other sirtuins in metabolism.
assessment.population: No new human feeding cohort.
assessment.result: Sirtuins are described as NAD⁺-dependent deacylases that connect metabolic state to protein regulation.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No dietary effect size.
assessment.evidence_summary: Supports sirtuins as consumers of NAD⁺.
assessment.limitations: A review of enzyme biology is not evidence that dietary niacin changes human cognition.

evidence_dependency: Covarrubias et al. (2021) is also the primary source for PM2-F1. Its appearance here is the consumption claim, not a second study.

scientific_findings.finding_label: The clock controls NAMPT in mice
scientific_findings.finding_summary: In mice and cells, the circadian clock controls NAMPT, and NAD⁺ rises and falls with that enzyme. This is not a human sleep-schedule result.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: The salvage enzyme is under clock control in these models. Keeping regular bedtimes has not been shown here to change NAD⁺ in people.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Circadian clock factors control NAMPT-mediated NAD⁺ biosynthesis in mice and cells, so NAD⁺ availability oscillates across the day in those systems.
scientific_findings.synthesis: One study reports a feedback cycle in which clock transcription factors control NAMPT and thereby NAD⁺ biosynthesis. A companion study reports that the NAD⁺-dependent deacetylase SIRT1 modulates CLOCK-dependent chromatin control, with NAD⁺ itself changing across the day. Both place the salvage enzyme inside a circadian loop. Neither assigns a bedtime or a meal time.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: The experiments are in mice and cells. They do not show that a regular sleep schedule, or restriction of sleep, changes NAD⁺ in people.

evidence_considered.label: Ramsey et al. (2009)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: The circadian clock controls NAMPT-mediated NAD⁺ biosynthesis and NAD⁺ oscillates across the day.

assessment.study: Mouse and cell experiments on clock control of NAMPT and NAD⁺.
assessment.population: Mice and cultured cells. No human sleep cohort.
assessment.result: Clock factors drive Nampt, and NAD⁺ levels oscillate with that control.
assessment.effect_magnitude: A daily oscillation in the model systems. No human effect size.
assessment.evidence_summary: Links the clock to nicotinamide salvage in mice.
assessment.limitations: Not a test of human sleep timing or dietary niacin.

evidence_considered.label: Nakahata et al. (2008)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: SIRT1, which uses NAD⁺, modulates CLOCK-mediated circadian control.

assessment.study: Cell and mouse experiments on SIRT1, CLOCK and oscillating NAD⁺.
assessment.population: Cultured cells and mice. No human participants.
assessment.result: SIRT1 binds the clock machinery and NAD⁺ levels change across the day in the reported system.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No human effect size.
assessment.evidence_summary: Connects NAD⁺ consumption by SIRT1 to circadian control in the model.
assessment.limitations: Does not test sleep schedules or niacin intake in people.

connected_supportive_evidence.label: Spiegel et al. (1999)
connected_supportive_evidence.why_relevant: The page had used this sleep-debt experiment as support for NAD⁺ synthesis.
connected_supportive_evidence.why_excluded: The study measured glucose tolerance and endocrine responses to sleep debt. It did not measure NAD⁺ or NAMPT.

scientific_findings.finding_label: High-dose niacin raised NAD⁺ in myopathy
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Five adults with mitochondrial myopathy and low NAD⁺ were given slow-release niacin, increased to 750–1,000 mg a day. Blood NAD⁺ rose, and muscle NAD⁺ reached the level of their controls.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: This is medical dosing in a deficiency disease. It is not evidence that an ordinary diet, or extra niacin once intake is adequate, raises NAD⁺ or helps attention.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: In adults with mitochondrial myopathy, escalating niacin to 750–1,000 mg/day increased blood NAD⁺ and restored muscle NAD⁺ to the matched-control level, without a cognitive endpoint.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Five adults with adult-onset mitochondrial myopathy and muscle mitochondrial DNA deletions, plus matched controls, received slow-release niacin. The dose started at 250 mg/day and rose to 750–1,000 mg/day. Patients were followed for up to 10 months and controls for 4 months. Blood NAD⁺ increased in the participants who continued, by up to 8-fold, and muscle NAD⁺ in the patients reached the control level. Muscle strength increased. Flushing occurred above 500 mg/day. Two controls stopped because of gastrointestinal irritation.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: The sample is five patients. The dose is far above ordinary niacin intake. There is no untreated comparison group, and attention, cognitive energy and recovery were not endpoints. The result does not transfer to people whose intake is already adequate.

evidence_considered.label: Pirinen et al. (2020)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: supplemental-formulation
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Slow-release niacin at 750–1,000 mg/day raised blood NAD⁺ and brought muscle NAD⁺ in mitochondrial myopathy to the control level.

assessment.study: Open niacin supplementation in adults with mitochondrial myopathy and in matched controls.
assessment.population: Five adults with adult-onset mitochondrial myopathy and matched controls. Two controls discontinued.
assessment.result: Blood NAD⁺ rose by up to 8-fold. Muscle NAD⁺ in patients reached the control level. Muscle strength increased. Cognition was not tested.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Up to an 8-fold rise in blood NAD⁺ at 750–1,000 mg/day.
assessment.evidence_summary: Pharmacological niacin can rebuild a deficient NAD⁺ pool in this disease.
assessment.limitations: Not an ordinary diet, not a randomised untreated comparison, and not a brain or attention outcome.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Training raised muscle NAMPT protein
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Twelve weeks of aerobic or resistance training increased NAMPT protein in skeletal muscle of young and older adults. The study did not measure NAD⁺ concentration.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Training changed the amount of the salvage enzyme in muscle. That is not a measurement of the NAD⁺ pool, and it is not a cognitive result.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Aerobic and resistance training increased skeletal-muscle NAMPT protein in young and older adults, without a reported change in NAD⁺ concentration.
scientific_findings.synthesis: NAMPT protein in skeletal muscle was lower at older ages across 57 people. Twelve weeks of aerobic training raised muscle NAMPT by about 12% in adults aged 35 or under and by about 28% in adults aged 55 or over. Resistance training raised it by about 25% and 30% in those same age groups. NRK2 and NMNAT1 and NMNAT3 protein did not change. In a separate group, six weeks of high-intensity interval training did not change NAMPT in abdominal fat.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: The endpoint is enzyme protein, not NAD⁺. Muscle NAMPT is not brain NAD⁺. Cognitive energy and recovery were not measured.

evidence_considered.label: de Guia et al. (2019)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Aerobic and resistance training increased skeletal-muscle NAMPT protein in young and older adults.

assessment.study: Twelve-week aerobic and resistance training, with NAMPT and related enzymes measured in muscle biopsies.
assessment.population: Adults aged 35 or under and adults aged 55 or over. A separate group provided abdominal fat biopsies.
assessment.result: Muscle NAMPT rose after both training modes. Other salvage enzymes in muscle did not. Fat NAMPT did not change after interval training.
assessment.effect_magnitude: About 12–28% after aerobic training and about 25–30% after resistance training, larger in the older groups.
assessment.evidence_summary: Training increases the amount of the rate-limiting salvage enzyme in human muscle.
assessment.limitations: NAMPT protein is not NAD⁺ concentration and not a cognitive endpoint.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Cognitive energy was not measured
scientific_findings.finding_summary: The ADHD cybrid study measured respiration, not NAD⁺. Cognitive energy was not an endpoint.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Lower respiration in that cell model is not an NAD⁺ result and not evidence that niacin changes cognitive energy.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: No assessed study measured NAD⁺ availability against cognitive energy. The ADHD cybrid experiment measured respiration without an NAD⁺ or cognitive-energy endpoint.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Verma and colleagues fused platelets from three boys with ADHD with mitochondria-depleted neuronal cells. Those cybrids respired less than control cybrids. The paper does not report NAD⁺ or NADH, and it does not test cognitive energy or diet. A narrative review of ADHD mitochondrial biomarkers does not add an NAD⁺ measurement.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Absence of an NAD⁺ measurement is not evidence against a biological link. It is evidence that this relationship has not been tested.

evidence_considered.label: Verma et al. (2016)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: ADHD cybrids respired less. NAD⁺ and cognitive energy were not measured.

assessment.study: Cybrid model using platelet mitochondria from boys with ADHD.
assessment.population: Three boys with ADHD, aged 10 and 13. No dietary arm.
assessment.result: Lower respiration and related mitochondrial changes in the cybrids. No NAD⁺ assay and no cognitive-energy test.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No NAD⁺ effect size.
assessment.evidence_summary: The study does not test this pool.
assessment.limitations: A respiration result cannot be read as an NAD⁺ or cognitive-energy result.

connected_supportive_evidence.label: Öğütlü et al. (2022)
connected_supportive_evidence.why_relevant: Reviews mitochondrial findings in ADHD, which the page had tied to NAD⁺.
connected_supportive_evidence.why_excluded: The review does not measure NAD⁺ or cognitive energy.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Recovery was not measured
scientific_findings.finding_summary: The ADHD mitochondrial review does not measure recovery and does not measure NAD⁺.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: A narrative link between mitochondrial strain and resilience is not a recovery result for this pool.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: No assessed study measured NAD⁺ salvage or NAD⁺ availability against recovery capacity.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Öğütlü and colleagues review mitochondrial biomarkers in ADHD. The review does not report a recovery test and does not report NAD⁺. It cannot establish that this pool changes recovery.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: An untested relationship stays unresolved. The review is not evidence that NAD⁺ is irrelevant to recovery.

evidence_considered.label: Öğütlü et al. (2022)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: The review summarises ADHD mitochondrial biomarkers and does not measure NAD⁺ or recovery.

assessment.study: Narrative review of mitochondrial findings in ADHD.
assessment.population: No new participants.
assessment.result: No NAD⁺ measurement and no recovery endpoint.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No NAD⁺ effect size.
assessment.evidence_summary: Does not test this phenome relationship.
assessment.limitations: A review of other mitochondrial markers is not an NAD⁺ recovery study.

evidence_dependency: Öğütlü et al. (2022) is connected supportive evidence on PM2-F6. Using it here is the same review, not a second measurement.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Oral NR supports measured blood NAD metabolism
scientific_findings.finding_statement: A small randomized crossover pharmacokinetic study found altered blood NAD metabolism after single oral NR-chloride doses; separate LC-MS work identified NR in cow milk.
scientific_findings.finding_summary: A small randomized crossover pharmacokinetic study found altered blood NAD metabolism after single oral NR-chloride doses; separate LC-MS work identified NR in cow milk.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Dietary nicotinamide riboside can supply the NAD precursor pool through supported salvage reactions, sustaining NAD-availability capacity.
scientific_findings.synthesis: A small randomized crossover pharmacokinetic study found altered blood NAD metabolism after single oral NR-chloride doses; separate LC-MS work identified NR in cow milk.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Supplemental NR chloride at 100–1000 mg is not an effective milk dose. Blood responses do not establish neuronal or mitochondrial NAD delivery, redox flux, superiority to adequate niacin or clinical benefit. Intestinal metabolism and tissue salvage can differ from the displayed intracellular NRK route; other NAD precursors remain alternatives. Numerical SEC remains pending full-method appraisal; no factor is forced.

title: Creatine–Phosphocreatine Energy Buffering
mission: Enable rapid ATP buffering so high-energy-demand tissues can meet sudden metabolic spikes.
summary: Provides a rapid ATP buffer through creatine–phosphocreatine cycling when cellular demand changes faster than oxidative ATP production can respond. Cerebral creatine depends on local synthesis, intercellular and blood–brain barrier transport, creatine-kinase activity and compartmentalisation. Exogenous creatine can alter cerebral total creatine or phosphocreatine in some people, but brain responses are smaller and less consistent than muscle responses, and concentration changes do not by themselves establish greater phosphocreatine flux or cognitive benefit.
dose_sensitivity: Brain uptake is modest and variable; effective supplemental exposure depends on dose, duration, baseline status, region and metabolic demand.
scientific_findings_intro: The creatine–phosphocreatine system is an intracellular energy buffer, not a single concentration marker. The findings below separate synthesis and transport, habitual dietary exposure, cerebral target engagement and functional outcomes. They support conditional intervention relevance while preserving the distinction between total creatine, phosphocreatine, ATP buffering and cognitive performance.

dietary_input_traceability.evidence_limitation: The brain also synthesises creatine, and exogenous exposure produces smaller and less consistent cerebral responses than skeletal-muscle responses.

phenome_relationships.rationale: Creatine–phosphocreatine buffering is positioned to stabilise ATP supply during changing demand. In a small crossover trial during acute sleep deprivation, a high single creatine dose altered cerebral high-energy phosphate measures and partially preserved cognitive performance {{cite:gordji-nejad_creatine_sleep_2024}}. This supports a conditional relationship under acute metabolic stress, not a universal energy effect.

Rapid ATP buffering is biologically relevant to recovery after energetic demand, but the reviewed human evidence primarily measures cerebral creatine, cognition during acute stress, or clinical contexts rather than recovery capacity itself {{cite:dolan_beyond_muscle_2019}}. The relationship therefore remains indirect and evidence-limited.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Cerebral creatine depends on synthesis, transport and compartmentalisation
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Brain creatine pools arise from endogenous synthesis and transporter-mediated movement between blood and neural cell types. Limited blood–brain barrier entry means cerebral creatine cannot be inferred from dietary exposure or muscle response alone.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: This establishes the biological system and its precursor requirements; it does not show that additional precursor intake increases cerebral creatine.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Cerebral creatine availability is jointly determined by endogenous synthesis, SLC6A8-mediated transport and cellular compartmentalisation, with more restricted exogenous uptake than in skeletal muscle.
scientific_findings.synthesis: The CNS review identifies creatine synthesis enzymes and the SLC6A8 transporter across neural compartments, alongside inefficient blood–brain barrier transfer. Arginine and glycine contribute to guanidinoacetate formation, and methionine-derived SAM provides the methyl group used to form creatine.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: This is review-level mechanistic and clinical-genetics evidence; it does not quantify ordinary dietary control of synthesis or identify a general intake threshold for healthy people.

evidence_considered.label: Béard & Braissant (2010)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: CNS creatine depends on endogenous synthesis and transporter-mediated movement, while blood–brain barrier entry is relatively inefficient.

assessment.study: Narrative review of CNS creatine synthesis, transport and creatine-deficiency disorders.
assessment.population: Mixed cellular, animal and human clinical-genetics evidence.
assessment.result: Identified local synthesis and SLC6A8-dependent transport as joint determinants of cerebral creatine availability.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No pooled effect estimate.
assessment.evidence_summary: Establishes the major biological determinants and precursor reactions represented by this PM.
assessment.limitations: Review-level synthesis does not quantify diet-to-brain responsiveness in healthy populations.

evidence_considered.label: Edison et al. (2007)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Renal arteriovenous measurements demonstrated guanidinoacetate production in humans and rats; arginine/citrulline infusion increased rat renal production, while glycine infusion did not.

assessment.population: Humans and rats; separate experimental arms.
assessment.result: Human arterial GAA 2.4 micromolar, renal arteriovenous difference -1.1 micromolar; rat infusion responses were precursor-specific.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Human A-V difference -1.1 micromolar; not cerebral production flux.
assessment.evidence_summary: Primary physiological production evidence complements curated AGAT/GAMT reactions.
assessment.limitations: Capacity of the endogenous synthesis route is distinct from a claim that extra amino-acid intake raises cerebral creatine, phosphocreatine buffering or cognition. AGAT feedback, GAMT methyl supply, organ exchange and SLC6A8-mediated tissue transport constrain delivery. Human renal GAA production is not a measurement of brain synthesis flux; rat arginine infusion and glycine null responses are not oral human efficacy experiments. Primary abstract inspected; no forced numerical SEC.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Low habitual dietary creatine does not necessarily lower brain total creatine
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Vegetarians reported much lower dietary creatine intake than omnivores but had comparable posterior-cingulate total creatine on proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Endogenous regulation can maintain a measured cerebral pool despite low habitual intake; one regional concentration measure does not establish phosphocreatine flux.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Habitual dietary creatine exposure does not map directly onto posterior-cingulate total creatine concentration in healthy adults.
scientific_findings.synthesis: A cross-sectional human comparison found substantially lower dietary creatine intake in vegetarians without a corresponding group difference in posterior-cingulate total creatine.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: The study was cross-sectional, measured one brain region and quantified total creatine rather than phosphocreatine turnover or ATP-buffering flux.

evidence_considered.label: Solis et al. (2014)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: habitual vegetarian or omnivorous diet
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Much lower dietary creatine intake in vegetarians was not accompanied by lower posterior-cingulate total creatine.

assessment.study: Cross-sectional proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy comparison.
assessment.population: Healthy vegetarian and omnivorous adults.
assessment.result: Posterior-cingulate total creatine did not differ significantly between dietary groups.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No interpretable intake-response effect estimate.
assessment.evidence_summary: Challenges a simple habitual dietary-creatine to cerebral-total-creatine model.
assessment.limitations: Small cross-sectional regional study; total creatine is not phosphocreatine flux or functional capacity.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Supplementation can raise cerebral creatine, but responses are modest and variable
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Across human spectroscopy studies, creatine supplementation often increased cerebral total creatine or phosphocreatine, usually by less than typical skeletal-muscle responses; some studies were null or reported different directions for total creatine and phosphocreatine.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Cerebral target engagement is possible but cannot be assumed from dose, muscle response or a single metabolite measure.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Exogenous creatine can alter cerebral total creatine or phosphocreatine, with smaller, region- and protocol-dependent responses than in skeletal muscle.
scientific_findings.synthesis: The review of human supplementation studies found that most reported a modest rise in cerebral creatine-related measures, while a minority were null and phosphocreatine responses were not uniformly positive. Dose, duration, population and spectroscopy method varied substantially.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: The evidence base was small and heterogeneous, and increased concentration does not by itself demonstrate faster creatine-kinase flux or functional benefit.

evidence_considered.label: Dolan et al. (2019)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: creatine supplementation
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Cerebral creatine-related measures were responsive in most reviewed supplementation studies, but changes were modest, heterogeneous and not universal.

assessment.study: Review of human supplementation studies measuring cerebral creatine or phosphocreatine.
assessment.population: Healthy and selected clinical human populations across heterogeneous protocols.
assessment.result: Most studies reported some cerebral increase, while others were null; responses were smaller than typical muscle responses.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Reviewed changes ranged from approximately null to low double-digit percentages.
assessment.evidence_summary: Establishes conditional cerebral target engagement while preserving protocol and measurement heterogeneity.
assessment.limitations: Review of a small, heterogeneous evidence base without an established optimal cerebral-loading protocol.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Cognitive effects of supplementation are domain- and population-dependent
scientific_findings.finding_summary: A systematic review of six randomised trials in healthy people found possible benefits for short-term memory and reasoning, but conflicting or null results across attention, executive control, reaction time, mental fatigue and several other domains.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Cognitive outcome evidence supports conditional investigation, not a general claim that creatine improves cognition.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Creatine supplementation does not produce a uniform cognitive benefit in healthy populations; observed effects vary by domain, age, dietary context and study design.
scientific_findings.synthesis: The systematic review found some support for short-term memory and reasoning while most other cognitive domains were inconsistent. Young participants often showed no change, and vegetarian status modified some memory findings but not other outcomes.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Only six small heterogeneous trials were included, and most did not pair cognitive outcomes with direct cerebral creatine or phosphocreatine measurement.

evidence_considered.label: Avgerinos et al. (2018)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: creatine supplementation
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Short-term memory and reasoning showed possible benefit, while many other cognitive domains were conflicting or unchanged.

assessment.study: Systematic review of six randomised controlled trials.
assessment.population: 281 healthy participants across varied ages and habitual diets.
assessment.result: Effects were domain- and population-dependent rather than uniformly positive.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No pooled overall effect estimate.
assessment.evidence_summary: Supports a constrained, context-dependent interpretation of cognitive supplementation evidence.
assessment.limitations: Small heterogeneous evidence base with limited direct cerebral target-engagement measurement.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Creatine partially preserved cognition during acute sleep deprivation
scientific_findings.finding_summary: In 15 healthy young adults, a high single creatine dose during 21 hours of sleep deprivation changed cerebral high-energy-phosphate measures and partially reduced deterioration in several cognitive tasks.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: This is direct human evidence linking an intervention, cerebral metabolic measures and function under acute stress; it is not a routine-use or sleep-replacement claim.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Under acute sleep deprivation, high-dose creatine can modify cerebral high-energy-phosphate measures and partially preserve cognitive performance.
scientific_findings.synthesis: A double-blind crossover trial combined proton and phosphorus magnetic resonance spectroscopy with repeated cognitive testing. Creatine changed phosphocreatine, ATP and total-creatine-related ratios and improved selected performance and processing-speed outcomes relative to placebo.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: The trial included 15 healthy young adults, used an unusually high acute dose and tested short-term sleep deprivation rather than routine cognitive function or long-term clinical outcomes.

evidence_considered.label: Gordji-Nejad et al. (2024)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: high-dose creatine during acute sleep deprivation
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Creatine altered cerebral high-energy-phosphate measures and partially preserved selected cognitive performance during sleep deprivation.

assessment.study: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled crossover trial with repeated MRS and cognitive testing.
assessment.population: Fifteen healthy adults aged 20–28 years.
assessment.result: A single 0.35 g/kg dose changed several cerebral metabolite ratios and improved selected cognitive outcomes over the sleep-deprivation night.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Outcome-specific changes; no general clinical effect size.
assessment.evidence_summary: Provides direct but small-sample human target-engagement and functional evidence under acute metabolic stress.
assessment.limitations: Small young sample, high acute dose and sleep-deprivation context limit generalisation.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Cooking heat converts some meat creatine to creatinine
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Controlled pork and cooked-ham experiments found more creatine-to-creatinine conversion with greater heat exposure, especially near the product surface.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Preparation can change food creatine retention, but this does not establish cerebral uptake or functional benefit.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Cooking time, temperature profile and sample location influence creatine retention and creatinine formation in pork matrices.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Creatine decreased and creatinine increased during controlled pork processing, with greater conversion in surface than core samples and differences between cooking programmes.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Evidence is limited to pork-loin and cooked-ham matrices and did not measure intake, cerebral creatine or function.

evidence_considered.label: Mora et al. (2008)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: controlled cooking of pork loin and cooked ham
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Greater heat exposure increased the creatinine-to-creatine ratio, particularly at the product surface.

assessment.study: Controlled food-chemistry experiments comparing pork cooking programmes and sample locations.
assessment.population: Pork loin, prepared cooked ham and commercial cooked-ham samples.
assessment.result: Creatine conversion varied with cooking method and was greater at the surface than the core.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Matrix- and location-specific differences; no human exposure estimate.
assessment.evidence_summary: Supports a food-preparation relationship for retaining creatine in pork matrices.
assessment.limitations: Food-composition evidence only; no human biological outcome.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Methionine supplies the methyl-donor route for creatine synthesis
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Dietary methionine availability affects methyl incorporation into hepatic creatine in neonatal piglets.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Dietary methionine availability affects methyl incorporation into hepatic creatine in neonatal piglets.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: This supports the substrate-supply relationship; it does not quantify cerebral creatine synthesis or an adult supplementation benefit.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Dietary methionine availability affects methyl incorporation into hepatic creatine in neonatal piglets.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Endogenous remethylation also supplies methionine. Neonatal-piglet isotope incorporation does not establish an adult intake target, cerebral delivery or benefit above adequacy. Methyl allocation, SAH inhibition, transport and other substrate availability constrain the route; no shared KC admission follows.

assessment.population: Twenty neonatal Yucatan miniature piglets.
assessment.result: Dietary methionine availability affects methyl incorporation into hepatic creatine in neonatal piglets.

assessment.evidence_summary: Primary abstract and published figure captions inspected; capacity rather than clinical efficacy.
assessment.limitations: Endogenous remethylation also supplies methionine. title: ROS Production and Control
mission: Regulate mitochondrial superoxide and hydrogen peroxide generation in response to metabolic conditions, preserving physiological redox signalling while limiting excessive oxidant production.
summary: Mitochondria produce oxidants as part of their response to changing energy demands. Keeping this production appropriately regulated allows cells to signal and adapt while limiting excessive oxidant exposure. This matters for understanding the metabolic environment in which brain cells function. The evidence here establishes source regulation and adaptive signalling in experimental models, alongside changes in oxidant emission in human muscle; these are different levels of biological observation.
dose_sensitivity: No general optimisation dose established. Experimental exposures are retained in source assessments, not translated into food prescriptions.

phenome_relationships.rationale: Elevated glutathione and oxidative-stress markers in paediatric ADHD case–control work link mitochondrial ROS handling to redox recovery context; GSH is required for mitochondrial lactate metabolism and ROS neutralisation — this PM governs ROS production/control balance, not GSH synthesis (BRS2/BRS3).

Oxidative-stress elevation in ADHD cohorts intersects stress-relevant redox tone — impaired ROS control may modulate allostatic load under repeated challenge without claiming oxidative stress causes ADHD.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Mitochondrial oxidant production is source- and state-dependent
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Specific mitochondrial electron-transfer sites generate superoxide and hydrogen peroxide; source-specific suppression can reduce oxidant production without inhibiting oxidative phosphorylation. Succinate oxidation during reperfusion can drive excessive production through reverse electron transport.
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Specific mitochondrial electron-transfer sites generate superoxide and hydrogen peroxide; source-specific suppression can reduce oxidant production without inhibiting oxidative phosphorylation. Succinate oxidation during reperfusion can drive excessive production through reverse electron transport.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Experimental suppressors and ischaemia models establish source regulation, not dietary effectiveness. These results do not imply that all mitochondrial ROS are harmful or that mitochondrial emission assays isolate gross production.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Specific mitochondrial electron-transfer sites generate superoxide and hydrogen peroxide; source-specific suppression can reduce oxidant production without inhibiting oxidative phosphorylation. Succinate oxidation during reperfusion can drive excessive production through reverse electron transport.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Experimental suppressors and ischaemia models establish source regulation, not dietary effectiveness. These results do not imply that all mitochondrial ROS are harmful or that mitochondrial emission assays isolate gross production.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Inactivity and training changed mitochondrial H2O2 emission
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Two weeks of leg immobilisation increased muscle mitochondrial H2O2 emission at a controlled membrane potential; six weeks of aerobic retraining restored emission and ATP-generating respiration toward baseline. Acute exercise responses were respiratory-state dependent in a separate study.
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Two weeks of leg immobilisation increased muscle mitochondrial H2O2 emission at a controlled membrane potential; six weeks of aerobic retraining restored emission and ATP-generating respiration toward baseline. Acute exercise responses were respiratory-state dependent in a separate study.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Measured emission is not pure source production. Immobilisation/retraining does not establish a universal exercise dose or a brain/ADHD effect. Acute and chronic exercise effects must not be collapsed into “exercise lowers ROS”.

title: Mitochondrial Protection (Redox Integrity)
mission: Preserve mitochondrial membrane and protein integrity through local protective mechanisms that limit oxidative injury and maintain organelle function.
summary: Mitochondria need intact membranes and proteins to keep their working machinery functional. Local protective systems help preserve those structures during oxidative strain. This provides a biological basis for considering protection in brain-cell energy metabolism, while the evidence assessed here comes from defined tissues and experimental models. Vitamin E and manganese support distinct protective capacities; their dietary supply must be distinguished from the amount that reaches and acts within mitochondria.
dose_sensitivity: No general optimisation dose established. Experimental exposures are retained in source assessments, not translated into food prescriptions.

phenome_relationships.rationale: Integrated mitochondrial membrane protection and redox integrity preserve energetic output when oxidative stress is elevated in paediatric ADHD — convergent with Verlaet glutathione/oxidative-stress findings and ADHD mitophagy reviews.

Mitophagy and mitochondrial quality-control biology reviewed in ADHD contexts support redox-resilience framing when oxidative insult is recurrent — mechanism boundary is organelle integrity, not pharmacological antioxidant treatment claims.

title: Carnitine-Mediated Fat Transport
mission: Enable long-chain fatty-acid transport into mitochondria so fat-derived ATP production can proceed.
summary: Transports long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria for β-oxidation (fatty-acid burning that generates ATP) via the carnitine shuttle system, a prerequisite step without which fat-derived energy production cannot occur regardless of how much fat is available. This transport step is a specific bottleneck distinct from glucose-based or ketone-based fuel pathways covered elsewhere. Dietary carnitine and substrate availability jointly determine how efficiently this shuttle keeps pace with fat-oxidation demand.
dose_sensitivity: Context-dependent support mechanism; more relevant where fat oxidation flexibility is a priority

phenome_relationships.rationale: Controlled carnitine supplementation improved behavioural and functional outcomes in children with ADHD — the strongest direct ADHD intervention anchor in BRS4, mapping fatty-acid transport into mitochondria to attention-relevant outcomes without generalising beyond trial context.

Carnitine-dependent fat oxidation supports mitochondrial substrate delivery for ATP production — trial evidence in ADHD children links this transport node to functional improvement alongside behavioural endpoints.

title: Ketone Utilisation Capacity
mission: Enable mitochondrial ketone utilisation so alternative fuel is available when glucose conditions shift.
summary: Supports capacity to transport, metabolise, and utilise ketone bodies (beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate, alternative fuels the liver produces when glucose availability falls) as mitochondrial energy substrates when glucose conditions change. This pathway provides metabolic fuel flexibility distinct from the carbohydrate- or fat-transport routes covered elsewhere, becoming physiologically relevant during fasting, prolonged exercise, or carbohydrate-restricted eating patterns. Mitochondrial ketone-oxidation enzyme capacity, not just circulating ketone levels, determines how effectively this alternative fuel is actually used.
dose_sensitivity: Context-dependent; ketone utilisation capacity depends on metabolic exposure, substrate availability, and sustained lifestyle patterns rather than single meal-level dosing alone

phenome_relationships.rationale: ADHD mitochondrial dysfunction reviews describe substrate-flexibility strain when oxidative phosphorylation is impaired — ketone utilisation is an indirect alternative-fuel pathway node without ADHD ketone-intervention outcomes in the hub set.

conversion_pathway.process: Hepatic mitochondrial ketogenesis proceeds through acetoacetyl-CoA formation, HMG-CoA synthase and HMG-CoA lyase to produce acetoacetate.
dependencies: Ketone release, circulation and brain monocarboxylate transport

title: Metabolic Fuel Switching
mission: Shape smooth transitions between glucose, fat, and ketone fuel pathways as physiological demand shifts.
summary: Enables transition between glucose-derived, fatty-acid-derived, and ketone-derived energy production pathways (metabolic fuel switching, the capacity to shift which substrate mitochondria burn) according to substrate availability and physiological demand. This mechanism represents the integration point across the individual transport and utilisation pathways covered by sibling mechanisms, rather than any single fuel route itself. Metabolic flexibility here — how readily the switch occurs — links directly to glycaemic context and cognitive energy stability across the day.
dose_sensitivity: Daily patterns of fuel exposure, glycaemic context, and sustained lifestyle practice influence switching capacity more than single-meal dosing alone

phenome_relationships.rationale: Narrative synthesis of ADHD mitochondrial biomarker and oxidative-stress literature supports fuel-switching flexibility as a modifiable bioenergetic context when respiration is compromised — direct ADHD fuel-switching outcome trials remain limited.

title: Mitochondrial Biogenesis
mission: Enable formation of new mitochondria so long-term energetic capacity can expand and adapt.
summary: Drives formation of new mitochondria through pathways such as PGC-1α, AMPK, and related transcriptional regulators (the master signalling network that senses energy demand and triggers organelle expansion) in response to repeated exercise and metabolic stimuli. This adaptive expansion increases mitochondrial density over weeks of consistent stimulus rather than through any single acute intervention. Macronutrient and cofactor sufficiency provide permissive substrate support, but the biogenesis signal itself originates primarily from physical activity.
dose_sensitivity: Exercise frequency and repeated signalling exposure are more important than meal-level dose alone

phenome_relationships.rationale: ADHD mitophagy and mitochondrial quality-control reviews link biogenesis/adaptation biology to long-term energetic restoration after repeated metabolic demand — diet and training provide permissive substrate context; direct ADHD biogenesis-outcome trials remain sparse.

title: Gut Barrier / Tight Junction Integrity
mission: Maintain epithelial tight junction integrity and selective permeability at the gut lining.
summary: The gut lining is a selective gate. Tight junctions, the seals between its cells, control which materials pass between them. Maintaining that selectivity helps protect the body while allowing normal exchange. Butyrate, cellular zinc and retinoid signalling affect epithelial functions in experimental models; glutamine has a condition-specific human permeability result. These findings identify different biological routes rather than a universal gut-repair supplement.

scientific_findings_intro: Butyrate and zinc experiments directly interrogate epithelial junction function. Retinoids influence differentiation and permeability, but their direction depends on the model. A selected postinfectious IBS trial found a glutamine response; heterogeneous supplementation evidence does not support a general regimen. Microbiota associations do not establish a barrier-to-cognition effect. [[4]](#pm-ref-4) [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[5]](#pm-ref-5) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) [[6]](#pm-ref-6) Alcohol studies identify a context-specific barrier stressor and recovery relationship; carotenoid absorption supports upstream delivery, and fermented-milk findings remain preparation- and population-specific.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Tight junctions govern selective paracellular permeability
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Intestinal epithelial tight junctions form regulated pore and leak pathways that determine selective paracellular passage.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: This supports the PM boundary around epithelial gate function. Downstream microbial-product containment and systemic inflammation remain outside it.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Intestinal tight-junction structure and regulation determine selective paracellular permeability, while epithelial injury can create a distinct unrestricted permeability pathway.
scientific_findings.synthesis: An authoritative mechanistic review distinguishes tight-junction-dependent pore and leak pathways from unrestricted flux caused by epithelial damage. In a mouse pneumonia model, increased permeability and claudin-2 were attenuated by oral LGG, providing intervention evidence that barrier permeability and junction-associated biology can move together under pathological conditions.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: The review establishes mechanism rather than dietary responsiveness. The LGG experiment was performed in young mice with experimental Pseudomonas pneumonia, not in healthy humans, and does not establish a generic fermented-food effect.

evidence_considered.label: Chanez-Paredes and Turner (2023)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Tight junctions define size- and charge-selective pore and leak pathways; epithelial damage produces a separate unrestricted pathway.

evidence_considered.label: Khailova et al. (2017)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Oral LGG attenuated pneumonia-induced intestinal permeability and claudin-2 elevation and supported mucin expression in mice.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Butyrate can support epithelial tight-junction assembly
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Microbial fermentation products, especially butyrate, can act directly on epithelial barrier biology.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: This supports a Direct butyrate relationship and a Derived fermentable-fibre provision relationship, with microbiota and fibre-specific limitations.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Butyrate can function as an epithelial metabolic substrate and promote intestinal tight-junction assembly, while fermentable dietary fibre lies upstream as microbial substrate provision for short-chain-fatty-acid production.
scientific_findings.synthesis: In Caco-2 monolayers, physiological butyrate increased transepithelial resistance, reduced inulin permeability and accelerated tight-junction assembly alongside AMPK activation. A broader review links microbial fermentation of dietary substrates to short-chain-fatty-acid production and intestinal barrier effects.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: The direct assembly experiment is an immortalised epithelial-cell model. Fibre-to-butyrate conversion varies by fibre structure and microbial ecology, and neither source establishes a universal human intake threshold, a generic effect of all fibre, or oral butyrate as necessary treatment.

evidence_considered.directional_finding: Butyrate increased barrier resistance, reduced inulin permeability and accelerated tight-junction assembly in Caco-2 monolayers.

evidence_considered.directional_finding: The review links microbial fermentation-derived short-chain fatty acids with epithelial barrier and gut-brain communication mechanisms.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Barrier markers and attention-related symptoms are associated, not causal
scientific_findings.finding_summary: One small cross-sectional ADHD study linked serum zonulin with hyperactivity, but it did not establish a causal tight-junction-to-attention pathway.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: The evidence is compatible with the proposed relationship but is too indirect to show that changing PM1 changes attention stability.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Current human evidence provides only indirect observational support for a relationship between intestinal barrier biology and attention-related symptoms.
scientific_findings.synthesis: In children with ADHD, serum zonulin was independently associated with hyperactivity and social-function scores. A separate microbiota study found lower Faecalibacterium abundance associated with parent-rated ADHD symptoms, but it did not measure barrier function. Together these studies support hypothesis generation, not a PM1-specific causal relationship.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Both studies are small and cross-sectional. Serum zonulin is an indirect permeability marker; neither study manipulated or directly quantified tight-junction integrity, and neither demonstrates that PM1 changes attention outcomes.

evidence_considered.directional_finding: Higher serum zonulin was independently associated with greater hyperactivity and social impairment in children with ADHD.

evidence_considered.directional_finding: Lower Faecalibacterium abundance was associated with parent-rated ADHD symptoms, but permeability and tight-junction function were not measured.

evidence_dependency: The two studies address different proxies and cannot be treated as independent replications of a PM1 → attention relationship.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Direct evidence for an Emotional Regulation relationship is absent
scientific_findings.finding_summary: The attached human study does not measure PM1 or emotional regulation.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Emotional Regulation remains a framework-level hypothesis rather than an evidence-established PM1 relationship.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: The bounded evidence assessment does not establish that gut tight-junction integrity modulates Emotional Regulation.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Jiang et al. measured faecal microbiota composition and parent-rated ADHD symptoms. It did not measure intestinal permeability, tight-junction function or emotional-regulation outcomes, so it cannot directly support the current PM1 → Emotional Regulation proposition.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: This is an evidence-gap adjudication, not evidence that no biological relationship exists. Targeted barrier measures and emotional-regulation outcomes would be needed to test the proposition.

scientific_hypotheses.title: Resistant Starch–Derived Butyrate and Tight-Junction Regulation
scientific_hypotheses.proposition: Dietary resistant starch may regulate epithelial paracellular tight-junction function through microbial butyrate production and local exposure.
scientific_hypotheses.rationale: Selected resistant-starch preparations support microbial butyrate production, and direct butyrate exposure can influence epithelial junction assembly. These separate observations motivate testing the joined dietary pathway; they do not establish it. The proposed five-link chain is: (1) dietary resistant-starch substrate reaches a capable microbial community; (2) utilisation and cross-feeding generate a context-dependent butyrate pool; (3) luminal butyrate becomes available to and is taken up by the epithelium; (4) cellular butyrate exposure engages pathways such as AMPK-related tight-junction assembly; (5) local engagement would produce a demonstrable paracellular tight-junction functional effect in the relevant host context. Evidence for separate links does not establish the complete chain. Moreau’s increased uptake followed healing; Peng’s cellular mechanism and the bounded human null/transcellular results must not be joined into an established dietary effect.

contextual.explanation: Supports community- and formulation-dependent upstream fermentation, not a downstream tight-junction mechanism.
Butyrate-exposed epithelial models inform plausibility, not dietary resistant-starch mediation.

evidence_sources.proposition: In RS3-fed colitic rats, increased mucosal butyrate utilisation followed healing.
evidence_sources.limitations: Infused labelled butyrate uptake was not tracing starch carbon. Histological healing and substrate use do not establish paracellular tight-junction mediation.

evidence_sources.label: Acute human colonic biopsy experiment (2020)
evidence_sources.proposition: Acute 5 or 25 mM butyrate pretreatment did not prevent induced hyperpermeability ex vivo.
evidence_sources.limitations: Chemical injury and acute exposure; not a universal refutation of dietary or chronic effects.

evidence_sources.label: Controlled potato/bagel dietary trial (2022)
evidence_sources.proposition: The tested potato diet lowered small-intestinal permeability indices but not the colonic probe; it did not establish butyrate-mediated tight-junction regulation.
evidence_sources.limitations: Metabolic syndrome, short dietary periods and surrogate permeability measures; formulation effects and alternative pathways remain.

evidence_sources.label: Scharf et al. (2025)
evidence_sources.proposition: Direct 100 mmol/L colonic butyrate perfusion for 90 minutes reduced induced transcellular hyperpermeability in IBS biopsies compared with pre-exposure.
evidence_sources.limitations: Transcellular outcome is not demonstrated paracellular tight-junction regulation. Direct perfusion is not dietary delivery and does not establish the resistant-starch pathway.

limitations: No joined dietary resistant-starch → butyrate → paracellular tight-junction mechanism has been established by the evidence reviewed here. This is a bounded assessment, not a claim that no such study exists anywhere.
Starch preparation, microbial degraders/cross-feeding, regional exposure and host state affect the pathway.
Faecal butyrate is not production flux or epithelial exposure; transcripts, electrical resistance, histology and paracellular marker flux are distinct endpoints.
Do not collapse human transcellular protection or small-intestinal permeability improvement into a colonic paracellular tight-junction result.
alternative_explanations: Other fermentation products, microbial shifts, altered bile acids, immune effects or nonfermentation food components may mediate a barrier result.
Mucosal healing may increase butyrate uptake rather than be caused by it.
required_evidence: A defined dietary preparation linked to local butyrate exposure and appropriate paracellular/junction endpoints, with credible causal mediation and microbial/host context addressed.
Starch-carbon tracing is one useful approach, not a mandatory exclusive admission criterion; perturbation, rescue and convergent mediation evidence may also be informative.
Separate paracellular from transcellular effects and measured exposure from inferred metabolite availability.

title: LPS / Endotoxin Containment
mission: Limit host exposure to bacterial endotoxin and related inflammatory microbial products.
summary: LPS transport and persistence depend on more than junction permeability. Lipid-carrier experiments and small human meal trials support exposure-specific changes in endotoxin readouts. Enzyme experiments show that microbial-product inactivation depends on substrate structure. Particular fermentable exposures changed mouse LPS measurements, while human fibre, butyrate and emulsifier findings are mixed. These results support bounded dietary influence, not one universal “detox” pattern or established cognitive benefit.
dose_sensitivity: Exposure-specific research protocols are not recommended intake targets. No routine dose for LPS containment or cognitive benefit is established.

title: Microbial Barrier–Immune Interface Support
mission: Support intestinal mucus maintenance and mucosal immune regulation through defined microbial activities.
summary: Some gut microbes help maintain the mucus layer that separates the intestinal contents from the gut lining, and they influence local immune responses. These functions matter because a protective mucus barrier reduces unwanted microbial contact, while appropriately regulated immunity helps prevent inflammatory injury. This PM concerns those protective microbial activities.
dose_sensitivity: Effects depend on the exact preparation, strain and experimental context; no human dosing or timing target is established.
references: [Jiang et al. (2018) — Gut Microbiota Profiles in Treatment-naïve Children with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#jiang_gut_2018)
[Pärtty et al. (2015) — A Randomized Trial](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#partty_possible_2015)
[Aarts et al. (2017) — Gut Microbiome in ADHD and Its Relation to Neural Reward Anticipation](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#aarts_gut_2017)
[Wang et al. (2022) — Effect of Bifidobacterium bifidum on Clinical Characteristics and Gut Microbiota in ADHD](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#wang_effect_2022)
[Prehn-Kristensen et al. (2018) — Reduced Microbiome Alpha Diversity in Young Patients with ADHD](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#prehn-kristensen_reduced_2018)
[Schroeder et al. (2018) — Bifidobacteria or Fiber Protects against Diet-Induced Microbiota-Mediated Colonic Mucus Deterioration](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#schroeder_bifidobacteria_2018)
[Mazmanian et al. (2008) — A microbial symbiosis factor prevents intestinal inflammatory disease](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#mazmanian_symbiosis_2008)
scientific_findings_intro: A specific strain preserved mucus growth, whereas an inulin preparation preserved mucus penetrability in Western-diet mice. A separate microbial-molecule experiment supports immune regulation. Human taxonomic or symptom studies do not identify the same effector pathways. [[6]](#pm-ref-6) [[7]](#pm-ref-7)

scientific_findings.finding_label: A defined strain and fibre preparation affect distinct mucus properties
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Microbial contributions to mucus function can be tested independently of taxon abundance.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: This is a strain-specific mouse result, not a generic Bifidobacterium effect or a human dietary requirement. The responsible microbial effector was not identified. Mucus growth, penetrability and epithelial tight-junction permeability are different endpoints.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Bifidobacterium longum NCC2705 can prevent impaired colonic mucus growth in a Western-diet mouse model.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Schroeder et al. compared B. longum NCC2705, oligofructose-enriched inulin and their combination. The strain prevented impaired mucus growth; inulin alone prevented increased mucus penetrability. These were distinct responses, and mucus thickness did not change.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: This is a strain-specific mouse result, not a generic Bifidobacterium effect or a human dietary requirement. The responsible microbial effector was not identified. Mucus growth, penetrability and epithelial tight-junction permeability are different endpoints.

evidence_considered.label: Schroeder et al. (2018)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: NCC2705 prevented the mucus growth defect, while inulin separately prevented increased penetrability.

assessment.study: Controlled Western-diet mouse intervention; Results and Figure 6
assessment.population: Mice receiving B. longum NCC2705, 1% oligofructose-enriched inulin, both, or vehicle for four weeks
assessment.result: Strain treatment preserved mucus growth; inulin preserved penetrability; neither changed thickness.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Mucus growth comparison: p=0.006 for strain alone, p=0.005 for the combination; inulin penetrability comparison: p=0.007.
assessment.evidence_summary: Measured host-interface functions distinguish the treatments; microbial abundance alone would not establish these effects.
assessment.limitations: No human effect or generic food claim; component mediation unresolved.

scientific_findings.finding_statement: Bacteroides fragilis polysaccharide A can protect against experimental intestinal inflammation through an IL-10-dependent immune response.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Mazmanian et al. compared PSA-expressing and PSA-deficient B. fragilis and tested purified PSA. Protection against experimental colitis required PSA and IL-10-producing CD4 cells; local pro-inflammatory responses were measured.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Experimental animal and cell evidence does not establish a generic Bacteroides benefit, a dietary admission, or efficacy in humans. The publisher abstract and figure descriptions were inspected; complete subscription results were not available.

title: Microbial Substrate-Processing Selection & Adaptation
mission: Adjust community substrate-processing capacity through resource competition and changes in microbial function.
summary: Gut microbes compete for available carbohydrates and adjust the enzymes used to break them down. This shapes which substrates the community can process and which organisms gain access to the products. Particular glycans and specialist degraders can change measured processing in experiments. Human dietary trials also show changes in processing potential, but more diversity or more turnover is not automatically healthier.
dose_sensitivity: Substrate structure and community composition affect processing; no optimal daily diversity count, timing or dose is established.
references: [Wastyk et al. (2021) — Gut-microbiota-targeted Diets Modulate Human Immune Status](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#wastyk_gut-microbiota-targeted_2021)
[Schleupner and Carmichael (2022) — Closing Research Gaps Through Female Inclusion in Study Design](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#schleupner_attention-deficithyperactivity_2022)
[Prehn-Kristensen et al. (2018) — Reduced Microbiome Alpha Diversity in Young Patients with ADHD](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#prehn-kristensen_reduced_2018)
[Steckler et al. (2024) — Dysbiosis and Decreased Short-chain Fatty Acids](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#steckler_disrupted_2024)
[Patnode et al. (2019) — Interspecies Competition Impacts Targeted Manipulation of Human Gut Bacteria by Fiber-Derived Glycans](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#patnode_interspecies_2019)
[Desai et al. (2016) — A Dietary Fiber-Deprived Gut Microbiota Degrades the Colonic Mucus Barrier and Enhances Pathogen Susceptibility](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#desai_fiber-deprived_2016)
[Ze et al. (2012) — Ruminococcus bromii is a keystone species for the degradation of resistant starch in the human colon](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#ze_resistant_starch_2012)

[Sonnenburg et al. (2010) — Specificity of polysaccharide use in intestinal bacteroides species determines diet-induced microbiota alterations.](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#sonnenburg_fructan_specificity_2010)
[Kiewiet et al. (2021) — Flexibility of Gut Microbiota in Ageing Individuals during Dietary Fiber Long-Chain Inulin Intake.](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#long_chain_inulin_elderly_2020)
scientific_findings_intro: Defined-community experiments connect glycan access, competition and processing machinery. Resistant-starch cultures show specialist-degrader dependence. A human dietary trial changed carbohydrate-processing gene potential; its fermented-food inflammatory findings remain useful but do not establish microbial mediation. [[5]](#pm-ref-5) [[6]](#pm-ref-6) [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[7]](#pm-ref-7)

scientific_findings.finding_label: Community competition changes glycan-processing functions
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Community context changes which microbes can access and process a resource.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Defined mouse communities do not establish a universal human response, benefit from greater diversity or an optimal turnover rate. Substrate use can also accompany adverse host effects. Specific SCFA, polyphenol and precursor conversions belong to PM5, PM6 and PM8.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Competition and functional acclimation can change community glycan processing even when several organisms possess relevant utilisation genes.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Patnode et al. manipulated fibre preparations and membership of defined human-derived bacterial communities in gnotobiotic mice. Utilisation-locus proteomics and genetic fitness screens identified resource-use machinery; glycan-coated beads measured degradation in vivo. Desai et al. separately showed substrate-dependent shifts toward host-mucin use in a defined community, with transcriptional and enzymatic readouts and mucus injury.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Defined mouse communities do not establish a universal human response, benefit from greater diversity or an optimal turnover rate. Substrate use can also accompany adverse host effects. Specific SCFA, polyphenol and precursor conversions belong to PM5, PM6 and PM8.

evidence_considered.label: Patnode et al. (2019)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Competitor manipulation changed resource-use fitness and protein expression; glycan degradation was measured directly.

assessment.study: Defined-community fibre interventions, competitor omission, proteomics, genetic screens and glycan-coated bead assays; Figures 3–5
assessment.population: Gnotobiotic mice colonised with defined human gut bacterial strains
assessment.result: Competition and acclimation altered utilisation machinery; bead assays resolved substrate-processing capacity.
assessment.effect_magnitude: GC–MS quantified glycan depletion from recovered beads; no generalised pooled effect size used.
assessment.evidence_summary: Distinguishes functional expression and measured degradation from gene potential and taxonomic composition.
assessment.limitations: Defined-community and artificial substrate assays; no demonstrated cognition or universal human benefit.

evidence_considered.label: Desai et al. (2016)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Fibre deprivation shifted community glycan-use readouts toward mucus substrates, with barrier erosion and increased pathogen susceptibility.

assessment.study: Defined-community dietary fibre deprivation; community transcriptional/enzymatic readouts and barrier outcomes
assessment.population: Gnotobiotic mice carrying a 14-species human-derived community
assessment.result: Host-glycan use increased under the studied deprivation conditions and was accompanied by mucus erosion.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No pooled quantitative magnitude extracted; directional experimental findings retained.
assessment.evidence_summary: Resource selection can have adverse as well as favourable host consequences.
assessment.limitations: Results passages retrieved; complete PDF opening timed out. Model-specific findings do not show all fibre deprivation acts through one route.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Dietary responses separate processing potential from immune outcomes
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Human dietary intervention can change processing potential without increased diversity; immune responses require separate interpretation.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: The prespecified cytokine-response score did not change. Gene abundance is functional potential, not enzyme flux; stool metabolite concentration is not production rate. Diversity and immune changes were accompanying results, not demonstrated causal mediation. No improvement in cognition surveys, glucose, lipids or blood pressure was established.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: High-fibre intake can increase metagenomic glycan-processing potential without increased diversity, while fermented-food-associated immune changes do not establish diversity-mediated benefit.
scientific_findings.synthesis: In Wastyk et al., 18 healthy adults were analysed in each free-living dietary arm after a four-week ramp and six-week maintenance. Fibre increased from 21.5 to 45.1 g/day; glycan-degrading CAZyme gene abundance increased with stable diversity. Residual stool carbohydrate increased with fibre intake, leaving processing sufficiency unresolved. Fermented foods increased from 0.4 to 6.3 servings/day; diversity increased and 19 of 93 circulating inflammatory proteins decreased, including IL-6, IL-10 and IL-12b.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: The prespecified cytokine-response score did not change. Gene abundance is functional potential, not enzyme flux; stool metabolite concentration is not production rate. Diversity and immune changes were accompanying results, not demonstrated causal mediation. No improvement in cognition surveys, glucose, lipids or blood pressure was established.

evidence_considered.label: Wastyk et al. (2021)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Fibre changed CAZyme potential without increased diversity; fermented foods changed diversity and inflammatory proteins without establishing mediation.

assessment.study: Free-living dietary trial; Figure 3C–E, Figures 5–6 and primary-outcome methods/Table S4
assessment.population: 18 healthy adults analysed per arm; high-fibre versus high-fermented-food dietary exposure
assessment.result: Distinct community-capacity and immune responses occurred across the two arms.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Fibre 21.5→45.1 g/day; fermented foods 0.4→6.3 servings/day; 19/93 inflammatory proteins decreased in that arm.
assessment.evidence_summary: Preserves the measured inflammatory response without attributing it to diversity or a defined taxon.
assessment.limitations: No untreated control arm or diversity-mediation test; primary cytokine-response score unchanged; potential, activity and host outcomes remain distinct.

evidence_considered.label: McDonald et al. (2018) — plant-variety gap context
evidence_considered.directional_finding: American Gut observational citizen-science cohort; Timothy Spector is a co-author. Self-reported plant variety associated with microbial diversity and selected taxa/metabolites.

assessment.study: Observational citizen-science cohort; dietary plant diversity analyses
assessment.population: Self-selected American Gut participants; analysis-specific subsets
assessment.result: Plant variety associated with diversity, selected taxa and stool metabolites.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No intervention effect or threshold estimated.
assessment.evidence_summary: Context for PM4-EG-PLANT-VARIETY-1 only; existing Finding proposition and SEC assessment unchanged.
assessment.limitations: Full-text dietary plant diversity section and methods inspected. No randomised plant-count intervention or threshold test; contextual evidence for the separate plant-variety gap, not replication of the Wastyk intervention.

evidence_considered.label: Stanford et al. (2025) — plant-variety gap context
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Randomised crossover in 25 adults with stage 3–4 CKD: at least 30 versus at most 15 plant foods weekly, six weeks per diet. Microbiome/metabolome and symptoms changed; uremic toxins did not consistently decrease across the cohort.

assessment.study: Randomised crossover; six weeks per diet and at least four-week washout
assessment.population: 25 Australian adults with stage 3–4 chronic kidney disease
assessment.result: Microbiome/metabolome and symptom changes; inconsistent cohort-wide uremic toxin reduction.
assessment.effect_magnitude: At least 30 versus at most 15 plant foods weekly; no threshold effect estimated.
assessment.evidence_summary: Context for PM4-EG-PLANT-VARIETY-1 only; existing Finding proposition and SEC assessment unchanged.
assessment.limitations: PubMed abstract and figure descriptions inspected; full-text retrieval unavailable. Population-specific dietary package; does not isolate a threshold at 30 or establish general-population substrate-processing flux. Requires full appraisal before any SOP admission.

evidence_considered.label: Creedon et al. (2026) — plant-variety gap context
evidence_considered.directional_finding: BIOME randomised 399 adults with low fibre intake; 349 analysed. A 30 g/day plant blend over six weeks changed microbial composition; richness decreased and between-group microbiome health-rank differences were not significant.

assessment.study: Six-week parallel randomised trial; plant blend versus croutons or probiotic
assessment.population: 399 randomised, 349 analysed; adults aged 35–65 with fibre intake below 20 g/day
assessment.result: Composition changed; richness decreased; no significant between-group microbiome health-rank difference.
assessment.effect_magnitude: 30 g/day blend versus 28 g/day croutons; 57 versus 14 changing species-level genome bins.
assessment.evidence_summary: Context for PM4-EG-PLANT-VARIETY-1 only; existing Finding proposition and SEC assessment unchanged.
assessment.limitations: Publisher full text inspected. Specific blend versus croutons/probiotic, not a plant-count dose-response test. Health ranks are association-derived, not direct metabolic pathway measurements. Commercial ZOE involvement; no admission or SEC reassessment in this gap review.

evidence_gaps.establishes: Defined glycan substrates and community composition influence processing. Wastyk's fibre and fermented-food interventions separate functional potential, diversity and immune outcomes.

evidence_gaps.title: 30 plants per week — a useful dietary target or a biological threshold?
evidence_gaps.establishes: McDonald et al. (2018), with Timothy Spector, reported observational associations between self-reported plant variety and microbial diversity, selected taxa and stool metabolites. The American Gut analyses compared extreme intake categories (more than 30 versus low variety), not an experimentally determined optimum. Stanford et al. (2025) subsequently tested at least 30 versus at most 15 plant foods weekly in 25 adults with stage 3–4 CKD, with microbiome/metabolome and symptom changes but no consistent cohort-wide reduction in uremic toxins. Creedon et al. (2026) tested a specific 30 g/day plant blend for six weeks: composition changed, richness decreased, and between-group microbiome health-rank differences were not significant.
evidence_gaps.cannot_establish: That 30 plants is a necessary, sufficient or optimal weekly threshold for PM4 substrate-processing capacity, or that any 30-plant pattern reproduces the effects of these tested interventions.
evidence_gaps.missing_link: The original cohort was self-selected and observational. Its analyses used more than 30 versus 10 or fewer plants (the metabolomics subset is described as fewer than 10); these are comparison categories, not a dose-response threshold. Later trials test a population-specific diet or a particular blend, not plant count independently of substrate amount, identity and preparation. Composition, gene potential and metabolite concentrations must not be equated with processing flux. The CKD paper's abstract and figures were inspected; full-text and supplementary appraisal remains necessary before intervention adjudication. No SOP is admitted by this record.
evidence_gaps.required_evidence: Controlled plant-variety comparisons across several intake levels, including around 30, with substrate quantity, composition and preparation addressed and PM-specific processing endpoints. Independently appraise the CKD and BIOME interventions for their exact populations and mechanisms; a useful tested practice need not establish a universal numerical threshold.
evidence_gaps.affected_relationship: Weekly plant-variety target → PM4 substrate-processing function

title: SCFA Production & Signalling
mission: Maintain short-chain fatty acid production and signalling that supports gut barrier and brain communication.
summary: Gut microbes ferment carbohydrates into short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), including acetate, propionate and butyrate. These products supply local cells and activate signalling pathways. The amount and mixture produced depend on the substrate and the microbial community. Human fermentation studies support particular inputs; cell experiments explain possible downstream actions without establishing cognitive benefit.

title: Polyphenol Biotransformation & Mitochondrial-Relevant Metabolite Generation
mission: Enable microbial activation of dietary polyphenols into bioactive metabolites.
summary: Gut microbes can convert some dietary polyphenols into different metabolites. Ellagitannins release ellagic acid, from which cooperating microbes can form urolithins. Not everyone completes this conversion to urolithin A. Understanding that variability separates microbial processing from taking the finished metabolite as a supplement.
dose_sensitivity: Repeated polyphenol exposure; responder variability expected

title: Vagal / ENS Signalling Modulation
mission: Maintain gut-to-brain nerve signalling through the vagus nerve and enteric nervous system.
summary: Specialised gut cells and nerves relay information from the intestinal contents to the brain. Experimental work identifies a fast glutamate-mediated connection to the vagus nerve. These are different routes and different endpoints.

title: Neurotransmitter Precursor Biotransformation & Availability
mission: Maintain gut-side processing that shapes neurotransmitter precursor availability.
summary: Gut microbes share substrates and compete for amino acids. Their processing can divert tryptophan into different metabolites before the host uses it. A tested pectin exposure redirected that processing in microbial communities and mice. These results explain gut-side precursor handling; they do not establish more brain serotonin, dopamine or better cognition.
dose_sensitivity: Requires repeated dietary pattern support; not a single-food effect

title: Glucose Appearance Kinetics
mission: Shape the rate of post-meal glucose appearance so metabolic and neuroendocrine systems face manageable, predictable load.
summary: Glucose entry begins with how food releases carbohydrate and how quickly the stomach delivers it to the intestine. Food structure, starch processing, defined fibre preparations and meal sequence can change this profile. This affects the immediate demand for insulin and helps explain different responses to similar carbohydrate loads. The practical routes are specific substitutions and preparation or sequencing protocols; choosing a fibre-rich food alone does not guarantee slower entry.
dose_sensitivity: Effects depend on the tested exposure, preparation and study population; no universal dose is established.
